(p-182) Surah Hud is Meccan, and it has one hundred and twenty-three verses.

﴿Alif-Lam-Ra﴾. Its place in the i'rab (grammatical analysis) is in the nominative, as the khabar (predicate) of an omitted mubtada' (subject). It is also said to be the mubtada', but the first view is the more evident, as was indicated in Surah Yunus. It may be in the accusative by supposing a verb suited to the context, such as "Recall" (udhkur) or "Recite" (iqra'), on the assumption that it is the name of the surah, which is the view on which most scholars agree. Or it has no place in i'rab, being recited in the manner of enumeration, as was explained concerning its counterparts.

The words of the Most High, ﴿a Book﴾, are the khabar of it on the second view, and the khabar of an omitted mubtada' on the remaining views.

﴿Its verses have been made firm﴾: they were arranged in a perfectly sound composition, not admitting any defect in any respect. Or they were made wise, because they contain the sublime and subtle wisdoms. Or they were protected from naskh (abrogation), understood in the general sense of change. Or they were supported by decisive proofs indicating that they are from God, Mighty and Majestic, or indicating the establishment of what they signify, in which case "verses" refers to all of them. Or it refers to the truth of the legal rulings they contain, in which case "verses" refers to the part of them that contains those rulings. This is so if "making firm" is explained as protection from naskh in the sense of replacing a legal ruling specifically. As for explaining it as protection from corruption, taking it from the expression "I made the mount firm" (ahkamtu al-dabbah) when one places a hakamah (bridle) on it to prevent it from bolting, this implies something that hardly befits the dignity of the noble verses, namely a tendency toward corruption were it not for the preventer. Moreover, attributing the making firm, in the aforementioned senses, to the verses of the Book rather than to the Book itself, especially in the senses that encompass each and every verse of it, indicates in a manner that is not hidden the excellent placement and the implication that it is at the utmost peak.

﴿Then they were detailed﴾: that is, they were made into divisions of rulings, proofs, admonitions and narratives. Or the great affairs of the servants concerning this life and the Hereafter were detailed in them, by way of metaphorical attribution. Explaining it as making them into verse after verse does not suit the context, because that is among the primary attributes, so it does not fit to join it to their being made firm with the particle indicating a delay (thumma). As for the first two meanings, although they coincide in time with making firm, since the verses have always been firm and detailed, and it is not that they were made firm or detailed after not being so, for the two actions are of the kind of the saying: "Glory be to Him who made the gnat small and the elephant large", nevertheless, since they are attributes of the verses in terms of the relation of some of them to others in a way that entails specific rulings and considerable effects, and with regard to the interests of the servants, it was appropriate to indicate that their rank is posterior to the rank of making firm. And if making them verse after verse is understood as separating some of them from others, it falls under this kind, but it is not on the same footing in entailing what it entails of rulings and effects. Or they were divided in the revelation into portions according to the interests. If the intended meaning is their revelation in portions in fact, then the delay is temporal. If the intended meaning is that they were in themselves such that their revelation is in portions as wisdom and interest require, then the delay is one of rank, because that is an inseparable attribute of them, deserving to be ordered upon the attribute of their being made firm. It is also read ("I made its verses firm, then I detailed them") in the first person singular form. And it is reported from Ikrimah and al-Dahhak: ﴿then they were detailed﴾, meaning they distinguished between truth and falsehood.

﴿From One who is Wise and Aware﴾: an adjective of the Book. It is described by this after having been described by the making firm of its verses and their detailing, which indicate the loftiness of its rank in essence, to make manifest the majesty of its status in terms of its attribution. Or it is a khabar after a khabar for the mentioned or omitted mubtada'. Or it is a relative clause (silah) of the two verbs. In the building of the two verbs in the passive voice, then the bringing of the agent under the title of the consummate wisdom and comprehensive knowledge of its sublime and subtle matters, indefinite with the indefiniteness of exaltation, and the linking of the two to it, not in the customary manner of attributing the actions to their doers, while observing the excellence of the correspondence, with eloquence and an indication of the grandeur of the two and their being in the most perfect state, is of a kind whose reality cannot be comprehended.

﴿Ala ta'budu illa Allah﴾ ("that you worship none but God") is a *maf'ul lahu* (object of purpose, an accusative noun stating the reason for an action). The *lam* (the particle "for") has been dropped from it, even though the usual condition for dropping it is absent. That condition is that the agent of the purpose clause must be the same as the agent of the main verb. The omission follows the regular rule for dropping the preposition before *an* (the verbal particle "that", *anna* type *masdariyya*, which turns the following clause into a verbal noun). It is as if it were said: "A Book whose verses were made firm and then detailed, so that you do not worship except God," that is, so that you abandon the worship of other than God, Mighty and Majestic, and devote yourselves purely to worshipping Him. Making the verses firm and detailing their meanings, as they have been detailed, calls people to faith and monotheism and to all the acts of obedience that follow from them.

It has also been said that *an* (*"that"*) is an explanatory particle (*mufassira*) for the sense of speech implicit in the word "detailed" (*tafsil*). That is, it means: "It was said: Do not worship except God."

﴿Inni lakum minhu﴾ ("Indeed I am to you, from Him," that is, on behalf of God, Exalted) *nadhir* ("a warner"), who warns you of His punishment if you do not abandon your disbelief and the worship of other than God, Exalted, ﴿wa-bashir﴾ ("and a bringer of good news"), who gives you the good news of His reward if you believe in Him and devote yourselves purely to His worship.

When the matters of the Book were mentioned, namely the firmness of its verses and their detailing, and the fact that this came from God, Exalted, and most of what was arranged in the course of this purpose was presented, namely the command to monotheism and the abandonment of associating partners with God, the statement that the one to whom this Book was revealed is a messenger sent from God, Exalted, was placed between this command and its two companions, namely seeking forgiveness (*istighfar*) and repentance (*tawba*). This was to convey his mission of delivering its rulings and to reinforce them with the supporting evidence of promise and threat. This indicates that monotheism holds the highest rank of importance, so much so that it was singled out for mention, and its obligation was emphasized through direct address after the Book. It also hints that just as monotheism is not realized in itself except together with the rule of prophethood, and the Messenger ﷺ, so likewise in mention neither of the two is separated from the other.

In the way the address was delivered, placing the warning before the good news corresponds to what was observed in the Book in placing negation before affirmation and clearing away before adorning, so that the parts of the speech respond to one another. It is also possible that God's words ﴿Ala ta'budu illa Allah﴾ are a separate statement, unconnected to what precedes it, delivered on the tongue of the Prophet ﷺ as an exhortation to them to hold to God's exclusive right to worship. It is as if the Prophet ﷺ said: "Abandon the worship of other than God," meaning: hold to it. The sense is: abandon the worship of other than God in a continuous manner. "Indeed I am to you" from God, Exalted, "a warner and a bringer of good news." That is, a warner who warns you of His punishment on the supposition that you continue in disbelief, and a bringer of good news who gives you the good news of His reward on the supposition that you abandon it and affirm His oneness.

Since the discussion of monotheism had preceded them, and this was emphasized by the address of the Messenger ﷺ in the manner of warning and good news, he began to mention what is part of its completion, in a way that includes a detailed explanation of what had been stated in summary in the description of the bringer of good news and the warner. Thus it was said:

﴿وَأنِ اسْتَغْفِرُوا رَبَّكُمْ﴾ This is conjoined (ma'tuf) to ﴿أنْ لا تَعْبُدُوا﴾ ("an la ta'budu," "that you not worship"), according to the two views mentioned. On the first view, *an* is a *masdariyya* particle (the "an" that turns the following clause into a verbal noun, the relative clause being its *silla*) because its *silla* may be an imperative or a prohibition, as in His saying ﴿وَأنْ أقِمْ وجْهَكَ لِلدِّينِ حَنِيفًا﴾ ("and that you set your face toward the religion, upright"). The reason is that what permits its *silla* to be a verb is only that it signifies the verbal noun, and this is present in both. The requirement that the *silla* of an ism relative pronoun be declarative (khabariyya) is only so that the relative clause can describe definites with sentences, and such sentences can describe definites only when they are declarative. The literal relative particle is not like this. Since declarative and imperative are equal in signifying the verbal noun, it is permissible for imperatives and prohibitions to be the *silla*, just as a verb may be. Thereby the *silla* is stripped of the meaning of command and prohibition, in the way that the verbal *silla* is stripped of the meaning of past and future.

﴿ثُمَّ تُوبُوا إلَيْهِ﴾ is conjoined to ﴿اسْتَغْفِرُوا﴾, and what is said about it is said about that. The meaning: what has been done of decisive ordering and detailed explanation was done so that you would single out God Most High for worship, and seek from Him the covering of the shirk that has come from you, then return to Him in obedience; or continue in what you are upon of monotheism and seeking forgiveness; or seek forgiveness from shirk and repent from sins.

On the second view, *an* is *mufassira* (explanatory), meaning: it was said in the course of the detailed explanation of the verses, "Do not worship except God, and seek His forgiveness, then repent to Him." The mention of the attribute of lordship (rububiyya) is an admonition to the addressees and a guidance to them toward the way of earnest supplication in asking, and a preparation for what follows it of enjoyment and bestowal of grace in His saying ﴿يُمَتِّعْكم مَتاعًا حَسَنًا﴾ ("He will let you enjoy a good enjoyment"). *Mata'an* (enjoyment) is in the accusative either as a verbal noun from which the extra letters are dropped, as in His saying ﴿أنْبَتَكم مِنَ الأرْضِ نَباتًا﴾ ("made you grow from the earth, a growth"), or as an object (maf'ul bihi), and it is a name for what is enjoyed of the benefits of this world, of wealth, children and other things. The meaning: He will let you live a pleasing life, in which nothing you desire is lost to you, and nothing of the troubles of life spoils it.

﴿إلى أجَلٍ مُسَمًّى﴾ ("until a specified term") means a term decreed with God, Mighty and Majestic, and it is the end of your lifespans. Since that is a limit beyond which no aspirant aspires, enjoyment running up to it takes, by custom, the place of permanence; or it means He will not destroy you with a punishment of total annihilation. ﴿وَيُؤْتِ كُلَّ ذِي فَضْلٍ﴾ ("and He will give every possessor of merit") in obedience and deed ﴿فَضْلَهُ﴾ ("his merit"), that is, a reward for his merit, either in this world or in the Hereafter. This is a completion of what was stated in summary about enjoyment until a specified term, and a clarification of what might make difficult the understanding of its wisdom from some things that happen in this world, namely the difference in condition between the two doers. For a person may have merit, in obedience and deed, yet is not given more enjoyment in this world than another who is lesser in merit; and sometimes the lesser one has more enjoyment. So it was said: "and He will give every person of merit the reward of his merit," either in this world, as happens in some cases, or in the Hereafter, and that is something that cannot be averted. This is a form of detailed explanation of what was summarized earlier in the good tidings. Then it turns to warning, and it was said: ﴿وَإنْ تَوَلَّوْا﴾ ("but if you turn away"), that is, if you turn away from what has been set before you of monotheism, seeking forgiveness, and repentance. It was placed after the good tidings in keeping with the pattern of mercy preceding wrath; or because punishment was attached to turning away from what was mentioned of monotheism, seeking forgiveness, and repentance, and that requires its prior mention. It is also read *tuwallu* (from *wallā*). ﴿فَإنِّي أخافُ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ ("then indeed I fear for you"), by the demand of compassion and tenderness, or I anticipate ﴿عَذابَ يَوْمٍ كَبِيرٍ﴾ ("the punishment of a great day"), which is the Day of Resurrection, described as great, just as it is described as mighty in His saying ﴿ألا يَظُنُّ أُولَئِكَ أنَّهم مَبْعُوثُونَ﴾ ﴿لِيَوْمٍ عَظِيمٍ﴾ ("Do those not imagine that they will be resurrected for a mighty day?"). It is great either because it is so in itself, or it is described with the attribute of what occurs in it, as it is described with heaviness in His saying ﴿ثَقُلَتْ في السَّماواتِ والأرْضِ﴾ ("heavy in the heavens and the earth"). It was also said: it is the day of hardships, and they were afflicted with a famine in which they ate carrion. Whichever it is, attributing the punishment to it conveys its terror and horror.

﴿To Allah is your return﴾: your return by death, then resurrection for recompense on a day like that day, not to any other. ﴿And He is Able over all things﴾: so within that generality falls His power to cause you to die, then to resurrect you and recompense you, and so He will punish you with its various kinds of punishment. This is an affirmation of what preceded regarding the greatness of the Day and a rationale for fear. When the content of the Book was conveyed to them through the tongue of the Prophet (ﷺ), and what should be conveyed of encouragement and warning was delivered to them, there arose in the mind of the listener the question: after they had heard such a speech, before which the solid mountains crumble, did they respond to it with acceptance, or did they persist in their turning away and their misguidance? So it was said, prefaced with the word of alerting, to indicate that what follows it of their shortcomings is a matter that must be understood and marvelled at:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 5:

﴿Surely they fold their breasts﴾ they turn away from the truth and deviate from it, meaning: they persist in what they were upon of turning away and aversion, for whoever turns away from something folds his breast away from it and draws in his side from it. This is a weighty meaning that suits what preceded it, and the allamah al-Zamakhshari (al-'Allama al-Zamakhshari) followed this path. But since turning away is not suitable as a cause for concealment in His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿that they may hide from Him﴾, he resorted to supposing an implied will, saying: "And they wish to hide from Allah, the Exalted, so that He does not inform His Messenger and the believers of their aversion." Making it, in directing the meaning toward it, a case of implication in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Strike the sea with your staff, and it parted﴾, meaning: he struck, and it parted. It is not hidden that the mind's inclination to insert the will between folding the breasts and concealment is not like its inclination to insert the striking between the command to it and the parting. Perhaps the more evident meaning is: they bend their breasts over what is in them of disbelief, aversion from the truth, and enmity toward the Prophet (ﷺ), in such a way that this is hidden and concealed within them, just as garments are folded over what is in them of concealed things. That this was not mentioned is either out of distaste for mentioning it, or as an indication that its manifestation makes its mention unnecessary, or so that the hearer's mind goes to everything in which there is no good among the matters mentioned, so that what is mentioned of their turning away from the truth that was presented to them enters it in the first instance; then the reason why that is a cause of concealment becomes evident.

And this is supported by what is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that it was revealed concerning al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, who was a man sweet of speech and good at conversing, who showed love to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while concealing in his heart what opposed it.

Ibn Shaddad said: it was revealed concerning some of the hypocrites, who, when he passed by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), would fold his chest and back, bow his head, and cover his face so that the Prophet (ﷺ) would not see him, as though he was only doing what he did because if the Prophet (ﷺ) saw him, he would not be able to stay away from attending his gathering and accompanying him, and perhaps that would lead to the manifestation of the disbelief and hypocrisy in his heart. It was also read (يَثْنَوْنِي صُدُورُهُمْ) with the ya' and the ta', from ithnawnā, on the pattern of if'awʿala from al-thany (folding), like ihlawlā from al-halāwa (sweetness), and it is a pattern of intensification. And from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: (لِتَثْنُونِي). It was also read (تَثْنُونَ), and its origin is tathnuwnan, from tafa'wa'ala from al-thunn, which is what is withered of the herbage and has become weak, meaning the yielding of their breasts to folding, as the withered plant is folded; or he meant the weakness of their faith and the softness of their hearts. It was also read (تَثْنُنَّ) from ithna'anna, if'alla from it, then it was hamzated, as it is said: ابْيَأضَّتْ and ادْهَأمَّتْ. It was also read (تَثْنَوِي) on the pattern of ترعوي.

﴿Surely when they cover themselves with their garments﴾ meaning: they wrap themselves in them for concealment, according to what is related from Ibn Shaddad; or when they retire to their beds and wrap themselves in their garments, for what occurs then is ordinarily the discourse of the soul. It was also said: a man of the disbelievers would enter his house, let down his curtain, bend his back, and wrap himself in his garment, and say: "Does Allah know what is in my heart?"

﴿He knows what they keep secret﴾ meaning: what they conceal in their hearts, ﴿and what they proclaim﴾, meaning: with respect to His all-encompassing knowledge, their secret and their open are equal, so how could what they might display be hidden from Him? The secret was placed before the open only to rebuke them from the outset for what they did, and as a notice of their exposure and the occurrence of what they fear, and to realize the equality between the two knowledges in the most eloquent manner, as if His knowledge of what they keep secret is older than His knowledge of what they proclaim. Its parallel is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: whether you conceal what is in your breasts or reveal it, Allah knows it﴾, where concealment is placed before revelation, contrary to what occurs in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whether you reveal what is in your selves or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it﴾, since in the latter the indication that accountability for what they conceal is more fitting than for what they reveal is not a purpose; rather the matter is the reverse. But here, the indication that the connection of His knowledge to what they keep secret is more fitting than to what they proclaim is an important purpose, along with both being on equal footing. How not, since His knowledge of His objects is not by way of the acquisition of an image, but rather the existence of each thing in itself is knowledge in relation to Him, mighty and majestic; and in this sense the situation does not differ between the manifest things and the hidden ones.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And I know what you reveal and what you were concealing﴾, since it was addressed to the angels, peace be upon them, whose station is too exalted for the requirement of emphasis and exaggeration in reporting the encompassment of Allah's knowledge of the outward and the inward, that method was not followed in it, though sufficiency was reached regarding it by what precedes it, His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿Indeed I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾. It may be that this is by way of consideration that the rank of the secret precedes the rank of the open, for nothing is made open except that it, or its beginnings, was previously concealed in the heart, so the connection of His knowledge, glory be to Him, to its first state precedes its connection to its second state.

﴿Indeed He is Knower of what is within the breasts﴾ is a reason for what preceded and a confirmation of it, standing in the place of the major premise of a syllogism. In the form of the intensive adjective (fa'il), and in the adorning of "the breasts" with the definite article of comprehensiveness, and in the expression of the inner thoughts by the title of their owners, there is an eloquence that no describer can describe, as if it were said: He is exceedingly comprehensive of the hidden thoughts of all people and their secrets concealed in their breasts, in such a way that they never depart from them at all; so how could what they keep secret and what they proclaim be hidden from Him? It is also possible that by "what is within the breasts" is meant the hearts, from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But it is the hearts within the breasts that become blind﴾, and the meaning is that He is Knower of the hearts and their states, so no secret of their secrets is hidden from Him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 6:

﴿And there is no creature on the earth but that its provision is upon Allah﴾. Its food, suitable for it in terms of its creation and in terms of its being brought to it by a natural way or a volitional one, since He has undertaken it out of bounty and mercy. It was stated in the form of an obligation (wujub) in consideration of the prior promise and to affirm that it will certainly reach it, and to induce the responsible (mukallafin) to place their trust in Him, Exalted is He, and to refrain from exhausting the soul in seeking it. ﴿And He knows its place of settlement﴾: the place of its lodging in the loins (aslab), ﴿and its place of storage﴾: its location in the wombs (arham) and what runs in their course of eggs and the like.

Each of the two names (al-ismayn) was specified with what was specified to it of the two places, because the drop of semen (nutfah), in relation to the loins, is in its natural receptacle and its innate origin; but in relation to the wombs and what runs in their course, it is deposited in them until a specified time. Or, its "settlement" (maskan) is from the earth when it came into being actually, and its "storage" (mawda') is from the materials and resting places when it was still potentially. Perhaps the mention of its place first (taqdim mahallaha) was in consideration of its final state, for the sake of harmony between it and the designation of its being a creature (dabbah) on the earth. The meaning: there is no creature on the earth but that Allah, Exalted is He, provides for it wherever it is, driving sustenance to it; and He knows its diverse materials, which are included in the ranks of the varying and developing predispositions (isti'dadat) in the differing stages, and its various resting places; and He bestows upon it, at every rank, what is suitable for it of the principles of its existence and its perfections that branch from that. The "storage" has been explained as its places in death, but this does not suit the context of undertaking its provision.

﴿All﴾ of the creatures, their provision, their settlement and their storage ﴿are in a Clear Book﴾, i.e., recorded in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), clear to whoever looks into it among the angels, peace be upon them, or manifesting what is recorded in it to the beholders. And since the matter has reached the point that He, Exalted is He, encompasses all the conditions of what is on the earth of creatures that are almost beyond counting, from the beginning of their origination to their end, the context required addressing the beginning of the creation of the heavens and the earth and the wisdom prompting that, so it was said:

The Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 11, Verse 7:

﴿He it is Who created the heavens and the earth in six days.﴾ The heavens in two days, the earth in two days, and what is upon it of kinds of animals, plants and other things in two days, as has been explained in the Surah (Ha Mim) al-Sajda. The creation of what is in the earth was not mentioned because it is among the completions of its creation. This is the secret of making the time of His creating it (the heavens) a completion of the time of the creation of the earth in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿in four days﴾, in completion of four days. By "days" is meant periods of time, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever turns his back to them on that day﴾, meaning in six periods of time, or in the measure of six days. For "day" in common usage is the time during which the sun is above the earth, and this cannot be conceived when there is no earth and no heaven. In creating them gradually, despite having full power to create them at once, there is evidence that He is capable and acts by choice, and an exhortation to deliberateness in affairs. As for specifying that number, it is a matter whose wisdom is known only to the All-Knowing of the unseen, may His wisdom be exalted. The use of the plural form for the heavens corresponds to the well-known indication that they are bodies differing in natures and varying in effects and rulings. ﴿And His Throne was﴾ before creating them ﴿upon the water﴾, with nothing beneath it except it, whether there was a gap between them and it was placed upon its back, as is reported in the narration. There is therefore no indication in this of the possibility of a void, for how could it be, since if it indicated anything it would indicate its existence, not merely its possibility. Nor does it indicate that water was the first thing that came into existence in the world after the Throne. It only indicates that their creation (the Throne and the water) preceded the creation of the heavens and the earth, without addressing the relation between them.

﴿That He may test you﴾ is connected to (khalaqa, "created"), meaning: He created the heavens and the earth and what is in them of created things, of which you are among the parts. He arranged in them everything you need for the beginnings of your existence and the means of your livelihood, and deposited within them, among their folds, wondrous crafts and lessons by which you may derive evidence for your religious aims, so that He may deal with you as one who tests you: ﴿which of you is best in deed﴾, so that He may then reward you with reward and punishment after the good are distinguished from the evil. The ranks of individuals of each of the two groups are distinguished according to the distinction of the levels of their knowledge and beliefs, which follow from their reflection upon the proofs, evidences and signs established in the heavens and the earth, and the levels of their deeds, which branch from that. For deed is not restricted to the knowledge of the limbs. This is why the Prophet (ﷺ) explained it by his saying: "Which of you is best in intellect, most scrupulous regarding the prohibitions of Allah, and quickest in obedience to Allah." For each of the heart and the body has a deed specific to it. Just as the first (the heart) is nobler than the second (the body), so too is the state of its deed. How could it not be so, when there is no deed without knowledge of Allah, may He be exalted, which is obligatory upon the servants, the most influential of all influences? Its path is theoretical: reflection upon the wonders of the works of the Sovereign, the Creator, and contemplation of His clear signs set up in the souls and the horizons. And there is no obedience without understanding what lies within the folds of the Wise Book of commands and prohibitions, and other matters that have a place in this domain.

It has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Do not prefer me over Yunus ibn Matta, for there was raised for him every day the like of the deeds of the people of the earth." They said: That was only the reflection on the matter of Allah, may He be exalted, which is the deed of the heart; for no one can, in a day, with his limbs, perform the like of the deeds of the people of the earth.

The construction of the verb of testing (ibtila', "to test") here, meaning its being followed by the interrogative particle (harf al-istifham), is not the well-known "suspension" (ta'liq) which requires that the object not be mentioned at all, and which is specific to verbs of the heart. Rather, it carries the sense of knowledge in view of its outcome, like "seeing" (al-nazar) and its like. For this reason it is treated as such by way of figurative representation (tamthil), or by way of contextual metaphor (isti'ara tab'iyya). The use of the comparative form (ahsan, "best") — although testing encompasses both groups with respect to their deeds, which are divided into good and bad, not merely into good and better — serves to indicate that what is intended in essence and as the principal aim of what has been mentioned, namely the bringing into being of those marvels in that wondrous pattern, is only the manifestation of the perfection of the goodness of the good-doers. And that this, being in the most complete of the fitting modes and the most excellent of graceful methods, necessitates acting upon its requirement, such that no one deviates from its clear ways. Rather, every individual is guided to what it directs him to of mere faith and obedience. Differences among them lie only in the degrees of these according to strength and weakness, abundance and scarcity. As for turning away from that and falling into the abysses of error, it is far from being included under "falling," let alone being regarded as the final cause of that wondrous creation. It is only a deed that proceeds from its doer through his evil choice, without any justification for it or any closeness to it. And there is no concealing what this contains of encouragement to ascend to the heights of knowledge and the stages of acts of obedience, and of warning against engaging in their opposites. And Allah, may He be exalted, knows best.

﴿And if you say: Indeed you will be resurrected after death﴾, in accordance with what the requirement of the testing entails, so that reward may follow, which branches from the manifestation of the levels of deeds: ﴿those who disbelieve will surely say﴾. If the address in His saying, may He be exalted, "Indeed you" is directed to all the responsible, then the relative pronoun with its clause is for specification, meaning: the disbelievers among them will say. If it is directed to the disbelievers among them, then it comes in the manner of censure: ﴿This is nothing but clear magic﴾, meaning: it is like it in deception or falsehood. "This" refers to the aforementioned statement or to the Qur'an. For the report about their being resurrected, although it is not necessarily a recited revelation (wahy matluww), nonetheless when they hear it they resort to the Qur'an, since it reports it in every place, and since it is a sign among them concerning this. So they deliberately deny it and call it magic, out of persistence in obstinacy and evasion of the paths of right guidance. It has been said: it refers to the resurrection itself, and the naming of it as magic is not suitable, for magic is only applied to something that exists apparently but has no real basis, whereas the resurrection itself, in their view, is pure non-existence.

The connection of this noble verse to what precedes it is either because the resurrection, as has been indicated, is among the completions of the aforementioned testing; so it is as if it were said: The matter is as mentioned, and yet if you inform them of one singular introduction to it, or a unique case of its completions, they do not falter in rejecting it, and they regard that as something without any validity at all, let alone affirming what is among its completions. Or it is because the resurrection is a new creation; so it is as if it were said: He is the One Who created all created things in the first place for this profound wisdom, and yet if you inform them that He will restore them a second time, which is easier for Him, they say what they say. Glory be to Allah above what they describe!

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read (illa sahir, "except a sorcerer"), taking the reference to be to the speaker, or to the Qur'an in the manner of (shi'r sha'ir, "the poetry of a poet"). It is also read with a fatha (anna-ka, "that you"), by including the meaning of (qulta, "you said") in the sense of (dhakarta, "you mentioned"), or by taking (anna-ka) to mean (anka, "about you") as in (la'alla-ka), that is: And if you mention, "Perhaps you will be resurrected," the expectation and anticipation being in view of the state of those addressed; that is, let them anticipate it and do not categorically pronounce its denial. Or it is a conversational accommodation with them in the way of agreeableness, lest they hasten to obstinacy and stubbornness while the decisive statement is striking their ears, unlike what they were accustomed to and what their fathers had been upon of denying resurrection. This would be more likely to prompt them to reflection and contemplation. As for what they did, may Allah fight them! How are they deluded!

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 8:

﴿And if We defer the punishment from them﴾ — the punishment that follows upon their being raised (ba'th), or the punishment promised in His saying, exalted is He: "But if they turn away, then I fear for you the punishment of a great day." It has been said: the punishment of the Day of Badr. And it is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that it refers to the killing of the mockers by Jibril, peace be upon him. The apparent meaning, however, is that what is intended is a punishment encompassing the disbelievers, not one specific to some of them, especially since it was not a promise that the criminals would hasten for.

﴿until a counted community﴾ — until a group of days that are few, because what counting encompasses is few. ﴿they will surely say, "What is holding it back?"﴾ — that is, what thing prevents it from coming? It is as though He intends it, but some preventer stops it. They were saying this only in the manner of hastening, as mockery, due to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿what they used to mock at﴾. Their intent was to deny its coming and its being withheld altogether, not to acknowledge it and inquire about what holds it back. ﴿Unquestionably, on the day it comes to them﴾ — that [punishment] — ﴿it will not be turned away from them﴾, meaning withheld. The sense is that if what is meant is the punishment of the Hereafter, no one will ever lift it; or if what is meant is the punishment of this world, no one will repel it from you, but rather it will befall you. And "the day" (yawma) is in the accusative, governed by the predicate of "laysa" which is placed before it. The Basrans used this to argue for the permissibility of placing it before "laysa," since the object follows its governing verb and therefore occurs only where its head occurs. It has been answered that adverbs of time permit what is not permitted elsewhere, by way of latitude; and that the object may be placed where the verb cannot be placed, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿As for the orphan, do not oppress [him]﴾ and ﴿As for the petitioner, do not repel [him]﴾, where "the orphan" and "the petitioner," although governed by the two jussive verbs, are placed before the prohibitive "la," while the two verbs cannot be placed before it. Abu Hayyan said: I have surveyed a considerable body of Arabic diwans and have found no instance of the predicate of "laysa" being placed before it, nor of its complement being placed before it, except what this noble verse indicates, and the verse of the poet:

﴿He refuses, and he only grows more obstinate, while I was stubborn in vice and I shall not yield.﴾

﴿And there befell them﴾ — that is, encompassed them — ﴿what they used to mock at﴾, that is, the punishment they used to hasten in mockery. Expressing it by the relative pronoun conveys its terrifying greatness, and indicates that the mockery contained in the relative clause is the cause of its descent and encompassing. Expressing it by the past tense follows the custom of Allah, exalted is He, in His reports, since such things, in their certainty and assurance, are as though they already exist. In this there is a grandeur and an indication of the exalted status of the One who informs, and an affirmation of the occurrence of what is reported, which is not hidden.

The commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 9:

﴿And if We let man taste mercy from Us﴾, i.e., We bestow upon him a blessing of health, security, wealth and other things, and We deliver it to him in such a way that he finds its pleasure.

﴿Then We withdraw it from him﴾, i.e., (p-190) We strip him of it. The mention of "withdrawing" (nazʿ) indicates the intensity of his attachment to it and his eagerness for it. ﴿Indeed, he is despairing﴾, extremely hopeless of the mercy of Allah, cutting off his hope of the return of its like, sooner or later, through the bounty of Allah the Exalted, due to the scarcity of his patience, his lack of reliance upon Him and his trust in Him. ﴿Ungrateful﴾, greatly ungrateful for the blessings that had preceded. In it there is an indication that the withdrawal occurred only because of their ingratitude for the blessings of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in which they were living. Its being placed after the description of their despair, although despair precedes it in time, is for the sake of preserving the rhyme (fawasil). Moreover, despair of the bounty of Allah, Glorified is He, and cutting off hope of the addition of its like in this world and of the delivery of its reward in the next, is also a form of ungratefulness for the blessing that had passed.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 10:

﴿And if We let him taste blessing after hardship has touched him﴾ such as health after sickness, wealth after poverty, and relief after distress. The expression of the touch of mercy and blessing with "taste" (al-dhawq), which indicates their pleasure and that they are things desired, and the expression of the touch of hardship with "touch" (al-mass), which implies that it is at the lowest of the degrees to which the name of encountering applies, together with the attribution of the first to God, Mighty and Majestic, and not the second, is of no small eloquence and indicates that His intention, exalted is He, is only to convey the desired good in the best manner, and that He only wills ease for His servants, not hardship; and they attain that [hardship] only through their own poor choice, a slight attainment, as if it merely brushes the skin without effect. As for the withdrawal of mercy, it proceeds from Him only by the dictate of the wisdom that calls for it, which is their ingratitude for it, as has already been mentioned. And the indefiniteness of "mercy" is in regard to the sense of its being withdrawn.

﴿Surely he will say: "The evils have departed from me"﴾ That is: the calamities that troubled me, and similar ones will not afflict me again, as is the custom of those evildoers, for anticipating the recurrence of their like is what clouds joy and spoils life. ﴿Indeed he is exultant﴾ (fariḥ), insolent and boastful in blessings, deceived by them, ﴿and boastful﴾ (fakhur) towards people for what he has been given of blessings, occupied thereby from fulfilling their due. The lam in "la-in" in the four verses is a preparatory lam for an oath, and its answer takes the place of the answer of the conditional clause.

﴿Except those who were patient﴾ over what afflicted them of adversity, whether before or after, out of faith in God and submission to His decree, ﴿and did righteous deeds﴾ out of gratitude for His past and present bounties. The lam in الإنسان (al-insān, "the human being") is either for generalizing the whole species (lil-istighrāq al-jins), in which case the exception (al-istithnā', exception) is connected (muttaṣil), or it is for a specific referent (lil-'ahd), in which case it is disconnected (munqaṭi'). ﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to the relative pronoun, in view of its being characterized by what is in the clause that follows it (ṣilah). The sense of distance in it indicates the exaltation of their rank and the remoteness of their station in excellence; that is, ﴿those﴾ who are described by those praiseworthy attributes. ﴿For them is forgiveness﴾, great, for their sins, however many they may be, ﴿and a reward﴾, a recompense for their good deeds, ﴿great.﴾

The connection of the three verses to what precedes them is that bestowing blessings and touching adversity are both a part of the category of trial, and they come as a detailed explanation of the general statement in God's words: ﴿that He may test you, which of you is best in deed﴾. The meaning is that each of bestowing blessing and withdrawing it, while being a trial for the human being, whether he will be grateful or ungrateful, does not guide him to the paths of right conduct; rather, in both states he swerves from it into the abysses of error. Thus no good deed appears from him except from the patient and the righteous. Alternatively, the connection is that their denial of resurrection and their mockery of punishment stem from their insolence and boastfulness, as if it were said: they did what they did because the nature of the human being is disposed to that.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 12:

(p-191) ﴿Then perhaps you would leave out some of what is revealed to you﴾ from the clear proofs indicating the reality of your prophethood, which proclaim that they come from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, for whoever has a listening ear. ﴿And your breast would be constricted by it﴾, that is: you would experience constriction of the breast by reciting it to them and conveying it to them in the course of the call and the argument. ﴿Lest they say﴾, meaning, because they would say, out of blindness to those proofs whose soundness is hardly hidden from anyone with even the slightest insight, and out of persistence in obstinacy, in the form of a demand: ﴿"Why has not a treasure been sent down to him"﴾, a precious hidden wealth that would indicate his truthfulness, ﴿"or an angel come with him"﴾ to confirm him. It was said: this was said by Abdullah ibn Umayya al-Makhzumi.

It is related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that the leaders of Makkah said: "O Muhammad, make the mountains of Makkah gold for us, if you are a messenger." Others said: "Bring us the angels so that they may testify to your prophethood." He said: "I am not able to do that," and so it was revealed. It is as if the Prophet (ﷺ), when he saw their audacity in demanding such great things, not content with the dazzling proofs which would have compelled them to accept, had they been people of intellect, and when he witnessed their persistence in arrogance, all the way to the extremes of hard and easy, hastening to respond with denial and mockery and calling it magic, his condition was likened to that of one who might be expected to have his breast constricted by reciting those shining verses to them and conveying them to them. Thus he was cautioned against this by the apprehension implied in "perhaps" (la'alla), and it was said:

﴿Indeed you are only a warner﴾; there is nothing upon you but warning with what has been revealed to you, without concern for what they answer with rejection or acceptance. ﴿And Allah is Guardian over all things﴾, preserving your states and theirs, so rely upon Him in all your affairs, for He will deal with them in a manner befitting their condition. Restricting oneself to the role of warner is, at its furthest reach, hitting the very mark.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 13:

﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾ This is a transition (idrab) by means of "am" (am al-munqati'ah, the disjunctive "am"), moving away from mention of their neglect of what is revealed, their indifference to it, and their failure to be convinced by the manifest miracles it contains, which indicate that it is from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and indicate the truth of His Prophet's prophethood (ﷺ), and beginning a mention of what they commit that is even worse and greater. In it there is the meaning of the interrogative hamzah (hamzat al-tawbikh wa'l-inkar wa'l-ta'ajjub), expressing rebuke, denial and astonishment. The hidden pronoun in "iftarahu" (he has invented it) refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the visible pronoun refers to what is revealed. That is: "Rather, do they say, 'He has invented it,' and it is not from Allah?"

﴿Say﴾: "If the matter is as you claim, ﴿then bring﴾ you too ﴿ten surahs like it﴾ in eloquence and excellence of composition." "Like it" is an attribute of "surahs," meaning similar to it. Its being singular may be either by considering the likeness of each one of them, or because agreement in number is not a required condition, so that a dual may be described by a singular, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Shall we believe two humans like us?﴾ Or it may be for the sake of indicating that the aspect of resemblance and the basis of likeness in all of them is one thing, namely the eloquence that leads to the level of inimitability, so that all of them are as one. ﴿Forged﴾ is another attribute of "surahs," placed after its attribute of being like what is revealed, because it is the attribute intended by the challenge, since by it their incapacity and their inability to produce a counter-challenge becomes evident. As for the attribute of "forgery," no purpose depends on it, nor does anything in the context of the challenge rest upon it; it is mentioned only in the manner of leniency and giving rein. Moreover, had the order been reversed, it might have been supposed that the intended meaning was similarity in forgery. The meaning is: "Bring ten surahs similar to it in eloquence, invented by yourselves, if it is true that I invented it, for you are more capable of that than I am, since you are Arabs, eloquent and articulate, who have practised the rudiments of that in speeches and poetry, have memorised the events and days, and have tried the methods of verse and prose."

﴿And call upon﴾ for assistance in the counter-challenge ﴿whomever you can﴾ to call upon and seek help from, of your gods whom you claim sustain you in all that you do and refrain from, and of the soothsayers and your guides to whose opinions you resort in difficulties so that they may aid you therein, ﴿other than Allah﴾ (min dun Allah), which is connected to "call upon," meaning: going beyond Allah, exalted is He. ﴿If you are truthful﴾ in claiming that I invented it, for that entails the possibility of producing its like, and that in turn entails your capacity to do so. The answer is omitted, indicated by what has been mentioned.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 14:

﴿Then if they do not respond to you﴾ That is: if they do not do what they were charged with, namely producing its like, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But if you do not﴾. It is expressed as "responding" to indicate that the Messenger ﷺ is in complete security regarding his command, as if his command to them to produce its like were a summons to a matter whose occurrence he desires. The pronoun in "lakum" (to you) refers to the Messenger ﷺ, and the plural is for honour, as in the saying of the one who said:

﴿Verse of poetry﴾ "And if you wish, I will forbid women other than you [to all men]."

Its first reading is "wa-lil-mu'minin" (and to the believers), because they are followers of him ﷺ in the matter of the challenge. In this there is a subtle reminder that their duty is not to separate from him ﷺ and to stand with him in opposing those who oppose him, as they used to do in jihad, and a guidance that this brings firmness in faith and tranquillity in certainty. For this reason His saying, mighty and majestic is He, "fa-'lamu" (then know) is linked to it. That is: know, when your incapacity to produce a counter-challenge has become evident to you despite their eagerness for it, a certain knowledge that borders on the eye of certainty, such that no room remains for any trace of doubt in any way, as if every other degree of knowledge were not knowledge. However, this is not to indicate the lowering of those degrees, but the elevation of this degree. By this the secret of introducing the word of doubt (in "if") together with the certainty of their non-response becomes clear, for placing all other degrees in the position of non-existence entails placing the certainty of non-response in the position of doubt concerning it. Or the meaning is: remain and persist in the knowledge you have been upon.

﴿Indeed it was sent down﴾ being accompanied ﴿with the knowledge of God﴾, which is specific to Him, such that minds and understandings cannot circle around it, possessing exclusively the features of inimitability, both in terms of the sublime arrangement and the report of the unseen. ﴿And that there is no god but He﴾: that is, know also that there is no partner to Him in divinity and its rulings, and that He is not able to do what anyone is able to do. ﴿Will you then be Muslims?﴾ That is: sincere in Islam, or steadfast upon it. This is of the kind of consolidation and elevation to the stations of certainty. It is also permissible that the address in all of it is to the polytheists, on the part of the Messenger ﷺ, included under the command of the challenge, and the pronoun in "lam yastajibu" (they do not respond) refers to "man istata'tum" (whom you can), that is: if your gods and all those to whom you cry out for help in your important and afflicting matters do not respond to you with aid and support, know that this lies outside the sphere of human power, and that it is sent down from the Creator of powers and decrees. Then the introduction of the word of doubt in that case, together with the certainty of non-response from your gods, is a mockery of them and a recording against them of the complete feebleness of their intellect. And the ordering of the command to knowledge upon the mere fact of non-response, insofar as it is preceded by supplication, which is preceded by their incapacity and distress, is as if it were said: if they do not respond to you when you turn to them after you have been compelled to that and the means have become constrained for you and the causes have overwhelmed you; or insofar as those from whom they seek help are, in their belief, stronger than them. Then when their incapacity becomes manifest through non-response, although that is before the manifestation of the incapacity of their own selves, their incapacity becomes more evident and clear. Know also that your gods are far removed from the rank of partnership in divinity and its rulings. ﴿Will you then enter into Islam?﴾, since no trace of doubt remains concerning its truth and the falsehood of the polytheism you were in; so that submission to the fact that the Qur'an is from God, exalted is He, enters it at the first level, or [it means]: you submit to the truth, which is that the Qur'an is from God, exalted is He, and you abandon what you were in of obstinacy and stubbornness. In this interrogation there is an emphatic obligation, since it carries the sense of a demand, and an alert to the existence of the obligating cause and the removal of excuse, and a despairing of their gods protecting them from the might of God, mighty is His authority. This, however, the first reading is more suitable to what preceded of His saying, exalted is He: "and your breast is constrained by it," and to what will come of His saying, exalted is He: "so do not be in doubt about it," and more closely connected with what follows, as you will be informed in detail.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 15:

﴿Whoever desires the life of this world and its adornment﴾ — i.e., what adorns and beautifies it, such as health, security, ample provision, many children, leadership, and other things. By "desire" is meant what occurs upon actually engaging in the deeds, not merely the inner wish of the heart, according to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We will pay them in full for their deeds therein﴾. The placing of (kāna, "was") before it indicates the continuity of this desire on their part, to the extent that they hardly desire the Hereafter at all. The intended meaning of "their deeds" is not all of their deeds, for not every wisher finds what he wishes for, nor does everyone attain everything he desires, since that is contingent upon the Will that operates in accordance with wisdom, as His saying, exalted is He, expresses: "Whoever desires the hasty [life], We hasten for him therein what We will, for whom We desire" [17:18]. Nor is it all of their deeds, but rather some of them, namely those deeds of righteousness which, by way of reward and recompense, bring about the matters mentioned. The word has been used and what is intended is its fruits. Thus the meaning is: We deliver to them the fruits of their deeds in this worldly life in full. It has been read as (yuwaff, "He pays"), attributed to God, glorified and exalted is He, and as (tuwaff, "it is paid"), with the feminine prefix on the passive form, with (a'maluhum, "their deeds") in the nominative; and it has been read as (nuwafi, "We pay"), with the light (tashdid-less) form and the nominative, since the condition is in the past tense, as in the line:

؎ Even if a friend comes to him on a day of hunger, he says, "My wealth is not absent, nor is it forbidden [to you]."

﴿And they therein﴾ — i.e., in the life of this world — ﴿will not be deprived﴾, i.e., they will not be diminished. This is expressed by "bakhs" (deprivation), which is the diminution of a right, although they have no trace of a right in what they are given, just as giving it is expressed by "tawfiyah" (full payment), which is the giving of rights, although their deeds are far from being deserving of that. This is an application of the matter to its outward state, a preservation of the forms of deeds, and an intensification in negating any shortfall, as if such a thing were a diminution of their rights, so that it does not fall under the occurrence or issuance from the Generous at all. The meaning is that they, therein specifically, are not diminished in the fruits of their deeds or their rewards in a complete and continuous diminution, nor are they deprived of them in a total deprivation. As for the Hereafter, they are in utter deprivation and certain despair, as His saying, exalted is He, declares:

"Those" ... etc. It is a reference to those mentioned, in terms of their desire for the life of this world, or in terms of their being paid their wages in full without deficiency, or in terms of both together. The sense of distance in it is to signal the distance of their rank in ill condition. That is: "Those who desire the life of this world and its adornment, who are paid in full for their deeds therein without deficiency" ﴿for whom there is in the Hereafter nothing but the Fire﴾, because their aspirations were directed toward this world, their works were confined to attaining it, and they have [in effect] forsaken its fruit, not intending anything else by them. Therefore, without doubt, there is for them in the Hereafter nothing but the Fire and its everlasting punishment.

﴿And what they did therein has become void﴾, meaning: in the Hereafter it becomes manifest that the deeds they performed, which would have led to reward had they been done for the Hereafter, have come to nothing; or [it means] what they did in the world of righteous deeds has come to nothing, since the condition for their being counted is sincerity. ﴿And vain is﴾, meaning: in itself, ﴿what they used to do﴾ in the course of pursuing worldly aims. Because the first has the nature of entailing reward and recompense, and its absence is due to its not being accompanied by faith and a sound intention, and because the second has no good aspect whatsoever, the first is connected with "has become void" (ḥubūṭ), which signals the cancellation of its reward, by the verbal form that indicates occurrence; and the second with "vain" (buṭlān), which makes clear that it is of a kind having no benefit whatsoever, by the nominal form that indicates that this is a necessary attribute of it, firmly established in it. The addition of "kāna" in the second and not the first is an indication that the performance of acts of righteousness by them, even if for a corrupt purpose, is not in continuity and permanence like the performance of the acts which are the preliminaries of their base aims. It has also been read as "wa-baṭala" (and became void) as a verb, meaning: its voidness became manifest, since it is known there that this and what it entails of worldly portions are of no benefit; or its worldly effect ceased, so it became void absolutely. It has also been read as "wa-bāṭilan mā kānū yaʿmalūn" (and vain what they used to do), with "mā" being indeterminate (ibhāmiyyah), or in the sense of a verbal noun, as in the saying of the poet:

"Nor one coming out of a mouth, a false speech."

And it is related from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, that what is meant by the words of the Exalted, "Whoever desires..." etc., are the Jews and Christians: if they gave to a beggar, or maintained ties of kinship, the recompense of that was hastened to them by expansion in provision and soundness in the body. It was also said: they are the hypocrites who fought with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and so they were given shares in the spoils. And you know well that this was only after the Hijrah, while the surah is Meccan.

It was also said: they are the people of showing off (riyā'), it is said to their reciters: "You wanted it to be said: so-and-so is a reciter," and indeed that has been said; and likewise for others among those who do acts of righteousness not for the sake of Allah the Exalted. According to this, it is necessary to restrict the saying of the Exalted, "for them there is nothing in the Hereafter but the Fire," to mean that for them, because of their showing-off deeds, there is nothing but that. What the eloquence of the noble composition requires is that what is meant by it is the disbelievers absolutely, such that those who disparage the Great Qur'an fall within them at the first level. For when the Exalted, the Mighty and Sublime, commanded His Prophet ﷺ and the believers to increase in knowledge and certainty that the Qur'an is sent down with the knowledge of Allah, and that no one else has any power over anything at all, and He roused them to steadfastness in Islam and firmness in it when the disbelievers' incapacity became evident, and [shown] that what they call upon besides Allah cannot oppose it, and it became clear that they are not upon anything at all, the situation required that some of their affairs be addressed, which might give the impression that they are upon something in some respect, namely their attaining immediate portions and their dominion over worldly aims, and the explanation that this is far from indicating that [they are upon the truth]. This has been explained most clearly. Then the encouragement toward what was mentioned, namely faith in the Qur'an, monotheism and Islam, was repeated, and it is said:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 17:

﴿Is one who is upon a clear proof from his Lord﴾: that is, a radiant proof of great significance, which indicates the truth of what he has been encouraged to hold firm to, namely Islam, and this is the Qur'an. Because of its status (or by interpreting "proof" in this way), the pronoun referring back to it is masculine in His words, exalted is He, ﴿and a witness from Him recites it﴾: that is, follows it, ﴿a witness﴾ who testifies that it is from Allah, exalted is He, and this is the inimitability (i'jaz) in its composition that is consistent in every sura of it, or what occurred in some of its verses of reports of the unseen. Both are attributes that accompany it and testify that it is from Allah, mighty and majestic is He. However, on the first interpretation, there is in the statement an allusion to the state of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers in their adherence to the Qur'an when its being sent down by the knowledge of Allah becomes clear through the testimony of its inimitability. ﴿From Him﴾: that is, from the Qur'an, without being separate from it, or from Allah, exalted is He, since each of them comes from Him, exalted is He, as testimony. On this interpretation it is also possible that the witness refers to the miracles manifested at the hands of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), since these too are among the witnesses accompanying the Qur'an that come from Him, exalted is He. Thus, the meaning of "one" (man) in His words, exalted is He, "Is one (afaman)" is everyone who possesses this praiseworthy attribute, and so it includes, primarily, those addressed in His words, exalted is He, "Then know" and "Will you then" (fahal antum). It has been said that it refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), and it has been said that it refers to the believers among the People of the Book, such as Abd Allah ibn Salam and his like. It has also been said that the "proof" means the evidence of reason, and the "witness" means the Qur'an, so the pronoun in "from Him" refers to Allah, exalted is He, or the "proof" is the Qur'an, and "recites it" comes from recitation (tilawa), and the "witness" is Gabriel, or the tongue of the Prophet (ﷺ), on the basis that the pronoun refers to him; or it comes from following (tuluww), and the "witness" is an angel who preserves it. The first view is the preferable one.

Since the intended meaning of the witness's following the proof is establishing testimony to its soundness, and its being from Allah following it in such a way that it never separates from it in any situation, for the Qur'an is a proof that remains over the course of time together with its witness, who testifies to its matter until the Day of Resurrection, to every believer and denier, the Book of Moses is conjoined in His words, mighty is He, saying: ﴿and before it was the Book of Moses﴾, to its doer (the witness), even though it preceded it in revelation. It is as though it were said: "Is one who is upon a clear proof from his Lord, and to which a witness from Him testifies, and another witness before it, which is the Book of Moses?" The one revealed later is mentioned first because it is a necessary attribute of it that does not separate from it, and because of its prominence in the attribute of following (tuluww). The indefiniteness in "proof" and "witness" is for magnification.

﴿As a guide﴾: that is, one followed in religion and one who is emulated. In the mention of this attribute in the context of explaining the following of the Book is what clearly reflects the magnification of the status of the one being followed. ﴿And a mercy﴾: that is, a great blessing upon those to whom it was sent down and those after them until the Day of Resurrection, in terms of its enduring rulings, supported by the Mighty Qur'an. These two are states (ḥal) of the Book.

﴿Those﴾: the ones described by that praiseworthy attribute, which is being upon a clear proof from Allah. Since that is an expression for mere adherence to it, and it may be by way of imitation (taqlid) of the great religious authorities of the past without having reached the subtle realities, He described them as ﴿believing in it﴾: that is, they affirm it with true affirmation, according to what the true witnesses testify, which express its truth. ﴿And whoever disbelieves in it﴾: that is, in the Qur'an, and does not affirm those true witnesses, ﴿of the factions﴾: from the people of Makkah and those who united with them against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). ﴿Then the Fire is his appointed place﴾: he will certainly enter it, as His words, exalted is He, state: ﴿They have in the Hereafter nothing but the Fire﴾. Making it an "appointed place" indicates that there are in it kinds of punishment that cannot be described.

﴿So do not be in doubt about it﴾: that is, about the matter of the Qur'an and its being from Allah, mighty and majestic is He, as the mentioned witnesses testify, and the virtue of whoever holds fast to it has become clear. ﴿That it is the truth from your Lord﴾, which will not make you lose in your religion or your worldly life. ﴿But most people do not believe﴾ in that, either because of the weakness of their insight and the corruption of their thinking, or because of their obstinacy and arrogance.

So "whoever" (man) in His words, exalted is He, ﴿Is one who is upon a clear proof from his Lord﴾ is the subject of a sentence whose predicate has been omitted, because the situation makes mentioning it unnecessary. Its estimated form is: "Is one who is upon a clear proof from his Lord like those whose deeds were mentioned and whose destiny and final outcome were made clear?" That is, there is a great disparity between them, such that their two fires can hardly be seen together. The placing of "fa" after the interrogative hamza is for denying that the assumption of equality follows from the attributes that were mentioned for them and the faults that were enumerated, as though it were said: "After the manifestation of their state in this world and the Hereafter, as has been described, could equality be supposed between them and one who was in the best of states in the immediate and the final, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Have you then taken, besides Him, protectors?﴾" That is: after you have known Him to be the Lord of the heavens and the earth, have you taken, besides Him, protectors? And His words, exalted is He: ﴿Is one who knows that what has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth like one who is blind?﴾?!

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 18:

﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah?﴾ By attributing to Him what does not befit Him, such as their saying that the angels are the daughters of Allah. Exalted is Allah far above that, a great exaltation. And their saying about their gods: "These are our intercessors with Allah." That is, they, along with their disbelief in the signs of Allah the Exalted, are fabricators against Him of a lie. Although this construction is framed as a denial that anyone could be more unjust than them, without addressing the denial or negation of equality, its intended purpose is consistently the denial and negation of equality, and the conveying that they are more unjust than every unjust person. This is indicated by the words of the Mighty and Majestic that follow: ﴿Without doubt, they are the greatest losers in the Hereafter.﴾ Thus, when it is said, "Who is more generous than so-and-so?" or "There is none more excellent than him," what is certainly meant is that he is more generous than every generous person and more excellent than every excellent person.

﴿Those﴾ are the ones described with the extreme injustice which is fabricating against Allah the Exalted. By this demonstrative, the need to attribute the presentation to their deeds is dispensed with, and it is sufficient to attribute it to them, where it is said: ﴿they will be presented﴾, because their presentation is from that standpoint, and by that title it is a presentation of their deeds in a more eloquent manner, since the presentation of a doer with his deed is more dreadful than the presentation of his deed in his absence. ﴿Before their Lord﴾, the Truth. In this there is an allusion to the falsity of their opinion in taking lords besides Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. ﴿And the witnesses will say﴾ at the presentation, from among the angels and the prophets, or from their own limbs. It is the plural of "shahid" or "shahid," like "ashab" and "ashraf": ﴿These are the ones who lied against their Lord﴾ by fabricating against Him. As if that were a matter so clear that it needs no testimony to its occurrence, and what needs testimony is only the identification of the one from whom it proceeded. Therefore they do not say, "These lied against their Lord." It is also possible that the intended "witnesses" are the attendees, namely all the people of the place of standing, according to what Qatadah and Muqatil said, and their saying: ﴿These are the ones who lied against their Lord﴾ would be a censure of them for that, given that He has called them as witnesses against them, as the words of the Exalted indicate: (and it says) without "and it testifies" ... etc., and as a preparation for what follows in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Surely the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers﴾ for the aforementioned fabrication. It is also possible that this, according to the first aspect, is part of the speech of Allah the Exalted, and in it is a great terrifying of what will befall them from the consequence of their injustice. O Allah, we seek refuge in You from disgrace before the heads of the witnesses.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 19:

﴿Those who bar⁠﴾ i.e., everyone who is able to bar it, or who engage in barring ﴿from the way of Allah﴾, from His upright religion, ﴿and seek to make it crooked﴾, deviant. That is, they describe it as such, though it is the furthest thing from that; or they seek to make its people deviate from it. It is said: "baghaytuka khayran aw sharran" (I sought for you good or evil), meaning I sought it on your behalf. This includes their denial of the Qur'an and their saying that it is not from Allah ﴿and they, of the Hereafter, they are disbelievers﴾, i.e., they describe it (the Way) as crooked, while in fact they disbelieve in the Hereafter, not that they believe in it and claim that it has an upright path which they guide people to. The repetition of the pronoun (hum) serves to emphasize their disbelief and to single them out for it, as if the disbelief of others were nothing in comparison to their disbelief.

**﴿Those⁠﴾** (with a description of their circumstances that necessitated destruction) **﴿were not able to escape⁠﴾** Allah, the Exalted, **escaping by themselves from His seizing them, were He to will that, ﴿in the earth⁠﴾** despite its vastness, even if they fled from it by every way of escape. **﴿And they had no protectors besides Allah⁠﴾** who would help them against His punishment. But that was delayed for a wisdom that required it. The plural [in "protectors"] is either in view of the individuals of disbelievers, as if it were said: "There was not for any one of them a protector," or in view of the multiplicity of what they used to call upon besides Allah, the Exalted; in that case it is a clarification of the state of their gods, that they had fallen from the rank of protection. **﴿The punishment will be doubled for them⁠﴾** is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) that includes the wisdom of delaying the seizing. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub read it with the doubling (tashdid).

**﴿They were not able to hear⁠﴾** because of the extreme deafness to the truth and their hatred of it, as if they were unable to hear. Since the ugliness of their state in not submitting to the Qur'an, whose means of reception is hearing, was greater than their ugliness in not accepting the other signs that are tied to sight, he (Allah) emphasized the negation of the first by denying them the ability (istita'a), and he sufficed with negating sight for the second. So the Exalted said: **﴿and they used not to see⁠﴾** because of their blindness to the signs of Allah spread out in the souls and the horizons. This is a resumptive statement that came as a rationale for the doubling of the punishment. It has also been said that it is a clarification of what was negated of the protection of the gods, for what does not hear and does not see is far removed from protection. The Exalted's statement **"The punishment will be doubled for them"** is an interjection placed between the two, censuring them from the outset for the evil of their final outcome.

Those are the ones described by the ugly traits mentioned, who have lost themselves by exchanging the worship of God, may His authority be exalted, for the worship of the gods, and what they used to fabricate, namely the gods and their intercession, has strayed from them. Or: they lost what they expended, and what they had gained was lost to them, so nothing remained with them except regret and remorse.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 22:

﴿La jarama﴾ (lit. "Undoubtedly" / "Certainly") has three possible readings:

The first: that "la" (لا) is a negation of what preceded it, and "jarama" is a verb meaning "haqqa" (حَقَّ, "it is true/certain"), and "anna" (أنَّ) together with what follows it in its clause is its subject. The meaning is: that act does not benefit them; it is certain ﴿that they, in the Hereafter, are the greatest losers﴾. This is the view of Sibawayh.

The second: "jarama" means "kasaba" (كَسَبَ, "earned/brought about"), and what follows it is its object, while its subject is what the speech implies, i.e., "that brought about their loss." The meaning is: nothing resulted from that except the manifestation of their loss.

The third: that "la jarama" means "la budda" (لا بُدَّ, "there is no doubt"), i.e., "there is no doubt that they, in the Hereafter, are the greatest losers."

In any case, its meaning is that they are greater losers than every loser, and thus it becomes clear that they are more unjust than every wrongdoer. These noble verses, as you see, confirm with the utmost emphasis the denial of equivalence, stated earlier, between one who is upon a clear proof from his Lord and one who desires the life of this world. For since they are more unjust than every wrongdoer and greater losers than every loser, no equivalence can be imagined between them and any of the unjust and losing transgressors; so what then is your thought about equivalence between them and one who is at the highest stages of perfection?

When the group of disbelievers, their deeds, and the explanation of their destiny and outcome had been mentioned, he began to explain the state of their opposites, namely the group of believers, and the praiseworthy consequences that their affair leads to, as a completion of the excellent qualities of theirs mentioned earlier in His saying, Exalted is He: "Is one who is upon a clear proof from his Lord..." (the verse), so that the stark contrast between the two in state and outcome may become clear. Thus it was said:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 23:

﴿Indeed, those who believe﴾ i.e., in everything that must be believed in (p-198), thereby including what we are concerned with: belief in the Qur'an, which is expressed by "being upon a clear proof from their Lord." This is only attained by listening to the revelation (wahy) and reflecting upon it, and by observing what leads to that, in the souls and on the horizons. Or [the meaning is] "they performed belief," as in [the usage] "yu'ti wa yamna'" (he gives and withholds).

﴿and do righteous deeds and humble themselves before their Lord﴾ i.e., they were at peace with Him and devoted themselves to His worship through submission and humility, from al-khabt (khabt), which is low, level ground. The meaning of akhbata is "he entered the khabt," just as ata'hama (he entered Tihama) and anjada (he entered Najd). ﴿Those﴾ who are described by these beautiful attributes ﴿are the companions of the Garden; therein they will abide forever﴾, i.e., will remain eternally. After the explanation of the difference between their two states in the intellectual sense, the explanation of their difference in the sensory sense was intended, so it was said:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 24:

﴿Mathal al-fariqayn﴾ (the likeness of the two groups) mentioned, i.e., their strange state; for the word mathal (likeness, parable) is applied only to what contains some strangeness of conditions and attributes. ﴿Like the blind and the deaf, and the seeing and the hearing﴾, i.e., like the state of these, so that their essences are like their essences. And although the statement could be taken as likening the first group to the blind and the deaf, and likening the second group to the seeing and the hearing, the one more emphatic, closer to what the word mathal indicates, and more suitable to what preceded regarding the description of the disbelievers as unable to hear and unable to see, is that it be taken as likening the first group to one who combines blindness and deafness, and likening the second group to one who combines sight and hearing, with the waw in His saying, "and the deaf" and in His saying, "and the hearing," being for conjoining attribute to attribute, as in the saying of one who said:

To the lordly king and the son of the valiant, and the lion of the battalion in the crowd.

In any case, the apparent meaning is that the condition indicated by the word mathal, which is the basis of the comparison, is what agrees with the mentioned conditions considered on the side of the likened-to: the first group's blindness to observing the signs of God set up in the world and looking at them with the eye of consideration, and their deafness to hearing the verses of the Noble Qur'an and receiving them with acceptance, as stated in His saying, ﴿They were not able to hear, and they used not to see﴾.
