This order was not observed here because the blind is more evident and more well-known in bad condition than the deaf, and because of the second group's use of each of their sights and hearings in what is mentioned, as it should be, which is implied by what preceded of faith, righteous deeds and humble submission, as explained there earlier. Therefore the comparison is not a representative (tamthili) comparison for all the states counted for each of the two groups from what has been mentioned, and what leads to it of doubled punishment and extreme loss for one of them, and of lasting bliss in the other. For considering that inclines toward the comparison being representative, by abstracting from the state of the first group in their mentioned deafness and blindness, and their falling because of that into doubled punishment and the loss beyond which there is no loss, a form, which is likened to a form abstracted from one who has lost the two faculties of sight and hearing, so that he stumbles in his course, falls into the pits of destruction, and finds no way to his goal; and abstracting from the state of the second group in using their faculties for the signs of God, the Exalted, as it should be, and their attaining the abode of eternity, a form, which is likened to a form abstracted from one who has sight and hearing and uses them in his affairs, so that he is guided to his path and attains his aim.

﴿Are they equal?﴾ meaning the two groups mentioned. The interrogation is denunciatory, reminding of what preceded regarding the denial of equivalence in His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Is one who is upon a clear proof from his Lord﴾ etc. ﴿(in) likeness﴾ i.e., in condition and attribute; it is a specification (tamyiz) from the subject of (yastawiyan). ﴿Will you not then take heed?﴾ i.e., do you doubt the non-equality and the disparity between them, or are you heedless of it so that you do not recollect it by reflecting on the parable struck for you? Then the denial falls upon both conjoined elements together. Or: do you hear this and yet not take heed? Then it refers to non-recollection after the establishment of what necessitates its existence, which is the parable struck, as in His saying, ﴿(Then if he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels?)﴾, where the fa' there is for denying turning back after the establishment of what necessitates its absence, from their knowledge that the messengers before the Messenger of God ﷺ had passed away. Or: will you not then do the recollecting? Or: will you not then reason? The meaning of the hamza is the denial of non-recollection and the deeming it unlikely to proceed from the addressees, and that it is not something that could occur. It is not of the kind of denial in His saying, ﴿Is one who is upon a clear proof from his Lord﴾ and His saying, ﴿Are they equal?﴾, for that is for negating likeness and negating equality.

Since it has been made clear from the opening of the noble surah up to this point that it is a Book whose verses are firmly established and whose matters are detailed, revealed concerning the affirmation of tawhid and the abandoning of the worship of other than God, Glorified is He, and that what was revealed to him is a warner and a bringer of good tidings from Him, the Exalted; and that within all this there was established what has a bearing on the realization of this aim, of encouragement and warning, and of binding the obstinate with what accompanies it of true evidences indicating that it is from God, the Exalted; and the consolation of the Messenger ﷺ for what afflicted him of constriction of breast arising from their shameful demands and their denial of him, and their calling the Qur'an at one time sorcery and at another fabrication; and the firming of the Messenger ﷺ and the believers in holding fast to it and acting upon its requirements in the most eloquent manner and most wondrous style, it began to realize and establish what has been mentioned by mentioning the stories of the prophets, may the blessings of God be upon them all, which include what the opening of the noble surah includes; so that this is confirmed by two means:

The first: that what he was commanded of tawhid and its branches is what all the prophets unanimously agreed upon.

The second: that this was known by the Messenger of God ﷺ only by way of revelation, so no doubt whatsoever remains about its truth; and so that he may be consoled by what he witnesses of the sufferings of the messengers before him from their peoples and their enduring of hardships at their hands. Thus it is said:

And We certainly sent Noah to his people. The *waw* is *al-waw al-ibtida'iyya* (the inceptive *waw*, which opens a new discourse), and the *lam* is the answer to an omitted oath (*qasam*). Its particle is the *ba'* and not the *waw*, as in Surat al-A'raf, so that two *waws* do not come together. This *lam* is hardly ever used except with *qad*, because it signals expectation (*tawaqquʿ*), and because the addressee, on hearing it, anticipates the occurrence of what it introduces. Noah is the son of Lamak, son of Mattushalakh, son of Idris, peace be upon them both, and he was the first prophet sent after him.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: He (ﷺ) was sent at the age of forty, remained calling his people for nine hundred and fifty years, lived sixty years after the Flood, and his lifespan was one thousand and fifty years.

Muqatil said: He was sent when he was one hundred years old. It was said: when he was fifty. It was said: when he was two hundred and fifty. He remained calling his people for nine hundred and fifty years and lived two hundred and fifty years after the Flood, so his lifespan was one thousand four hundred and fifty years.

﴿Indeed I am to you a plain warner.﴾ The *inni* is read with *kasra* (*bi-al-kasr*), on the intention of a verb of saying, meaning: so he said, or saying. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read it with *fath* (*bi-al-fath*), on the assumption of an omitted preposition, meaning: We sent him while (*multabisan*) with that statement, which is "Indeed I am to you a warner." When the preposition is attached to it, it takes *fath*, as *inna* does in *ka'anna*. The meaning with *kasra* is as in your saying: "Indeed Zayd is like a lion." Mention is made only of his (ﷺ) being a warner, not because his call was only by way of warning, do you not see His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So I said: Ask forgiveness of your Lord, indeed He is ever Forgiving﴾ ﴿He will send the sky upon you in abundant rain﴾ ... etc., but because they did not seize the spoils of his good tidings (ﷺ). ﴿Plain﴾: I make clear to you what necessitates the punishment and the way of escape from it, since warning is the announcement of what is to be feared, not merely for the sake of frightening and alarming, but for the sake of taking precaution against it. Thus it relates to both of its attributes.

(p-200) ﴿That you worship none but Allah﴾. That is, "that you not worship," where "an" is a *masdariyyah* (a particle that turns the following verb into a verbal noun), and the *ba'* (with) is connected to *arsalna* (We sent). The "la" is *nahiyah* (prohibitive): "We sent him while bringing them the prohibition of association (shirk)." However, some description of his attributes and conditions, ﷺ, was placed between them, namely that he is a clear warner, so that it would be more readily accepted. This was not done at the beginning of the sura, lest the Book be separated from its content by something that is not one of its attributes or conditions. Alternatively, *an* is *mufassirah* (explanatory), connected to it, or to *nadhir* (warner), or it is an object of *mubin* (clear). According to the reading with *fath* (the vowel on the *alif* of *an*), it is a substitute for "Indeed I am to you a clear warner," and a specification of what necessitates the occurrence of the feared outcome, and a clarification of the way of escape, which is the worship of Allah, exalted is He.

His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿Indeed I fear for you the punishment of a painful day﴾ is a reason for the requirement of the prohibition, an explicit statement of the feared outcome, and a confirmation of the warning. By "a painful day" is meant the Day of Resurrection, or the Day of the Flood. Describing it as "painful" is a metaphorical attribution for emphasis, as in "its day is fasting." This statement, and what is similar to it in meaning, which he ﷺ said during the course of the call, as is attributed to him in the other suras, since it was not uttered by him ﷺ only once but he would repeat it to them over that lengthy period, as His, exalted is He, saying indicates: ﴿My Lord, I have called my people night and day﴾ and the verses that follow, is conjoined to the act of sending that accompanies it, or to the implied speech after it, whose answer, which addresses the conditions of the believers who followed him ﷺ after the "lataya" and the "allati" (i.e., after much hardship), is introduced by the *fa'* of sequence (*fa'* al-ta'qib), so it was said:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 27:

﴿So the chiefs (al-mala') among those of his people who disbelieved said﴾. That is, the nobles among them. It comes from their saying "so-and-so is full (mali') of such-and-such," meaning he is capable of it, because they are filled with the sufficiency of affairs. Or because they fill hearts with awe and assemblies with dignity. Or because they are filled with forbearance and sound opinions. Describing them with disbelief serves to censure them and to record this against them from the outset, not because some of their nobles were not disbelievers.

﴿We see you only as a human like ourselves﴾. Their meaning is: you are only a human like us, and there is no excellence in you that distinguishes you above us with what you claim of prophethood. Had it been so, we would have seen it. This is not to say that such a thing is impossible, but that we do not see it. The same applies to their saying: ﴿And we see none following you except those who are our lowest (arafilana) in judgment at first glance﴾. Both verbs are from sight of the eye (ru'yat al-'ayn).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿only a human like us﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl, a qualifier of the state) from the object (maf'ul, the direct object), and likewise His saying ﴿following you﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause from it, either in its own state, or with the implied qad (قد) according to those who stipulate that. It is also possible that the verb is from sight of the heart (ru'yat al-qalb), which is the apparent reading. In that case the two are the second object (al-maf'ul al-thani). The predication of the opinion in the first case relates to the likeness (al-mithliyya), not to humanness (al-bashariyya) alone.

They did not state this categorically, though they were certain of it and insistent upon it, as a display that this had not been said by them at random, but after reflection and deliberation on the matter. For this reason they limited themselves to that supposition in what follows. And it is an allusion, from the outset, to the view of one who is clear-sighted. Thus their saying ﴿and we do not see you﴾ is an answer to what might be raised against them: that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace (ﷺ), is not like them, since he witnessed the proofs of his prophethood, and took the opportunity to follow him, one who has an eye that sees and a heart that perceives. So they claimed that these are our lowest (arafilana), that is, our basest and most inferior, the plural of arfal (أرْذَلٍ), for it has by dominance come to function as a noun, like al-akbar and al-akabir. Or it is the plural of arful (أرْذُلٍ), the plural of radhl (رَذْلٍ), like akalib, aklub and kalb. They mean that their following you carries no weight, since they have no solidity of intellect and no originality of judgment. This was from them at first glance (bady al-ra'y), that is, its outward appearance, without deep reflection, from al-badw (البدو), or at its beginning, from al-bad' (البدء). The yā' (ي) is substituted for a hamza (ء) because of the kasra before it. Abu 'Amr read it with it. Its accusative is adverbial (ẓarfiyya, adverbial of time) by omission of the annexed term, meaning: at the time of the occurrence of bady al-ra'y. The governing element is (ittaba'aka, "followed you").

They regarded them as base despite their being people of sound intellect because of their poverty. When they knew only the outward aspect of the worldly life, the nobler in their eyes was the one with more of it in portion, and the baser was the one deprived of it. They did not comprehend that this does not weigh with Allah the wing of a gnat, and that bliss is only the bliss of the Hereafter, and that the noble is the one who attains it and the base is the one who is deprived of it. We seek refuge in Allah, exalted is He, from that.

﴿And we do not see for you﴾, that is, for you and your followers, so the addressee was given precedence over the absent ones, ﴿over us any merit﴾. They mean that their following you does not indicate your prophethood, nor does it bring them any virtue that would necessitate our following you. Their restriction here to denying the sight of merit, after their explicit statement of their baseness earlier, is considered in light of their prior and subsequent condition. Their meaning is that they were base before following you, and that we see in you and in them after following no merit over us.

﴿Rather, we think you are liars﴾, all of you, since your speech is one and your claim is one, or you in the claim of prophethood and they in affirming you. Their restriction to supposition is a caution on their part against attributing to themselves rash judgment, and a courtesy toward him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace (ﷺ), by way of display, in the manner of fairness.

This is the commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 28:

﴿He said, "O my people, tell me﴾, i.e., inform me. This implies the feebleness of their opinion mentioned above. ﴿If I am upon a clear proof﴾, an evident demonstration, ﴿from my Lord﴾, and a witness that testifies to the truth of my claim, ﴿and He has given me mercy from Himself﴾, which is prophethood. It is permissible that the mercy is the proof itself, mentioned to indicate that, although it is a proof from God Most High, it is also a great mercy and blessing from Him. In that case, the reason for the singular pronoun in His words ﴿so it was made obscure to you﴾ is evident. If by the mercy is meant prophethood and by the proof is meant the evidence that establishes its validity, then the singular is used to refer to each of them, or because the pronoun refers to the proof and it suffices with that, since its obscurity entails the obscurity of prophethood, or because a different verb is understood after "proof." The meaning of "was made obscure" (ʿummiyat) is "was concealed." It was also read (ʿamiyat), meaning "became hidden." Its reality is that just as a proof is made seeing and insightful, it can be made blind, because the blind man neither guides himself nor guides others. In the recitation of Ubayy (fa-ʿammāhā ʿalaykum), it is attributed to God, Mighty and Majestic:

﴿Shall we compel you to it?﴾, i.e., shall we force you to be guided by it? This is the response to "tell me," and it serves in place of the response to the conditional. Abu ʿAmr read it with the vowel of the mim dropped (idghām-free reduction of the vowel). Where two object pronouns occur together, and the more definite of them has been placed first, the second may be joined or separated. It is joined, as in His words ﴿So God will suffice you against them﴾ and ﴿while you dislike it﴾, i.e., you choose it without reflecting upon it. The summary of the answer is: tell me, if I am upon a proof whose indication of the validity of my claim is clear, but which is hidden from you, and which you take for granted, can we compel you to accept it while you turn away from it without reflecting upon it? That is, that cannot be. Its apparent sense suggests that it came from him (ﷺ) as an expression of despair of compelling them and of abstaining from disputing with them, like His words ﴿and my advice will not benefit you﴾, etc. But it is understood to mean that his intention (ﷺ) was to turn them back from turning away from it and to urge them to reflect upon it, by directing the denial at compulsion while they are averse to it, not at compulsion in general.

That said, it is permissible that the proof means the rational evidence, which is the criterion of excellence, by which individual humans are distinguished from one another, and on which honor with God, Mighty and Majestic, and selection for messengership depend. Being upon it means holding fast to it and remaining steadfast in it (p-202). Its obscurity to the disbelievers, on the basis that the pronoun refers to the proof, is their failure to perceive that he (ﷺ) was upon it. By mercy is meant prophethood, whose exclusivity to him among them they denied. The meaning is: you claimed that the station of prophethood is attained only by one who has a virtue over the rest of people which entails his exclusive possession of it to the exclusion of them. Tell me, if I surpassed you in an added distinction and the acquisition of a virtue from my Lord, and He gave me prophethood from Himself in accordance with it, so that this proof was hidden from you: you did not hit upon it, did not attain it, and did not know of my possession of it and my being upon it until now, so that you claimed I am like you. While it is established in itself, shall we compel you to accept my prophethood which follows from it, while you are unwilling? The interrogation is then for the purpose of inducing acknowledgment, which is most suitable to the context of argument. In that case his (ﷺ) words are a reply to the doubts they slipped into the midst of their speech about his being a human being: at best he would be like them, with no superiority over them, and a cutting off of the root of their feeble opinions.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 29:

﴿And O my people, I ask of you no wealth for it﴾, that is, for what I have said during your call, ﴿wealth﴾ which you would pay to me after your faith and your following of me, so that this would be a reward for me in return for your guidance. ﴿My reward is only from Allah﴾, who will reward me in the Hereafter. In expressing it thus, when it was attributed to them as wealth, there is what is not hidden of distinction. ﴿And I will not drive away those who have believed﴾. This is a response to what they hinted at with their saying: ﴿And we do not see you followed except by those who are our lowest [in rank]﴾, meaning that if the nobles had followed him, they would have agreed with him, and that following the poor is a hindrance for them from that, as they stated explicitly in their saying: ﴿Shall we believe in you while the lowest follow you?﴾ So that was a request from them to drive them away, and a conditioning of their faith upon that, out of disdain at being aligned with them in one row, may he be blessed and granted peace.

﴿Indeed, they are going to meet their Lord﴾ is a justification for his refusal (ﷺ) to drive them away, that is: indeed they are triumphant in the Hereafter by meeting Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. It is as if it was said: I will not drive them away nor distance them from my assembly, because they are brought near in the presence of holiness. The mention of the attribute of lordship is for the sake of cultivating the obligation of caring for them and the necessity of refraining from driving them away. Or it means that they are believers in this world in meeting their Lord, certain of it, knowing that they will undoubtedly meet Him, so how could I drive them away? Interpreting it to mean that they will meet Him and He will recompense them for what is in their hearts of sound, firm faith, as has become clear to me, or otherwise, of what you know them by, namely that their faith is built on surface opinion without examination and reflection. But it is not incumbent upon me to split open their hearts and learn the secret of that from them, so that I might drive them away if the matter is as you claim. The certainty of the consequence of Allah's wrath, the Mighty and Majestic, upon driving them away, as will come, forbids this.

Also, they only said that their following of you is according to surface opinion without reflection and contemplation, and this can hardly be a basis for driving them away in this world or for being held to account in the Hereafter. Its utmost is that they would not be at the rank of the certain, and the claim that building faith on apparent opinion leads to renouncing it upon reflection, so it is as if they said: they followed you without reflection, so they will not remain steadfast upon your religion, rather they will apostatize from it, is an obvious far-fetched claim.

﴿But I see you as a people who are ignorant﴾ of everything that ought to be known, and included in it is their ignorance of the meeting with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and of their station with Him, and of the necessity of driving them away resulting in Allah's wrath, as will come, and of the feebleness of their opinion in requesting that, and making their faith conditional upon it out of disdain at being aligned with them in one row, and their assumption that baseness is by poverty and nobility by wealth. And the choice of the verbal form is to indicate renewal and continuation. Or it means: you act foolishly toward the believers by attributing to them baseness.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 30:

﴿And O my people, who would help me against Allah?﴾ [who would] repel the descent of His wrath upon me ﴿if I drive them away﴾. For that is a matter that cannot be averted, since driving them away is an injustice that necessarily brings about the descent of wrath, decisively. It was not stated explicitly, as an indication that it is too evident to need explanation, especially since what hints at their condition has been mentioned beforehand. It is as if it were said: "Who would repel from me the anger of Allah, Exalted is He, if I drive them away, when they stand in such a station of honour and nearness?" As indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Will you not then remember?﴾ That is: will you persist in the ignorance mentioned above, so that you do not remember what has been said of their condition, until you recognize that what you are doing is far from being right? And because this reason is presented in a particular way, clearly indicating the obligation to refrain from driving them away, it has been set apart from the previous reasoning and introduced with "O my people."

And I do not say to you, when I claim prophethood (nubuwwah), "With me are the treasuries of God." That is, His provision and wealth, so that you might infer from their absence that I am lying, by your saying: "We see no superiority of yours over us; rather, we think you are liars." For prophethood is too exalted to be attained through worldly means, and claiming it has nothing to do with claiming wealth and status.

"Nor do I know the unseen (al-ghayb)." That is, in my saying "I am a clear warner to you" and "I fear for you the punishment of a painful day," I do not claim knowledge of the unseen, so that you should hasten to deny and dismiss me.

"Nor do I say I am an angel," so that you would say: "We see you only as a human like ourselves." For humanity is not an obstacle to prophethood but one of its foundations. The meaning is that you have taken the lack of these three things as a pretext for denying me, while in fact I do not claim any of them, and what I do claim is not connected to any of them, but relates only to the inner excellences by which the ranks of humans differ.

"Nor do I say," by way of accommodating you as you say, "to those whom your eyes look down upon." That is, those you disdain and despise. The verb is from (zarāhu idhā ʿābahu), "he found fault with him." Attributing the looking-down to their eyes, in view of their saying "We see none following you except our lowest," is either to indicate that this is due to the shortness of their vision, and if they had reflected on their situation they would not have done this; that is, I do not say concerning those whom you have deemed base for their poverty, from among the believers, that "God will not grant them any good," in this world or the next. For perhaps God will grant them the good of both abodes.

If you say: this statement is not one the disbelievers deny, nor one they suppose he (ﷺ) might make, either originally or as a consequence, unlike the claim of angelhood, knowledge of the unseen, and possession of the treasuries, which he (ﷺ) denied of himself by way of disavowal and disassociation. Then on what basis is his denial of this joined to his denial of those? I say: it is because both denials refute their false analogy, which they clung to earlier. For they claimed that prophethood entails the aforementioned matters, and that it cannot be attained by one who lacks those qualities, since finding its place and seizing its opportunities is not the custom of the base. So he (ﷺ) answered by denying all of that together. It is as if he said: I do not say that the existence of those things is a necessity of prophethood, nor that the lack of wealth and status is an obstacle to good.

"God knows best what is in their souls," that is, of faith. The mention of only the denial of the stated saying, although he (ﷺ) is certain that God, glorified is He, will grant them great good in both abodes, and that they are in firm certainty of faith, is done in accordance with the custom of fairness toward the people, and in sufficiency by opposing their words, and as guidance (p-204) for them toward the path of right guidance: that it is fitting for everyone not to pronounce a judgment except on what he knows with certainty, and to build his affairs upon clear evidence, and not to speculate about what he has no manifest proof for.

"Then indeed I would be, if I said that, among the wrongdoers" — that is, by degrading their rank and diminishing their rights, or among those who wrong themselves by this, since its burden returns to themselves. In this there is an allusion that they are wrongdoers in their disdain and their looking down upon them. It was also said: if I said any of what was mentioned, namely claiming angelhood, knowledge of the unseen, and possession of the treasuries, which is far-fetched, because the consequence of those statements suffices without needing the reason that one would be counted among the wrongdoers.

﴿They said, "O Noah, you have argued with us"﴾ (khāṣamtanā), ﴿"and you have multiplied our arguing"﴾ (fa-aktharta jidālanā). That is, you prolonged it, or you brought it in all its forms. The multiplying of argument is realized only after its basis has occurred, which is why it is linked to the preceding clause with the particle fa- ("then"). Or it means that you intended it and so multiplied it, as in His saying: ﴿"When you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah"﴾. When he (ﷺ) refuted them, presented clear proofs whose meanings were evident and arguments that the intellects receive with acceptance, and silenced them by rejecting their false doubts, their stratagems were exhausted and their pretexts failed them. They said: ﴿"Then bring us what you threaten us with"﴾ of the punishment alluded to in his saying, "Indeed I fear for you the punishment of a painful day" (11:26), on the assumption that the intended meaning of "the day" is not the Day of Resurrection. ﴿"If you are one of the truthful"﴾ in what you say.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 33:

﴿He said: "Only Allah will bring it to you, if He wills"﴾. That is, this matter is not entrusted to me, nor is it within my power; rather, Allah will take charge of it, the One whom you have disbelieved in and disobeyed. He will bring it to you, sooner or later, if His will, which follows wisdom (hikmah), is attached to it. There is in this, as is evident, a magnification (tahwil) of what is promised. It is as if it were said: bringing it about is a matter beyond the scope of human capacities, and only Allah, Mighty and Majestic, does it. ﴿And you cannot escape Him﴾, by fleeing or by repelling, as you repel me in speech.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 34:**

﴿And my counsel will not benefit you﴾. *Nusḥ* (sincere counsel) is a comprehensive term covering everything in speech or action around which good revolves. Its reality is the purifying of the will to do good and the guiding toward it. Its opposite is *ghishsh* (deceit). It has also been said: it is informing someone of the place of error so that it may be avoided, and of the place of right guidance so that it may be followed. ﴿If I desire to counsel you﴾ is a conditional clause whose apodosis has been omitted, because what preceded it indicates it. The estimated sense is: "If I desire to counsel you, my counsel will not benefit you." This clause is evidence for what was omitted from the apodosis of His words, exalted is He: ﴿If God desires to lead you astray﴾. The estimated sense is: "If God desires to lead you astray, then if I desire to counsel you, my counsel will not benefit you." This is according to what the Basrans (*al-Baṣriyyūn*, the grammarians of Basra) held, namely that the apodosis (*jawāb*, the consequent of the conditional) may not precede the condition (*al-shart*). As for the Kufans (*al-Kūfiyyūn*, the grammarians of Kufa), who held that it is permissible, then His words, exalted and high, ﴿and my counsel will not benefit you﴾ are the apodosis of the first condition, and the clause is the apodosis of the second condition. In either estimation, the apodosis is linked to the first condition, and its being linked to it is dependent upon the second condition.

This statement is connected to their words: "You have disputed with us and multiplied our disputation" (ﷺ) uttered it, to show his inability to compel them with proofs and clear evidences because of their persistence in obstinacy, and to announce that what had preceded from him was not by way of argument and contention, but by way of counsel to them and compassion for them, and that he had spared no effort in guiding them to the truth and directing them to its clear path, and in purifying his counsel for them. However, this would not benefit them at the time of God's will to lead them astray. The restriction of the non-benefit of counsel to His will, although it is certainly realized, is for the announcement that his counsel was concurrent with the will and with concern for it, and in order to achieve the correspondence between that and what stands opposite it of His will, exalted is He, to lead them astray. The mention is limited to the mere will to lead astray, not to the leading astray itself, since He did not say "if God leads you astray," for the sake of emphasis on the overpowering majesty of His Presence, exalted and high. This indicates that his counsel, concurrent with concern for them, does not profit them when God, glorified is He, merely wills to lead them astray, so how much more so when that is realized and created in them. The insertion of (*kāna*, "was") indicates that God's will precedes in time just as it precedes in rank, and indicates its renewal and continuity.

What relates to their words "bring us what you promise us" was placed before this statement, namely His words: ﴿Only God will bring it to you, if He wills﴾, as a response to them from the outset, and as a recording against them of the descent of punishment, together with what it contains of the connection of the answer to the question. In it is evidence that God's will may validly be connected to leading astray, and that the opposite of His will does not occur.

It has also been said: the meaning of ﴿(that He lead you astray)﴾ is that He destroy you, from *ghawā al-faṣīl ghawan*, when the young camel is bloated and perishes.

﴿He is your Lord﴾, your Creator and the Owner of your affair, ﴿and to Him you will be returned﴾, so He will recompense you for your deeds without doubt.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 35:

﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾ Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "It refers to Nuh (peace be upon him)." The meaning is: "Rather, do the people of Nuh say, 'Nuh has invented what he has brought, attributing it to Allah, Mighty and Majestic'?" Say, O Nuh, ﴿If I have invented it,﴾ by mere supposition, ﴿then upon me is my crime (ijram).﴾ That is, my sin and the burden of my crime, which is the earning of sin (kasb al-dhanb). It has also been read in the plural form (ijrami/ajrami as an alternative reading, meaning "my sins"), and the earlier scholars supported this by explaining it as "my sins" (athami). ﴿And I am free from what you commit (tujrimun)﴾ of your crime in ascribing the invention to me. So there is no justification for your turning away from me and your hostility towards me.

Muqatil said: "It refers to Muhammad (ﷺ)." The meaning is: "Rather, do the polytheists of Makkah say, 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) has invented the report of Nuh'?" It seems that it was brought in the midst of the narrative when a portion of it was being related, to affirm its truth, to confirm its occurrence, and to arouse the listeners' desire to hear it, especially since a group of it was narrated that is connected to what took place between him (ﷺ) and his people of argument, while another group remained independent and connected to their punishment.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 36:

﴿And it was revealed to Noah that none of your people will believe except those who have already believed.﴾ That is, those who persist in disbelief. This is a declaration to him ﷺ that they will not believe, and an announcement that their belief is like an impossibility whose expectation is not valid. ﴿Except those who have already believed⦆ — except those from whom there has already been found what was expected of their belief. This exception follows the pattern of His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿except what has already passed﴾, and ﴿So do not grieve over what they have been doing﴾, meaning: do not grieve with the grief of one who is wretched and humbled, nor be distressed by what they were engaged in of denial, mockery and harm during this long period, for their actions have come to an end and the time for retribution against them has arrived.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 37:

﴿And build the ark﴾ while being [kept] ﴿under Our eyes﴾, i.e., under Our protection and care, as if with him there were guardians and watchers from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, who guard him with their eyes from the transgression of the disbelievers and from deviation in the craft; ﴿and by Our revelation﴾ to you of how you are to make it, and Our teaching and inspiration.

From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: he did not know how to build the ark, so Allah the Exalted revealed to him that he should make it like the breast of a bird. The imperative here denotes obligation, since there is no way to preserve the soul from drowning except by it, so it is obligatory just as preservation is obligatory. The definite article (al-) may be for a known reference, meaning that this is directed by Allah's revelation to him, peace be upon him, that He would destroy them by drowning and would save him and those with him by means of something he would make by His command and revelation, of such-and-such a shape and such-and-such a name; or it may be for the genus.

It was said: he built it, peace be upon him, in two years; and it was said: in four hundred years. It was made of teak wood and was made in three decks: in the first deck were carried the wild animals, predators and creeping creatures; in the middle deck, the beasts and livestock; and in the upper deck, the human race, he and those with him, along with what they needed of provisions. He also carried the body of Adam, peace be upon him. It was said: he placed in the first the beasts and wild animals, in the second the humans, and in the upper the birds. It was said: its length was three hundred cubits, its width fifty cubits, and its height thirty cubits. Al-Hasan said: its length was one thousand two hundred cubits, and its width six hundred cubits.

It is also said that the disciples said to Jesus, peace be upon him: "If only you would send us a man who witnessed the ship, so he could tell us about it." He set off with them until they reached a mound of dust. He took a handful of that dust and said: "Do you know who this is?" They said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "This is Ka'b ibn Ham." He then struck it with his staff and said: "Rise by Allah's permission!" And behold, he was standing, shaking the dust from his head, and he had grown white-haired. Jesus, peace be upon him, said to him: "Is this how you died?" He said: "No, I died while I was young, but I thought it was the Hour, so from that point I turned gray." He said: "Tell us about Noah's ship." He said: "Its length was one thousand two hundred cubits and its width six hundred cubits, and it had three levels: one level for the beasts and wild animals, one level for the humans, and one level for the birds." Then he said: "Return, by Allah's permission, as you were," and he returned to dust.

﴿And do not address Me concerning those who have done wrong﴾, i.e., do not argue with Me about them, nor ask Me to ward off punishment from them. In this there is an emphasis that is absent if it were said: "do not ask Me about them." Since the statement contains something that hints at causation, the reason is emphasized, so it is said: ﴿Indeed, they are to be drowned﴾, i.e., they are decreed to be drowned; the decree has already passed and the pen has dried, so there is no way to avert it, and the proof has been established against them, so there remains only that they be made an example for those who take warning and a lesson for others.

﴿وَيَصْنَعُ الفُلْكَ﴾ "And he was building the ship." This is a narration of a past situation, meant to bring its remarkable image before the mind. It is also said that the implied sense is "And he began to build the ship," or "he set about building it," and that "began" was omitted, leaving "was building." Either way, it suits the continuity understood from the clause that serves as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) for his pronoun, namely His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whenever a company of his people passed by him, they mocked him﴾, meaning they ridiculed him for building the ship. This was either because they did not know what a ship was, nor how to use it and benefit from it, so they marvelled at it and mocked him. Or it was because he was building it in a barren desert, in the farthest place from water, and at a time of his might, a great might. They used to laugh among themselves and say: "O Noah, you have become a carpenter after you were a prophet!" It is also said that he (peace be upon him) used to warn them of drowning, but when his stay among them lengthened and they saw from him neither a sign nor a trace of it, they considered it among the impossible. Then, when they saw him occupied with the means of deliverance from it, they did what they did. The core of all of this is their denial that his work could have a praiseworthy outcome, together with the great hardships that he bore, which were nearly unbearable, and their deeming him ignorant (istijhāl) of this matter, peace be upon him.

﴿قالَ إنْ تَسْخَرُوا مِنّا﴾ "He said: If you mock us," considering us ignorant (mustajhilīn) in what we are engaged in, ﴿فَإنّا نَسْخَرُ مِنكُمْ﴾ "then we shall mock you," that is, we shall deem you ignorant in what you are upon. The application of "mocking" to him is by way of mushākalah (rhetorical correspondence of wording). The pronoun in "minnā" (from us) is plural either because their mockery of him (ﷺ) is also mockery of the believers, or because they used to mock them as well, but it was sufficient to mention their mockery of him (ﷺ). For this reason, all of them became subject to retribution in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿then we shall mock you﴾ ... etc., so the speech is balanced on both sides. The linking of his (ﷺ) deeming them ignorant to what they did of mockery is in terms of his manifesting it and addressing them directly (ﷺ), as ignorant in what they do and leave undone. This is a consistent matter with no connection to their mockery of them. However, he (ﷺ) did not rush to manifest it, following the path of good character. He manifested it only as a recompense for what they had done after the great and the small (i.e., after every kind of harm). Their mockery was continuous and renewed according to the renewal of their passing by him, and he did not answer them each time. Otherwise it would have been said: "And he would say: If you mock us..." etc. Rather, he answered them only after their harm reached its utmost limit, as the resumptive construction (istināf) indicates. It is as though a questioner asked: "What did Noah do when they reached this extent with him?" and it was answered: "He said: If you mock us," that is, if you attribute us to ignorance in what we are occupied with of preparation and direct engagement in the means of deliverance from the punishment, and you mock us because of it, ﴿then we shall mock you﴾, that is, we attribute you to it in what you are in of turning away when seeking refuge through faith and obedience, and of persistence in disbelief and sins, and of exposing yourselves to the causes of the descent of the wrath of God, Exalted is He, of which your deeming us ignorant and your mockery of us are among the parts. The comparison in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿as you mock﴾ is either in mere certainty and occurrence, or in recurrence and repetition, according to what proceeded from a company after a company, and not in the modes and states that befit the dignity of the Prophet (ﷺ). Both matters are realized at present. It is also said: "We shall mock you in the future with a mockery like your mockery, when drowning falls upon you in this world and burning in the Hereafter." Perhaps its meaning is: "We shall treat you as the treatment of one who does that," because mockery itself is hardly fitting for the station of prophethood. Yet even so, this has no soundness, because their condition at that time was not something unsuited to mockery, or what is similar to it. So reflect.

﴿So you will come to know who will be given a punishment that disgraces him﴾, which is the punishment of drowning, ﴿and upon whom will descend﴾ like the descent of a debt that has fallen due, ﴿a lasting punishment﴾, which is the lasting punishment of the Fire. This is a forceful threat. The phrase "who" (man) refers to them, and it may be an interrogative in the position of the nominative (ḥayyiz al-rafʿ), or a relative pronoun in the position of the accusative (maḥall al-naṣb) governed by "you will know" (taʿlamūn). What follows it fills the role of two objects, or of one object if knowledge (al-ʿilm) is taken in the sense of recognition (al-maʿrifa).

Since the basis of their mockery was their considering him (ﷺ) a fool for undergoing the severe hardships, in case of what would hardly fall within the bounds of possibility in their opinion, namely the flood, and for enduring the difficulties of building the ship, and they used to regard it as a punishment, it was said: after their considering him a fool, "So you will come to know who will be given the punishment". The meaning is: what I am engaged in does not contain a punishment that will reach me; so you will come to know who is the one being punished. Knowledge, after their considering him a fool, indeed hit its target. Describing the punishment as disgracing is because mockery and ridicule usually bring disgrace and shame. Mentioning the descent of the lasting punishment is for the sake of exaggeration in the threat, and specifying it as "like a debt that has fallen due" and the expression "will come upon him" for the first are in the highest degree of eloquence.

(p-208)﴿until, when Our command came﴾. *Hatta* (until) is the particle with which a sentence is begun. It has entered upon the conditional sentence, and it is nonetheless the limit (*ghayah*) for His words, "and he would fashion," and what lies between them is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in it. "And they would mock him" is the response (*jawab*) to *kullama* (whenever). It has been said that it is a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*) on the assumption of a questioner's question, as we have mentioned. It has also been said that it is the response itself, and "they would mock him" is a substitute (*badal*) for "passed by" (*marra*), or a qualifier (*sifah*) for "chiefs" (*mala'*). You have known that the correct view is the first, because the purpose is to show the extent of their harming him ﷺ and his bearing their harm, not his hastening (ﷺ) to answer them whenever something from their speech that harmed him occurred.

﴿and the oven (*tannur*) boiled over﴾. Water gushed forth from it and rose violently, just as a cooking pot boils with its bubbling. The *tannur* is the bread oven, and this is the view of the majority.

It has been narrated that it was said to Nuh, upon him be peace: "When you see water boiling forth from the oven, board the ship, you and whoever is with you." When the water gushed forth, his wife informed him, and he boarded. It has also been said that it was the oven of Adam, upon him be peace, and it was made of stone, and it passed to Nuh. The water gushed from it, though it is the furthest thing from water, by way of breaking the customary course (*kharq al-'adah*). It was in Kufa, at the place of its mosque, on the right of one entering from the side of the Gate of Kindah. The building of the ship took place at that place, or in India, or at a place in Syria called 'Ayn Warda.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and 'Ikrimah and al-Zuhri that the *tannur* is the surface of the earth.

It is narrated from Qatadah that it is the most noble place on earth, that is, its highest part.

It is narrated from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that "the oven boiled over" means the dawn broke.

﴿We said: "Carry in it"﴾, that is, in the ship, and this is the response of *idha* (when). ﴿of every kind﴾, that is, of every species that is necessary on the earth. ﴿two mates﴾. The *zawj* (mate) is that which has a counterpart of its own kind, so the male is a mate to the female just as she is a mate to him. It may also be applied to the two of them together, in which case it is opposed to the single (*fard*). To remove that possibility it was said: ﴿two﴾, each of them being a mate to the other. It has been read with the construct (*idafah*). This was placed before his family and the rest of the believers because he was foremost in what he was commanded to carry, since it requires him to engage in the work of distinguishing one from another and specifying the mates, for it is narrated that he ﷺ said: "My Lord, how shall I carry from every kind two, two?" So Allah, exalted is He, gathered to him the beasts of prey, the birds, and others, and he began striking with his hands into each kind, so the male fell into his right hand and the female into his left, and he placed them in the ship. As for humans, they enter the ark by their own choice, so the sense of carrying is lightened in their case. Or, because the ship is carried only through the handling of humans, and they enter it only after carrying it themselves.

﴿and your family﴾ is conjoined to "two mates," or to "two." What is meant is his wife, his sons, and their wives. ﴿except him against whom the word has already gone forth﴾, that he is among the drowned because of their wrongdoing, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and do not plead with Me concerning those who have done wrong﴾, and so on, to the end of the verse. What is meant by him is his son Kan'an and his mother Wa'ilah, for both of them were disbelievers. The exception is disjunctive (*munqati'*) if by "family" is meant those who are family in faith, and this is the apparent meaning, as you will know. It is connected (*muttasil*) if by it is meant those who are family by kinship. Knowledge of their conditions and the investigation of their deeds suffices for the soundness of the exception. *'Ala* (against) was used because what has preceded harms them, just as the *lam* (for) was used for what benefits them, in His mighty and majestic saying: ﴿and certainly Our word has preceded for Our servants, the messengers﴾, and His saying: ﴿indeed those for whom the best (reward) from Us has preceded﴾.

﴿and whoever believed﴾ from among others. The singular is used for the family among them because of the stated exception, and the singular form is chosen for "believed" in keeping with the wording of "whoever" (*man*), to indicate their fewness, as His mighty saying expresses it: ﴿and none believed with him except a few﴾. It has been said that they were eight: Nuh, upon him be peace, his family, his three sons, and their wives.

It is narrated from Ibn Ishaq that they were ten: five men and five women. It is also narrated from him that they were ten besides their wives. It has been said that they were seventy-two men and women, and Nuh's sons were Sam, Ham, and Yafith, with their wives, so the total is seventy-eight, half of them men and half women. The consideration of "with him" (*ma'iyyah*) in their belief is to hint at being with him in the place of security and salvation.

"وَقالَ" — that is, Noah, peace be upon him, said to those believers who were with him, as his words indicate: ﴿Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ Had the pronoun referred back to God Most High, it would have been fitting to say: "Indeed, your Lord." This may have been after the loading into the ship of what he had been commanded to carry of the pairs, as if it were said: "So he carried the pairs, or he put them into the ship, and said to the believers: ﴿Embark therein﴾," just as its like will come in His words, Most High: ﴿(while it runs with them)﴾. Riding (rukub) means being raised above something that is in motion, and it is transitive by itself; its use here with the word "fi" (in) is not because what was commanded was that they be inside it rather than above it, as has been thought. Rather, the most apparent reports say that he (peace be upon him) placed the wild animals and their like in the lowest deck, the cattle in the middle, and he and those with him rode in the upper part. Rather, it is for the sake of observing the aspect of place and location within the ship. The secret in this is that the meaning of riding is being above something that has motion, either voluntary motion, as with an animal, or compelled motion, as with a ship, a wheel, and the like. When it is used of the first, it gives the object its original due, so one says: "I rode the horse," and to this belongs the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿and the horses and mules and donkeys, that you may ride them﴾. If it is used of the second, it hints at the place-character of the object by means of the word "fi" (in), so one says: "I rode in the ship," and to this belongs the noble verse, and the saying of the Mighty and Majestic, speaking: ﴿So when they embark in the ship﴾, and the saying of the Most High: ﴿So they both set out until, when they embarked in the ship, he made a hole in it﴾.

"Bismillah" is related to "irkabu" (embark) and is a circumstantial clause (hal) from its subject, meaning: embark, mentioning the name of God Most High, or saying "in the name of God." ﴿Its course and its anchoring﴾ is in the accusative as an adverb of time, meaning: at the time of its running and its anchoring, on the basis that both are nouns of time, or they are verbal nouns like "the running" and "the anchoring" with the time omitted, as in your saying: "I will come to you the rights of the star." Or they are nouns of place, governed by what is in "bismillah" of the meaning of a verb, or by the intention of saying. It is permissible that "bismillah majriha wa mursaha" be an independent sentence, consisting of a subject and predicate, in the position of a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of the ship, meaning: embark therein, running and anchoring by the name of God, in the sense of a decree, like His saying, Most High: "Enter them, abiding therein." Or it is an abrupt sentence on the basis that Noah commanded them to embark therein, then informed them that its running and its anchoring are in the name of God Most High; so these two would be two statements of his, peace be upon him. It was said: when he, peace be upon him, wished to set it running, he would say: "In the name of God," and it would run; and when he wished to anchor it, he would say: "In the name of God," and it would anchor. It is also permissible that the word "name" be superfluous, as in His saying: ﴿a provision for their wives, a year's maintenance without expulsion﴾; and then "the name of peace upon you both," and "God" is intended to mean its running and its anchoring, that is, by His power and His command. It was read "mujriha wa mursiha" in the form of the active participle, in the genitive position as two attributes of God, Mighty and Majestic; and "majraha wa marsaha" with an open mim, as two verbal nouns, or two nouns of time, or two nouns of place, from "jara" and "rasa."

﴿Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving﴾ of sins and faults, ﴿Merciful﴾ to His servants, and for this reason He saved you from this calamity and the general disaster. Had it not been for that, He would not have done it. In this is an indication that their deliverance was not because of their deserving it, but purely by the grace of God, Glorified is He, His forgiveness and His mercy, according to the view of the People of the Sunna.

﴿And it runs with them﴾ is related to an omitted element indicated by the command to board. That is: they boarded it, saying the name of God, and it ran with them, enveloping them ﴿amid waves like mountains﴾. The "wave" (mawj) is what rises from the water when it is agitated, and each wave of that is like a mountain in its height and its piling up. As for what has been said, that the water covered everything between heaven and earth and the ship ran within it like a fish, this is not established. The well-known view is that the water rose above the highest mountains by fifteen cubits, or forty cubits. Even if that is sound, this running was before the matter grew severe, as is indicated by God's words: ﴿And Noah called to his son﴾. For that can only be imagined before the connection between the ship and the land was cut, since at that point it would be possible for what took place between Noah, upon him be peace, and his son to occur, namely the exchange of calling him to the ship and his answer that he would seek refuge on a mountain. It was also read as (ibnaha wa-ibnahu), with the alif omitted, on the basis that the pronoun refers to his wife, who was his stepson (rabib). As for what is said, that he was born of an illegitimate union, based on God's words ﴿but they both betrayed them﴾, this is a grave accusation of something whose enormity cannot be measured, for the dignity of the prophets, may God's blessings and peace be upon them, is too exalted to be pointed at with the finger of slander. The betrayal meant is betrayal in religion. It was also read as (ibnah), in the lamentation form (nudba, a mournful address), and because it is a quoted utterance (hikaya), the letter of the ending was permitted to be dropped. You should know that the calling to the ship does not suit this, for it is explicit that despair had not yet occurred in his life. ﴿And he was in a place apart﴾, that is, a place in which he had isolated himself from his father, his brothers and his people, such that the address "board" did not reach him, and he needed the aforementioned call. It was also said: "in a place apart from the disbelievers," having separated himself from them, and Noah thought that he intended to part from them, which is why he invited him to the ship. It was also said: he was feigning to his father, so he thought him a believer. It was also said: he knew that he was a disbeliever up to that time, but upon him be peace, thought that at the sight of those terrors he would desist from what he was upon and accept faith. It was also said: what preceded in God's words ﴿except those against whom the word has already gone forth﴾ was not explicit in including his son, but was rather like something ambiguous, and paternal compassion moved him toward that.

﴿O my son﴾ is read with a fatha on the ya', by limiting it to the alif that replaces the ya' of possession in your saying "ya bunayya" (O my little son). It was also read with a kasra on the ya', by limiting it to the ya' of possession, or the ya' fell and the alif fell because of the meeting of two sukun, since the ra' after them is sakin.

﴿Board with us﴾: Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read with idgham (assimilation) of the ba' into the mim, because they are close in point of articulation. The verb "board" was used without mention of the ship, to make it clear and to indicate the narrowness of the situation, where the choking precedes the recitation, while the sense of "with" dispenses with that. ﴿And do not be with the disbelievers﴾, that is, in place: on the surface of the earth outside the ship, not in religion, even though that is among what his boarding with him, upon him be peace, requires, just as boarding with him requires that he be with him in faith. This is because he, upon him be peace, was keen to warn against destruction, so the prohibition against disbelief does not suit that.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 43:

﴿He said, "I will take refuge on a mountain that will protect me from the water."﴾ Of the mountains, ﴿that will protect me﴾ by its height ﴿from the water.﴾ He supposed that this was like other waters in the usual seasons of floods, from which one may sometimes escape by climbing to high ground. But how could he do that, when the flood had already reached the heights (al-zubā)? He was also ignorant that this flood was sent to destroy the disbelievers, and that there was no escape from it except by seeking refuge in the place of safety for the believers. Therefore, peace be upon him, he wished to make clear to his son the true state of affairs and to turn him away from that impossible idea. The apparent course would have been to respond in a way that matches his statement and addresses what he claimed about the mountain, namely that it would protect him from the water, by saying, "It will not protect you from it," which would negate the attribute of protection from it only, without addressing its negation from anything else, or negating the thing itself altogether. However, peace be upon him, when he ﴿said, "There is no protector today from the command of God"﴾, he adopted the method of generic negation (nafy al-jins, the negation of a whole class), which covers all individual instances of protectors, both in essence and in attribute, as in the saying, "There is no caller in it and no answerer," meaning, "No one among the people." This is for the sake of emphasis (mubālagha) in denying that the mountain is a protector in both of the two aspects mentioned. He added "today" to draw attention to the fact that this is not like other days in which events occur and usual calamities befall, from which one may sometimes be rescued by resorting to some ordinary means. He expressed the water, in the place where it would have been referred to by pronoun, as ﴿the command of God﴾, meaning His punishment, which was alluded to when it was said, ﴿until when Our command came﴾, in order to magnify its importance, to inspire awe about its matter, and to alert his son to his error in calling it "water," which suggests that it is like other waters from which one escapes by fleeing to some known refuges. It also gives the reason for the stated negation, for the command of God cannot be overcome, and His punishment cannot be averted. It also prepares for restricting protection to the presence of God, exalted is His protection, by the exception, as if it were said, "There is no protector from the command of God except Him." It was said, ﴿except for him on whom He has mercy﴾, to magnify His sublime station by means of ambiguity followed by explanation, and by generality followed by detail, and to indicate that His mercy is the cause in this matter, in accordance with the fact that His mercy precedes His wrath. All of this is for the utmost care of him, peace be upon him, in securing what he hoped for, namely the salvation of his son, by explaining the gravity of the calamity, cutting off his vain hopes, turning him away from excuses that would avail him nothing, and guiding him to seek refuge in the true Refuge, exalted is His protection. It was also said: there is no place that protects from the command of God except the place of the one on whom God has mercy, which is the Ark (al-fulk). It was also said: the meaning of "no protector" is "no one having protection, except him on whom God, exalted, has mercy."

﴿And the wave came between them﴾, meaning between Noah and his son, so that what was between them of conversation was cut off, not between his son and the mountain. This is because of His words, exalted is He, ﴿and he was among the drowned﴾, since this follows only from the wave intervening between him, peace be upon him, and his son, not between him and the mountain, because the mountain was far from being a protector, even if no wave came between him and the one who sought refuge in it. In this there is an indication of the destruction of all the other disbelievers in the most eloquent manner, so that this became a matter of certain occurrence that needed no explanation. The use of "kāna" (was) rather than "ṣāra" (became) is an emphasis on his being among them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 44:

﴿And it was said: "O earth, swallow your water"﴾. That is: soak it up (inshafi). The verb ibla'i (swallow) is borrowed for it from the way an animal swallows what it eats, to indicate that this is not like the usual, gradual soaking up (al-nashf al-mu'tad al-tadriji). ﴿Your water﴾: that is, the water of the Flood that is on your surface, not the waters that are customary in it from springs and rivers. It is expressed as "water" after it was expressed in what preceded as "the command of God, the Exalted," because the context is one of diminishing and reduction, not one of magnification and awe. ﴿And, O sky, withhold﴾: that is, hold back from sending down rain. It is said: "the sky cleared (aqla'at al-sama')" when its rain ceased, and "the fever cleared (aqla'at al-humma)" meaning it subsided. ﴿And the water subsided﴾: that is, the water between the sky and the earth decreased. ﴿And the matter was decreed﴾: that is, what God, the Exalted, had promised Noah was accomplished, namely the destruction of his people and the salvation of him and his family; or the matter was completed. ﴿And it came to rest﴾: that is, the Ark settled ﴿on al-Judi﴾, which is a mountain at Mosul, or in Syria, or at Amul.

It is related that he, peace be upon him, boarded the Ark on the tenth of Rajab and disembarked from it on the tenth of Muharram, so he fasted that day in gratitude, and it became a Sunnah.

﴿And it was said: "Away with the wrongdoing people!"﴾: that is, destruction for them. The mention of the attribute of wrongdoing indicates that it is the reason for their destruction, and it serves as a reminder of God, the Exalted's, words that preceded: ﴿And do not address Me concerning those who did wrong; indeed, they are to be drowned﴾. The noble verse has reached the furthest of the degrees of miraculousness and has taken hold of the forelock of the choicest excellences. Skilled and meticulous scholars have undertaken to detail it, and by my life, that is beyond what the describers can describe. It is therefore fitting for us to be brief in this matter, and to leave the matter to the reflection of people of understanding. And God has the knowledge of the Book.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 45:

﴿And Noah called out to his Lord﴾. That is, he intended this, as is shown by the particle "fa" (so, then) in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so he said, "My Lord, indeed my son is of my family"﴾, and You had promised me to save them within the command to load them into the ark. Or the calling was in its literal sense, and the "fa" serves to detail what was summarized in it. ﴿And indeed Your promise is the truth﴾. That is, Your promise of that, or: indeed every promise You make is true, admitting no failure; thus the specific promise in question enters into it as a primary instance. ﴿And You are the most just of judges﴾, because You are the most knowing of them and the most just of them; or, You are more wise than those endowed with wisdom, since the judge in respect of wisdom is like the armored one in respect of armor. This supplication of his, peace be upon him, followed the manner of the supplication of Job, peace be upon him: ﴿When he called to his Lord, "Indeed, adversity has touched me, and You are the most merciful of the merciful"﴾.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 11, verse 46:**

﴿He said, "O Noah!"﴾ Since his supplication, peace be upon him, was based on reminding Allah, exalted is His remembrance, of His promise, and that promise was based on Kan'an being of his family, the first thing negated was that he was of his family, through the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, he is not of your family.﴾ That is: he is not of them at all, because the basis of family membership is religious kinship, and there is no connection between the believer and the disbeliever. Or it means: he is not of your family whom I commanded you to carry in the ship, since he was excluded from them by the exception. Under both interpretations, he is not among those who were promised deliverance. Then the reason for his not being of them was given by way of an explanatory resumption (*istinaf tahqiqi*, a clause that resumes the discourse to confirm and explain), through the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, his deed is unrighteous.﴾ The original form is *innahu dhu 'amalin ghayri salih* (indeed he is one whose deed is unrighteous), but the deed itself was made the subject for emphasis, as in the verse of al-Khansa':

*Fa-innama hiya iqbalun wa-idbaru*

*For it is but advance and retreat.*

And "unrighteous" (*ghayru salih*) is used in place of "corrupt" (*fasid*), either because the corrupt may sometimes be applied to what has been corrupted while it is by nature capable of being righteous, and so it is not explicit for what is purely corrupt, such as murder and injustices; or to hint that the deliverance of those who were saved was only because of their righteousness. Al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read: *innahu 'amila ghayra salih* (indeed he did an unrighteous deed), that is, *'amalan ghayra salih* (an unrighteous deed, as an absolute object, *maf'ul mutlaq*).

Since his supplication, peace be upon him, was based on what was mentioned, namely the belief that Kan'an was of his family, and since that has been negated and confirmed by explaining its cause, the prohibition against asking for his deliverance was made to follow from this. However, the prohibition was expressed in a general form that includes this case by primary inclusion. So it was said: ﴿So do not ask Me,⦆ that is: once you have come to understand the clear reality, ﴿about that of which you have no knowledge⦆ — that is, a request whose fulfilment you do not know with certainty to be right and in accordance with wisdom, if *ma* refers to the thing asked for, which is the object of the verb "ask"; or a request you do not know to be right, if *ma* refers to the verbal noun, which is an absolute object. In that case the prohibition explicitly applies to both what is known to be corrupt and what is of doubtful status. It is also permissible that the meaning be: about that of which you have no knowledge that it is right or wrong, in which case the prohibition applies to what is of doubtful status, and the status of what is known to be corrupt is understood from it by the stronger implication. Under both interpretations, it is general and includes the matter at hand, as we have explained.

As you see, this is clear evidence that his calling out to his Lord, mighty and exalted is He, was not an inquiry about the reason his son was not saved, despite the prior promise to save his family, and that son being of them, as has been said. For the prohibition against inquiring about what one does not know is not in accord with wisdom, since not knowing something is a reason to inquire about it, not to abandon it. Rather, it was a supplication from him for his son's deliverance when the waves came between them. He did not yet know of his destruction, either because the waves brought him close to the ship through the crashing of the billows, or because they brought the ship close to him. It was also said: or because he was saved on the summit of a mountain. But the mention of the promise in the supplication refutes this, since the promise was specific to deliverance in the ship. And the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿There is no protector today from the command of Allah except for those upon whom He has mercy⦆ show that the mere separation of the waves between them does not necessitate his destruction, let alone knowledge of it, because it is evident that Allah could preserve him by His mercy. He had been promised the deliverance of his family, and his son was not openly disbelieving, as we have explained, so it is not permissible for him, peace be upon him, to invite his son to the ship or to ask his Lord to save him. His son's withdrawal from him, peace be upon him, and his intention to take refuge on the mountain, is not explicit proof of persistence in disbelief, because it is evident that this may have been out of ignorance that deliverance is confined to the ship, and his supposition that the mountain functions in the same way, or out of aversion to being confined in the ship. Rather, his words, ﴿I will betake myself to a mountain that will protect me from the water⦆, after Noah, peace be upon him, had said to him, ﴿and do not be with the disbelievers,⦆ perhaps gave him hope regarding his faith, since he did not say, "I will be with them," or "we will take refuge," or "it will protect us." For singling himself out in attributing the two actions mentioned perhaps indicates his separation from the disbelievers, his withdrawal from them, and his compliance with some of what Noah, peace be upon him, had commanded him. However, if he, peace be upon him, had reflected on his son's situation with due reflection, and examined his conditions in everything he did and left undone, he would not have been uncertain that he was not a believer and that he was the one excluded from his family. For this reason it was said: ﴿I admonish you lest you be among the ignorant,⦆ and by this the leaving of what is better was expressed.

It was also read: *fa-la tas'alnin* (without the pronominal *ya'* of possession, *ya' al-idafa*), and with the heavy *nun* (*nun al-thaqila*), with a *ya'* and without a *ya'*.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 47:

﴿He said: "My Lord, I seek refuge in You from asking You about that of which I have no knowledge."﴾ That is: I request from You hereafter ﴿that of which I have no knowledge﴾, i.e., a thing requested whose attainment I do not know to be in accordance with wisdom; or a request whose rightness I do not know, whether it is known to be corrupt or its state is ambiguous; or a request of which I do not know whether it is right or wrong, as has passed.

This is a repentance from him, peace be upon him, for what had occurred from him. He did not say "I seek refuge in You from it" or "from that," for the sake of emphasis in repentance, to show eagerness and readiness for it, and for blessing through mentioning what Allah Most High had taught him. It is more eloquent than saying "I repent to You for asking You," because of what it contains of indicating that this matter is a dreadful and prohibited thing, from which there is no escape except by seeking refuge in Allah Most High, and that His power is insufficient to deliver one from hardships except by that. ﴿And unless You forgive me﴾ what proceeded from me of the aforementioned request, ﴿and have mercy on me﴾ by accepting my repentance, ﴿I will be among the losers﴾, having lost deeds because of that. For neglecting the thanks of Allah Most High, especially upon the arrival of such a great blessing as salvation and the destruction of enemies, and occupying oneself with what does not concern one, especially with regard to the beginnings of the deliverance of one about whom it was said: "Indeed, he is not of your family; indeed, it is unrighteous conduct" (إنَّهُ عَمَلٌ غَيْرُ صالِحٍ), and pleading to Allah Most High concerning his matter, is a transaction that is not profitable, and a manifest loss.

And the delay in mentioning this call after the narration of the command that came down upon the earth and the sky, and what follows it of the cessation of the flood, the fulfillment of the command, the settling of the ark upon al-Judi, and the invocation for destruction upon the wrongdoers, although its proper place is to be mentioned right after His saying Most High: ﴿So he was among the drowned﴾, as occurred in reality, since at that time the supplication for deliverance could be conceived, not after knowledge of destruction, is not for what has been said about it being an independent purpose of significance, namely making the kinship of religion overshadow the kinship of lineage, and that in matters of fundamental religious belief nothing should be advanced except after certainty, by analogy with what occurred in the story of the cow, in mentioning the command to slaughter it before mentioning the murdered man who is the beginning of the story. Its proper order would have been: "And when you killed a soul and disputed concerning it, and We said: Strike him with part of it" as established in its place. The change of order there is to indicate the completeness of the bad state of the Jews by enumerating their various crimes, and to repeat the rebuke upon them with each type separately. So His saying Most High: ﴿And when Moses said to his people, "Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow"﴾ ... etc., is for rebuking them for mockery, for not hastening to comply, and what follows from that; and His saying Most High: ﴿And when you killed a soul﴾ ... etc., is for rebuking the killing of a forbidden soul and what follows from it of grave matters. Had the story been related in its natural order, the purpose, which is the repetition of rebuke, would have been lost, and it would have been thought that the whole was a single rebuke.

As for what we are dealing with, it is not something in which such a subtlety can be observed at all, and what has been mentioned about making religious kinship overshadow lineal kinship... etc., is not lost even if speech were arranged in the order of occurrence. Rather, because mentioning this call, as you see, requires mentioning what passed of the answer, which requires mentioning what passed of his repentance, peace be upon him, whose mention leads to mentioning its acceptance within the command that came down upon him, peace be upon him, to descend from the ark with peace and the abundant blessings upon him and upon the believers, as will come in detail. There is no doubt that these meanings are interwoven, such that the noble verses containing them can hardly be separated from one another, and that this is only completed with the completion of the story. And there is no doubt that this happens only with the completion of the flood. Therefore the situation necessarily required mentioning its completion before this call, and that occurs at the mention of Canaan being among the drowned. For this subtlety, the excellence of the placement of the concise and eloquent expression increased. There is another benefit in it, which is the explicit statement of his destruction from the very beginning. Had the second call been mentioned right after His saying Most High: "﴿So he was among the drowned﴾", it might have been supposed from the beginning, until His saying: "﴿Indeed, he is not of your family﴾", that he would be saved through the supplication of him, peace be upon him. So his destruction was stated explicitly from the beginning. Then was mentioned the command that came down upon the earth and the sky, which is an expression of the eternal divine will's attachment to what was mentioned of the gushing forth and the cessation, and it was made clear that the command of Allah reached its place, its decree proceeded and its judgment prevailed over them, with the destruction of those who perished and the deliverance of those who were saved, upon the completion of that flood and the settling of the ark upon al-Judi. Thus the story was related up to this stage, and this was made clear with the best of clarity. Then was touched upon what occurred in the midst of that of what passed between Noah, peace be upon him, and the Lord of Majesty, exalted be His wisdom. So after his repentance, peace be upon him, its acceptance was mentioned, with His saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 48:

﴿It was said: "O Noah, descend"﴾ That is: come down from the ship. It is also read with a dammah on the ba' (ihbit). ﴿with peace﴾ accompanied by safety from hardships, which is ﴿from Us﴾; or, with peace and greeting from Us upon you, as He said: ﴿Peace upon Noah among the worlds.﴾ ﴿And blessings upon you﴾ That is: good things that increase in your offspring and in what sustains your livelihood and theirs, of all kinds of provision. It is also read as (barakatin). This is a proclamation and good tidings from Allah the Exalted of the acceptance of his repentance and his deliverance from loss, through the abundant flow of all kinds of good upon him in every (p-215) what comes and what goes. ﴿And upon nations﴾ arising ﴿from those who are with you﴾ until the Day of Resurrection, branching out from them. So "min" here is for the beginning of origin (ibtida'iyyah), and what is meant is the believing nations, descended from those with him until the Day of Resurrection. ﴿And nations We shall give enjoyment to, then a painful punishment from Us will touch them.﴾ That is: and from them (among them), taken as a predicate that has been omitted because of what preceded it.
