For the mention of the blessed nations branching from them as an indefinite noun indicates that some of those who branch from them are not upon their description; that is, not everyone who branches from them is a Muslim and blessed, rather among them are nations who are given enjoyment in this world and punished in the Hereafter. On this basis, those who were with Noah (peace be upon him) are not explicitly described as Muslims and blessed; rather, this is understood from their being with Noah (peace and blessings be upon him) and from their descendants being so by the indication of the text. It is also permissible that "min" be explanatory (bayaniyyah), meaning: and upon nations who are those who are with you. They were called "nations" because they are factions united together and separate groups, or because all nations branched from them. In that case, the nations referred to in His saying, "And nations We shall give enjoyment to," would be some of the nations branching from them, namely the disbelieving nations descended from them until the Day of Resurrection, and the matter of the believing nations arising from them remains vague, neither addressed nor indicated by that. There is some obscurity in the indication of the mentioned part on its omitted predicate, because the mentioned "min" is explanatory while the omitted one is partitive or for beginning of origin, so reflect.

﴿Then there will touch them﴾ either in the Hereafter, or in this world as well, ﴿from Us, a painful punishment.﴾

From Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi: every believing man and woman until the Day of Resurrection entered into that peace, and everything after it of enjoyment and punishment belongs to every disbeliever. From Ibn Zayd: they descended, and Allah was pleased with them; then He brought forth from them offspring, some of whom He showed mercy to and some of whom He punished. It was said: what is meant by the nations given enjoyment are the people of Hud, Salih, Lut and Shu'ayb (peace be upon them), and by the punishment what befell them.

﴿Tilka﴾ ("That") is a demonstrative referring to the story of Nuh (peace be upon him) that has been related. It may be used either because the events, having already passed, are treated as distant in status, or to indicate the high rank of the story. It is a *mubtada'* (subject of a nominal sentence), whose predicate (*khabar*) is ﴿min anba'i al-ghayb﴾ ("among the news of the unseen"). That is, it is of the same kind as the unseen news, meaning it is not among the ordinary reports, but is unique in itself, distinct from everything else. Or it means some of it is. ﴿Nuhiha ilayka﴾ ("We reveal it to you") is a second predicate, with the pronoun referring to the story, meaning "revealed to you." Or the predicate is the phrase itself, with ﴿min anba'i﴾ attached to it, so the use of the present tense serves to bring the scene vividly before the mind. Or it is a *hal* (circumstantial clause) describing ﴿anba' al-ghayb﴾, meaning "revealed to you."

﴿Ma kunta ta'lamuha anta wa la qawmuka﴾ ("You did not know it, nor did your people") is another predicate, meaning that it was unknown to you and to your people. ﴿Min qabli hadha﴾ ("before this") means before Our revealing it to you and informing you of it. Or it means before this knowledge which you acquired through revelation. Or it means before this time. Or it is a *hal* from the pronoun in (*nuhiha*) or the *kaf* in (*ilayka*), meaning that you and your people were ignorant of it. Mentioning their ignorance is a reminder that he (peace be upon him) did not learn it from others, since he did not mix with anyone else, and that his people, despite their large number, did not know it, so how could any one of them know it?

﴿Fasbir﴾ ("So be patient") is a consequence of the revelation, or of the knowledge derived from it, which is indicated by His saying: "You did not know it, nor did your people, before this." That is: since We have revealed it to you, or you have come to know it through this, then be patient with the hardships of conveying the message and the harm from your people, just as Nuh was patient, as you have heard, with various kinds of trials over this long period. This relates to what preceded His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So perhaps you will leave aside some of what is revealed to you﴾ ... etc. ﴿Inna al-'aqibata﴾ ("Indeed, the final outcome") is victory in this world and success in the Hereafter ﴿li-al-muttaqin﴾ ("is for the righteous"), as you witnessed in the case of Nuh (peace be upon him) and his people, and you have in him a good example. Thus it is (p-216) a consolation to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and a reason for the command to be patient. For the fact that the good outcome belongs to the righteous, and that is at the furthest degree of taqwa, while all believers are righteous, is something that consoles him ﷺ, eases his burdens, and removes whatever constriction of his chest may arise. This applies if taqwa is taken to mean its first degree, namely guarding oneself against the everlasting punishment by disavowing shirk, and on this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He made them hold to the word of taqwa﴾. It may also be that the third degree of it is meant, which is to purify oneself from whatever occupies the heart away from the Truth, and to devote oneself wholeheartedly to Him. This is the true taqwa required by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Fear Allah as He should be feared﴾. For taqwa in this sense includes the patience mentioned. So it is as if it were said: "Be patient, for the outcome belongs to those who are patient."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 50:

﴿And to ʿĀd﴾ is related to an implied verb that is conjoined to His words, exalted is He, "We sent" (أرْسَلْنا) in the account of Noah. It is the verb that governs His words, exalted is He, ﴿their brother﴾, meaning: and We sent to ʿĀd their brother, that is, one of them by lineage, as in their saying: "O brother of the Arabs." Placing the prepositional phrase before the object here is to avoid a pronoun referring to something not yet mentioned (al-hidhar ʿan al-idmar qabla al-dhikr). It is also said that it is related to the verb mentioned earlier, and "their brother" is conjoined to "Noah." This has been discussed in Surat al-Aʿraf.

His words, exalted is He, ﴿Hud﴾ are an explicative apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) to "their brother." He (ﷺ) was one of them. He is Hud son of ʿAbd Allah son of Rabah son of al-Khulud son of al-ʿAws son of Iram son of Sam son of Noah, peace be upon him. It is also said: Hud son of Shalih son of Arfakhshadh son of Sam son of Noah, cousin of the father of ʿĀd. He was made one of them because they would understand his speech best, know his condition best, and be most inclined to follow him.

He said: since the mention of his being sent (ﷺ) to them invites the question of what he said to them and called them to, it is answered by way of resumption (istiʾnaf), so it is said: He said: ﴿O my people, worship Allah﴾, meaning: make Him one, as His words, exalted is He, indicate: ﴿You have no god other than Him﴾. This is a resumptive clause that serves as an explanation of the worship that is commanded and as the reason for the command, as if it were said: single Him out for worship and do not associate anything with Him, since you have no god besides Him. The word (غَيْرُهُ) "ghayruhu" with a nominative ending (بِالرَّفْعِ) is an attribute of (إلَهٍ) "ilah" in terms of its grammatical position (bi-iʿtibar mahallih), and it has also been read with a genitive ending (بِالجَرِّ), taking it according to its surface form (lafzih).

﴿You are not﴾ (إنْ أنْتُمْ): you are not, by your taking idols as partners to Him, or by your saying that Allah commanded you to worship them, ﴿except fabricators﴾ against Him, exalted is He far above that with great exaltation.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 51:

﴿O my people, I ask of you no wage for it. My wage is only from the One who originated me.﴾ Every prophet addressed his people with this statement, to remove what they might suppose ( izahah), and to make the advice pure (imhad al-nasihah), for advice that is mixed with greed is far removed from having any effect. The use of the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) serves to magnify (tafkhim) the one referred to, and making the relative clause (silah) the act of origination (fitrah) is because it is the earliest of the blessings overflowing from the presence of God, Exalted, which warrant gratitude; gratitude can only be realized by proceeding in accordance with the dominant requirement of His command, turning away from worldly aims, among which is wages.

﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾ That is: Are you heedless of this matter? Or: Will you not reflect upon it so that you understand it? Or: Are you ignorant of everything, so that you understand nothing at all? For this is something that should not be hidden from any of the intelligent.

O my people, seek forgiveness from your Lord, that is: ask Him for His forgiveness for the sins of the past that you have committed, through faith and obedience, ﴿then turn to Him in repentance﴾, that is: seek nearness to Him through repentance. Also, disavowing others (al-tabarru' min al-ghayr) can only come after faith in God Most High and eagerness for what is with Him. ﴿He will send the sky upon you in abundant rain﴾, that is: the rain, ﴿frequent in its showers﴾, that is: abundant in its pouring. ﴿And He will add strength to your strength﴾, added to and joined with your existing strength, that is: He will multiply it for you. He encouraged them with abundant rain because they were people of crops and buildings. It is also said that God Most High withheld the rain from them and made the wombs of their women barren for three years, so he (peace be upon him) promised them abundant rains and the multiplication of strength through procreation, upon faith and repentance. ﴿And do not turn away﴾, that is: do not turn away from what I have called you to, ﴿as criminals﴾, persisting in what you were upon of criminal conduct.

They said, "O Hud, you have brought us no clear proof (bayyinah)," meaning: no argument that demonstrates the soundness of your claim. They said this out of extreme obstinacy and because they paid no regard to the clear proofs (al-bayyinat) that had come to them, which are too many to be counted. ﴿And we are not going to abandon our gods﴾, meaning: we are not going to abandon their worship ﴿on your word﴾, meaning: coming from you. That is, our abandoning them does not proceed from your saying. The construction attributes the state of description to the thing described, and its meaning is causation (ta'lil) in its most eloquent form, since it indicates that your word is an efficient cause. The particles bi (with) and li (for) do not convey this. This is like their statement, reported in Surat al-A'raf: ﴿Have you come to us that we may worship God alone and forsake what our fathers used to worship?﴾ ﴿And we are not going to believe you﴾, meaning: we will not accept as true anything of what you bring or what you leave aside. This includes what he called them to of monotheism and abandoning the worship of the gods. In this there is an indication, which is plain, of their severe stubbornness and of their excess in arrogance.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 54:

﴿In naqulu illa i'taraka﴾ That is: we say nothing except our saying: "i'taraka", meaning, "has afflicted you" ﴿ba'du alihatina bi-su'in﴾ "some of our gods with harm", namely with madness, for your reviling them, your turning people away from their worship, and your lowering them from the rank of divinity and worship-worthiness by what you said earlier: "You have no god other than Him. You are only inventors of falsehood" (Qur'an 11:50). The indefinite in (su') is for minimization, as if they did not exaggerate the harm, as is indicated by the attribution of this to "some" of their gods rather than all of them. The clause is the object of the saying, and (illa) is superfluous (laghw), because the exception is an incomplete (mufarragh) one. This statement confirms what was mentioned earlier of their saying: "We will not abandon our gods because of your words, and we will not believe you" (Qur'an 11:53). Their belief that he, peace and blessings be upon him, is as they claimed, and far be it from him, requires that they not take his words into account and regard them as among the nonsense, let alone believe in them and act upon their implications. They mean: we do not regard your speech except as among the kind of ravings that issue from madmen, which admit neither truth nor falsehood, so how could we believe him, trust him and act upon what it requires?! They have pursued, in their course of opposition and obstinacy, a path of escalation from the lower to the higher: first they reported that he had not brought a clear proof, though what he brought might be a valid argument in itself even if not clearly indicative of the intended meaning; second, they spoke of abandoning compliance with his words, saying "We will not abandon our gods because of your words," although such compliance was attainable by their affirming him, peace and blessings be upon him, in what he said; then they negated their affirmation of him, peace and blessings be upon him, saying "We will not believe you," though his speech is of a kind that admits affirmation; then they negated from him even that rank, by what they said, saying what they said. May God fight them; how are they deluded?

Abu al-Su'ud, Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, on Surah 11 (Hud), verse 55:

﴿He said: "Indeed I call God to witness, and you bear witness that I am free of what you associate﴾ (p-218) ﴿apart from Him﴾. That is, of your associating apart from God; that is, without Him having sent down any authority for it, as He said in Surat al-A'raf: ﴿Do you dispute with me about names you have named, you and your fathers, for which God has sent down no authority?﴾ Or, "of what you associate" refers to the gods other than God. He answered with this their foolish statement, which is based on the belief that their gods have the power to harm or benefit, and that they are far removed from that. Since what first came from him, upon him be blessings and peace, concerning their gods, namely that they are far removed from divinity, came only within the context of the command to worship God Most High and to single Him out for it, and this was difficult for them and they regarded it as something that brings about some loss, so much so that they claimed that their gods would afflict him, upon him be blessings and peace, with harm, as recompense for his treatment of them, he, upon him be blessings and peace, declared the truth plainly and proclaimed it, when he informed them of his long-standing disavowal of them with a nominal sentence introduced by "inna" (indeed), and he called God to witness to that, and commanded them to hear it and bear witness to it, in contempt of them. Then he commanded them to gather together with all their gods, without exception, as is suggested by their saying "some of our gods," and to cooperate in bringing their scheming against him, upon him be blessings and peace, and he forbade them from delaying or postponing in that, saying: ﴿So scheme against me, all of you together, and give me no respite﴾. That is: if what you have hinted at is true, that your gods are able to harm whoever touches them or turns away from worshipping them, even indirectly, then I am free of them. So be you, together with them, all of you, and set about your scheme against me, and do not allow me any reprieve nor show me any leniency in that. The "fa" (so) here marks the command as a consequence of their claim about the power of their gods to do what they said and of his disavowal, both together. And this is among the greatest of miracles, for he, upon him be blessings and peace, was a single man facing a vast multitude and a great host of the stubborn, harsh, and mighty people of 'Ad, and he addressed them with what he addressed them, belittled them and their gods, and incited them to engage in the beginnings of opposition and harm, and urged them to take up the means of enmity and hostility. Yet they were unable to carry out anything of what they were charged with, and their incapacity was manifestly clear. How could it be otherwise, when he had taken refuge in a firm and lofty pillar and held fast to a strong rope? For he said:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 56:

﴿Indeed I have put my trust in Allah, my Lord and your Lord.﴾ That is, even if you exert your utmost effort to harm me, you will not be able to do anything of what you intend against me, for I rely upon Allah the Exalted. The past tense has been used here (تَوَكَّلْتُ, "I have put my trust") because it is more indicative of the (immediate) performance of the act (al-inshā', i.e., the speech act itself), which suits the context; and (it expresses that) I am confident in His protection and in His guarding me from your mischief. He is my Owner and your Owner; nothing proceeds from you, and no matter befalls me except by His will and His decree. Then he substantiated this with His saying: ﴿There is no creature but that He holds its forelock.﴾ That is: none but that He is its Owner and has power over it, directing it as He wills, it being unable to resist Him; for seizing by the forelock is a figure of speech for this (complete control).

﴿Indeed my Lord is on a straight path.﴾ This is a reason for what trust (tawakkul) implies, namely their inability to harm him. That is: He is upon the truth and justice, so He will hardly let you dominate me, since one who seeks refuge in Him is not lost before Him, and no oppressor can encroach upon Him (yaftāt, i.e., act against Him without right). Restricting the mention to the Lord's being attributed to Himself (i.e., "my Lord") is either by way of sufficiency, since the intended meaning is clear, or because the benefit of His being the Owner of them (the people) as well also returns to him, upon him be prayers and peace.

(p-219) ﴿Fa-in tawallaw﴾ means: "if you turn away," with one of the two tā' elided, i.e., "if you persist in the turning away and aversion you have been engaged in." ﴿Then I have indeed conveyed to you what I was sent with to you﴾ means: I am not blamed for any shortcoming in conveying (the message), and you were left without excuse (maḥjūjīn), since the truth reached you and you refused anything but denial and obstinate rejection. ﴿And my Lord will bring after you a people other than you﴾ is a resumption (istiʼnāf) containing a threat to them: that God Most High will destroy them and install other people in their homes and possessions. Alternatively, it is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the answer introduced by the fā' (of "fa-qad abligtukum"). This is supported by the reading of Ibn Masʿūd (may Allah be pleased with him) in the jussive mood, coordinated with the place (ʿaṭf ʿalā al-mawḍiʿ), as if it were said: "If you turn away, He will excuse me, destroy you, and install others in your place." In the restriction of the addition of the Lord to him (peace be upon him) there is a symbol of the gentleness toward him and the destruction of those addressed. ﴿And you will not harm Him﴾ by your turning away ﴿in any way﴾ of harm, because that is impossible for Him. Whoever reads (yastakhlif) in the jussive mood drops the nūn from it.

﴿Indeed my Lord is, over all things, Guardian (ḥafīẓ)﴾ means: a watchful, dominating Overseer, so your deeds are not hidden from Him and He will repay you according to them. Or: a Guardian who prevails over all things, so how could anything harm Him, since He is the Guardian of all?

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 58:**

﴿When Our command came﴾, that is: Our punishment descended. In expressing it as "command," attributed to His Own pronoun, may He be exalted in majesty, and in describing its descent as "coming," there is evident magnification and awe-inspiring force; or the sense is that Our command came with the punishment. ﴿We saved Hud and those who believed with him﴾, and they were four thousand, ﴿by a mercy﴾ great, belonging to them ﴿from Us﴾, which is the faith that We bestowed upon them by granting them success in it and guiding them to it. ﴿And We saved them from a severe punishment﴾, that is: that deliverance was a deliverance from a severe punishment, namely the scorching winds (al-samum) which would enter the noses of the disbelievers and exit from their posteriors, cutting them into pieces. It has been said that by the second [deliverance] is meant deliverance from the punishment of the Hereafter, and there is no punishment more severe or more intense than it. This deliverance, although not restricted to the coming of the command, was mentioned to complete the blessing upon them, and as an allusion that just as the destroyed were punished in this world with the scorching winds, they are punished in the Hereafter with the severe punishment.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 59:**

﴿And those were ʿĀd﴾. The demonstrative noun (ism al-ishara, "those") is feminine, in view of the tribe (al-qabila), or because the reference is to their graves and remains (athar). ﴿They denied the signs of their Lord﴾: they disbelieved in them after they had become certain of them. ﴿And disobeyed His messengers﴾: he used the plural "messengers" (al-rusul), although only Hud, peace be upon him, was sent to them, in order to make their condition appear more grievous and to show the completeness of their disbelief and obstinacy, by indicating that their disobedience to him (peace be upon him) is disobedience to all the messengers, past and future, since their word is united upon monotheism (tawhid). [Compare the verse:] ﴿We make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾. Accordingly, "the signs" may be taken to mean what Hud and the other prophets, peace be upon them all, brought. This is more fitting with all that precedes, namely all the signs, and with what follows in His saying: ﴿And they followed the command of every obstinate tyrant﴾, referring to their great men and leaders who called to misguidance and to the denial of the messengers. It is as if it were said: they disobeyed every messenger and followed the command of every tyrant. This description, however, does not extend to every individual among them in the way that the denial of the signs and the disobedience of the messengers did, for following a command is a trait of the lowly rather than of the leaders. (p-220) ʿAnid is an intensive form (fa'il) from ʿanada, ʿanadan and ʿandan, meaning to transgress. The meaning is: they disobeyed the one who called them to guidance, and they obeyed the one who drove them to ruin.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 60:

﴿And they were followed in this world by a curse﴾: a distancing from mercy and from every good. That is, the curse was made to cling to them. This is expressed by "following" for emphasis, as if it never left them, however far they went. Rather, it revolves around them wherever they turn. Because it occurs in the company of their following their leaders, the meaning is that when they followed them, they were made to follow that curse as a recompense for their conduct, a fitting recompense. ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection﴾: that is, they will also be made to follow a curse on the Day of Resurrection, which is the everlasting punishment of the Fire. It is elided because the first mention indicates it, and to signal that each of the two states is a distinct type, not to be combined in a single clause, such that it would be said: "they were followed in this world and on the Day of Resurrection by a curse." This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And ordain for us in this world good, and in the Hereafter﴾, signaling the difference between the two kinds of good. The worldly good is such things as health, sufficiency, and success in goodness, while the otherworldly good is reward and mercy.

﴿Indeed, ʿĀd disbelieved their Lord﴾: that is, they disbelieved in their Lord, or in the blessing of their Lord, treating it as the opposite of gratitude, which is thankfulness; or they denied it. ﴿Away with ʿĀd!﴾: a supplication against them for destruction, even though they were already destroyed, and in whatever manner of destruction, to record against them that they deserved destruction and merited annihilation. The repetition of the interjective particle (ḥarf al-tanbīh) and the restatement of "ʿĀd" serve to intensify the depiction of their condition and to urge reflection upon their story. ﴿the people of Hud﴾: an explanatory apposition (ʿaṭf al-bayān, apposition clarifying the preceding noun) to "ʿĀd." Its benefit is to distinguish them from the second ʿĀd, the ʿĀd of Iram, and to indicate that their deserving distance was due to what took place between them and Hud, peace be upon him, for they were his people.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 61:

﴿And to Thamud [We sent] their brother Salih.﴾ This is a conjunction with what preceded in the words of the Exalted: ﴿And to 'Ad [We sent] their brother Hud.﴾ Thamud is a tribe of the Arabs, named after their great forefather Thamud ibn 'Abir ibn Iram ibn Sam. It has been said that they were named thus for the scarcity of their water (al-thamd), which is little water. Salih, upon him be peace, is the son of 'Ubayd ibn Asaf ibn Mashij ibn 'Ubayd ibn Jadir ibn Thamud. Since the report of his being sent to them is liable to prompt the question, "What did he say to them?", the answer is given in a resumptive manner: ﴿He said: O my people, worship Allah﴾, i.e., Him alone. This is justified by the words: ﴿You have no god other than Him.﴾ Then, in what moves them to faith and monotheism and urges them to increase sincerity in it, He adds the words: ﴿He brought you into being from the earth﴾, i.e., He is the One who formed and created you from it, and no other? This is a restriction of rebuttal (qasr qalb) or a restriction of exclusion (qasr ifrad), for the creation of Adam, upon him be peace, from it is a creation of all the individuals of mankind from it, for what has passed many times: that the creation of him, upon him be peace, was not confined to himself, but was a prototype comprising in summary form the creation of all his offspring who will exist until the Day of Resurrection. It has also been said: the creation of Adam, upon him be peace, and the production of the substances of the drops from which his progeny were created from the dust is a production of all creation from the earth. So reflect.

﴿And He settled you therein﴾ from 'umr (life/lifespan), i.e., He granted you long life and preserved you.

﴿therein﴾ Or from 'imarah (cultivation/habitation), i.e., (p-221) He empowered you to build it, or commanded you to do so. It has also been said that it is from 'umra (the grant of use for life), meaning He let you have your dwellings for your lifetimes, and He inherits them from you after your lifetimes have ended, or He made you inhabitants of your dwellings, living in them for the duration of your lives, then you leave them to others like you.

﴿So seek His forgiveness, then turn to Him in repentance﴾, for what has been detailed of the varieties of favour calls for seeking forgiveness for the negligence that occurred from them, and for repentance from the abominations they were engaged in. It has been further explained what necessitates this, so it is said: ﴿Indeed my Lord is near﴾, i.e., near in mercy, as in His saying, ﴿Indeed the mercy of Allah is near to the good-doers﴾, ﴿responsive﴾ to whoever calls upon Him and asks of Him. A subtle point has been observed in the noble arrangement: the mention of the motivating cause, which precedes the command to seek forgiveness and repent, is placed first, and the mention of the outcome, which comes later in existence than both of them, namely the answering, is placed after it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 62:

﴿They said: "O Salih, you were indeed among us a man of whom great hopes were held."﴾ That is: we used to hope from you, because of the signs of rectitude and the indications of right guidance we used to see in you, that you would become our leader and our counselor in matters.

And from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, (it means): a virtuous and excellent man whom we would place above all of us. It was also said: we used to hope that you would enter our religion and agree with us in what we are upon, ﴿before this﴾, namely the call to Tawhid (monotheism) and the abandonment of worshipping the deities which you have undertaken, or before this time; so it was as if they had not been, until now, in despair of that, even after the call to the truth. But now our hope in you has come to an end. And Talha read: (مَرْجُوءًا) with a long vowel (madd) and a hamza.

﴿Do you forbid us to worship what our fathers worshipped?﴾ That is: what they worshipped. The shift to the present tense (imperfect) is to narrate a past state. ﴿And indeed we are in grave doubt about that to which you invite us﴾ concerning Tawhid, abandoning the worship of idols, and other matters such as seeking forgiveness and repentance. ﴿Disquieting﴾ means: causing doubt, from (arabahu), meaning he caused him to fall into doubt, that is, unease of the soul and absence of tranquility; or from (araba), when one is possessed of doubt. Whichever it is, the attribution is metaphorical (majazi), and the tanwin in it and in (شَكٍّ) is for magnification (tafkhim).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 63:

﴿He said: "O my people, tell me, if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord, and He has given me mercy from Himself"﴾. That is: inform me, ﴿if I am﴾ in reality ﴿upon clear evidence﴾, that is, a manifest proof, a demonstration, and insight, ﴿from my Lord﴾, my Sustainer and the one who manages my affairs, ﴿and He has given me from Himself﴾, from His side, ﴿mercy﴾, that is, prophethood. And these matters, although they are certain to occur, are introduced with the word of doubt in consideration of the state of those addressed and for the sake of good discourse, in order to bring them down from their obstinacy.

﴿So who will help me against Allah﴾, that is, who will save me from His punishment. The shift to the explicit noun is for the sake of increased awe. The fa' (so) indicates the consequence of denying help in light of what preceded of the granting of prophethood, and of his being upon clear evidence from his Lord, on the supposition of disobedience, as expressed by the words of the Exalted: ﴿if I disobey Him﴾, that is, by being lax in conveying the message and by going along with you in what you do and leave undone. For disobedience from one whose condition is that (i.e., a prophet) is more remote, the accountability for it more binding, and the denial of his being helped more inclusive.

﴿Then you would add nothing to me﴾ in that case by your attributing me to yourselves, as their saying indicates: "You were among us a man of hope before this" — that is, you would not benefit me, since there is no root of loss in me that you could increase, ﴿other than making me a loser﴾, that is, other than making me a loser by nullifying my deeds and exposing me to the wrath of Allah, the Exalted. Or: "you would add nothing to me by what you say, other than attributing you to loss and saying to you: 'Indeed you are the losers.'" So the increase is upon its meaning. The fa' indicates the consequence of the absence of increase upon the negation of a helper, which is implied by denying it on the supposition of disobedience, together with the certainty of what negates it, namely that he, upon him be peace, is upon clear evidence from his Lord and has been given prophethood.

**"O my people, this is the she-camel of God"** The annexation (*idafah*, the grammatical construction linking "she-camel" to "God") serves to honor her and to draw attention to the fact that she is distinct from all other camels in her creation and in her character. **"A sign for you"**: a miracle indicating the truthfulness of my prophethood. It is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) describing "the she-camel of God," and the governing element is the sense of the verb contained in "this" (*hadhihi*). The phrase **"for you"** (*lakum*) is also a circumstantial clause, describing "a sign" (*ayah*). It is placed before the noun because "sign" is indefinite (*nakirah*); had it been placed after, it would have been an adjective (*sifah*) of it. It is also permissible for "she-camel of God" to be a substitute (*badal*) for "this," or an explicative apposition (*ʿatf bayan*), and for "for you" to be the predicate (*khabar*) and also the governing element of "a sign."

**"So leave her"** (*fa-dharuha*): let her be and her affairs. **"to eat in God's earth"** (*takul fi ardi Allah*): to graze on its plants and drink its water. The annexation of the earth to God, exalted is He, is to foster the sense that she deserves this, and it provides the reason for the command to leave her to her own affairs. **"And do not touch her with harm"** (*wa la tamassuha bi-su'*): the prohibition against interfering with her in any way that might harm her is emphasized, in that she is forbidden from being touched, which is the first step toward striking her and the beginning of doing evil. In other words: do not strike her, do not drive her away, and do not approach her with any kind of harm, let alone hamstring her or kill her. **"Lest a near punishment seize you"**: that is, a punishment that is close in coming.

It is related that they asked him to bring forth from a rock called al-Kathibah a she-camel that was pregnant in its tenth month, large-bellied, thick-furred, and hollow-flanked, and they said: "If you do that, we will believe you." So Salih, upon him be peace, took from them a covenant: "If I do that, will you truly believe?" They said: "Yes." So he prayed and called upon his Lord, and the rock writhed like a woman in labor who is giving birth, and it split open, releasing a pregnant she-camel exactly as they had described, while they were watching. Then she gave birth to a young one like her in size. Jundu' ibn ʿAmr believed in him, together with a group of people. But Dawab ibn ʿAmr, al-Hubab, the chief of their idols, and Rabab, their soothsayer, prevented the rest from believing. The she-camel remained with her young one, grazing on the trees and coming to the water every other day. She would not lift her head from the well until she had drunk all of its water. Then she would spread her legs, and they would milk her as much as they wished until their vessels were full, so they drank and stored. She used to spend the summer at the upper part of the valley, and their livestock would flee from her to the lower part of it; and she spent the winter in the lower part, and their herds would flee to the upper part. This troubled them greatly.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 65:

﴿So they hamstrung her.﴾ It is said: Unayzah, the mother of Ghanm, and Sadaqah bint al-Mukhtar adorned the hamstringing for them. So they hamstrung her and divided her meat. Then her foal climbed a mountain called Qarrah and cried out three times. Salih said to them: "Catch the foal; perhaps it will lift the punishment from you." But they could not catch it. The rock split after its crying, and it entered it. ﴿Then he said﴾ to them, Salih: ﴿"Enjoy yourselves"﴾, that is, live, ﴿"in your homes"﴾, that is, in your dwellings, or in the world, ﴿"for three days."﴾ It is said he told them: "Tomorrow your faces will become yellow, the day after tomorrow red, and on the third day black, and then the punishment will seize you at morning."

﴿That﴾ is a reference to what is indicated by the command to enjoy oneself for three days, with the punishment descending after them. The meaning of distance in it (the demonstrative "that") is to magnify it. ﴿"is a promise not to be denied"﴾, that is, not denied in it. The preposition has been omitted due to the well-known extension of usage (ittisa'), as in his saying:

*And a day we witnessed it safe and populated.*

Or it means "not denied": as if the one promising said to him, "Will you keep it with me?" If he keeps it, he confirms him; otherwise he denies him. Or it means "a promise that is not a lie," with the word functioning as a verbal noun (masdar), like *al-majlud* and *al-ma'qul*.(p-223)

﴿So when Our command came﴾, meaning Our punishment, or Our command for it to descend, and in this there is a terrifying awe (tahwil) that is not hidden. ﴿We saved Salih and those who believed with him﴾. The phrase ﴿by a mercy﴾ is connected either to ﴿saved﴾ or to ﴿believed﴾. ﴿By a mercy﴾ means because of a great mercy ﴿from Us﴾. For Salih, this mercy is prophethood (al-nubuwwah), and for the believers it is faith (al-iman), as has passed, or it means they were accompanied by mercy and compassion from Us. ﴿And from the disgrace of that day﴾, meaning: and We saved them from the disgrace of that day, which is their destruction by the Blast, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We saved them from a severe punishment﴾, in the sense that this saving was a saving from the disgrace of that day, that is, from its humiliation and abasement, or their humiliation and exposure on the Day of Resurrection, as the severe punishment was interpreted to mean earlier. Thus the meaning is: We saved them from the punishment of the Day of Resurrection after We saved them from the punishment of this world. From Nafi', with a fatha, on the basis that the mudaf (the annexed noun) takes its declension (bina') from the mudaf ilayhi (the noun it is annexed to), namely the word ﴿yawmi'idhin﴾ here and in al-Ma'arij, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿from the punishment of that day﴾. It was also read with tanwin and the accusative of ﴿yawma'idhin﴾.

﴿Indeed your Lord﴾: the address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). ﴿He is the Strong, the Mighty﴾, the One capable of everything and the One who overpowers everything, and no one else. Because the report of the saving of the allies, especially when announcing the arrival of punishment, is of greater importance, He mentioned it first. Then He reported the destruction of the enemies, saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 67:

﴿And the cry seized those who did wrong﴾. He shifted from the pronoun to the explicit noun, to record their wrongdoing against them and to signal that wrongdoing was the cause (ʿilliyyah) for the descent of the punishment upon them. ﴿The cry﴾, that is, the cry of Jibril, upon him be prayers and peace. It has also been said that there came upon them from the sky a cry containing the sound of every thunderbolt and the sound of everything on the earth, so their hearts were torn apart within their chests. In Surah al-A'raf: ﴿So the quake seized them﴾. Perhaps it occurred after the cry, which was followed by the agitation of the air. ﴿So they became﴾, that is, they turned to be ﴿in their homes﴾, that is, their lands or their dwellings, ﴿prostrate﴾ (jathimin), lifeless, dead, not moving. What is meant is that they were in this state at the very beginning of the descent of the punishment upon them, without convulsion or movement, as happens at a usual death. What this indicates of the severity of the seizing and its swiftness is not hidden. O Allah, we seek refuge in You from the descent of Your wrath. It has been said: when they saw the signs that Salih had explained, of yellowing of their faces, reddening and blackening, they resolved to kill him, upon him be prayers and peace, but Allah the Exalted delivered him to the land of Palestine. When it was the forenoon of the fourth day, which was the day of Saturday, they applied spices and shrouded themselves in leather sheets, and then the cry came upon them, so their hearts were torn apart and they perished.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 68:

﴿As if they had never prospered therein﴾ That is: as if they were in their lands or their dwellings. The phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: they became prostrate, resembling those who never existed and never dwelt in any place at all. ﴿Behold! Indeed Thamud﴾ The noun is placed in the position of the pronoun for the sake of added clarity. Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) read it with tanwin (nunation) here and in Surah al-Najm, while Hafs read it without tanwin here, in Surah al-Furqan, and in Surah al-'Ankabut.

﴿They disbelieved in their Lord﴾ Their disbelief is stated explicitly even though it is already known from what preceded regarding their circumstances, in order to censure their condition and to give the reason for their deserving the invocation against them of distance and destruction in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Away with Thamud!﴾ Al-Kisa'i read it with tanwin.(p-224)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 69:

﴿And indeed Our messengers came to Ibrahim﴾ — they were the angels.

From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, they were Jibril and two angels. It was also said: they were Jibril, Mika'il and Israfil, peace be upon them. Al-Dahhak said: they were nine. From Muhammad ibn Ka'b: Jibril and with him seven. From al-Suddi: eleven, in the forms of handsome youths with bright faces. From Muqatil: they were twelve angels. The coming with the good tidings is ascribed to them without the word "sent," because they were not sent to him (peace be upon him), but rather to the people of Lut, as He, exalted is He, says: ﴿Indeed, We have been sent to the people of Lut﴾. They came to him only to bring good tidings. Since the purpose of the noble surah is to mention the evil conduct of past nations toward the messengers sent to them, and the punishment that befell them because of that, and since not all of the people of Ibrahim (peace and blessings be upon him) were among those struck by punishment, but only the people of Lut from among them, the style that had been consistent in what preceded was changed. Compare His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And to 'Ad, their brother Hud﴾ and ﴿And to Thamud, their brother Salih﴾; then it reverted to it where it says: "And to Madyan, their brother Shu'ayb."

﴿with the good tidings﴾ — that is, accompanied by them. It was said: these are good tidings in general, encompassing the good news of a son from Sarah, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So We gave her the good news of Ishaq﴾ ... the verse, and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So We gave him the good news of a forbearing boy﴾, and His saying: ﴿And they gave him the good news of a knowing boy﴾. And it is also good news of his not being harmed, by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then when the fear had left Ibrahim and the good tidings had come to him﴾, because of the evident connection of the disputation to their coming, as will come. It was also said: it is the good tidings of the destruction of the people of Lut, but his disputing with them (peace be upon him) about them rules this out. The most apparent view is that it is the good tidings of a son, and you will come to know the secret of the disputation's connection to that.

Since the report of their coming with good tidings is a prompt for the listener to ask what they said, it is answered: they ﴿said: "Peace"﴾ — that is, "We greet you with peace" or "We say peace to you." It is permissible that its accusative be governed by "said," meaning: they said a word of peace, or they mentioned peace. ﴿He said: "Peace"﴾ — that is, "Peace be upon you," or "Peace is upon you." He greeted them with a greeting better than theirs. It was read as "salima" like "harima" in "haram," and Ibn Abi 'Abla read "qala salaman." It is also reported from him that he read both with the nominative.

﴿Then he did not delay﴾ — that is, Ibrahim — ﴿in bringing a calf﴾, that is, in bringing it, or his bringing a calf was not delayed. ﴿roasted﴾ — that is, cooked in hot stones in a trench. It was also said: fat, whose grease drips, based on the saying "a fat calf," from "hanadhtu al-faras" when you made the horse sweat with a cover.

﴿So when he saw their hands not reaching toward it﴾: they were not extending their hands to the food. ﴿He was alarmed by them﴾, meaning he disliked them (ankarahum). It is said that nakirahu, ankarahu and istankarahu have the same meaning. He disliked them because, when a guest arrived at their place and did not eat of their food, they assumed he had not come with good intent. It has been narrated that they would dip arrows that were in their hands into the meat, and their hands did not reach it. This disapproval on his part, peace be upon him, relates to their aforementioned action. As for his disapproval concerning their persons, it has no connection with seeing that they did not eat. It occurred upon seeing them because they were not of the kind of people he was accustomed to among men. Do you not see the words of God the Exalted in Surat al-Dhariyat: ﴿A peace, a people unknown﴾? ﴿And he sensed fear of them﴾, meaning he perceived or harbored, on their account, ﴿fear﴾, when he supposed that their descent was for a matter that God the Exalted disapproved of, or for the punishment of his people. The explicit object (al-maf'ul al-sarih) has been placed after the adverbial phrase (al-zarf) because the intended meaning is to inform that he, peace be upon him, sensed from their direction something which was fear, not that he sensed fear from their direction and not from the direction of others. Its verification is that delaying what should be placed first makes the soul await it, so that when it arrives it settles in more firmly.

﴿They said: Do not fear﴾. They did not say this merely upon seeing signs of fear in him, to remove it from him, but after he had made it known to them. God the Exalted said in Surat al-Hijr: ﴿He said: Indeed we are apprehensive of you﴾, and that is not mentioned here, being sufficient with that.

﴿Indeed we have been sent﴾. Its apparent meaning is that it is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) having the sense of giving a reason for the aforementioned prohibition, just as the words of God the Exalted ﴿Indeed We give you good news﴾ are a reason for that. For their being sent to another people necessitates his safety from fear, meaning: we have been sent with punishment ﴿to the people of Lut﴾ specifically. However, it is not so, for the words of God the Exalted ﴿He said: What is your business, O messengers?﴾ ﴿They said: Indeed we have been sent to a guilty people﴾ are explicit that they said this in answer to his question, peace be upon him, and the speech has been abbreviated, being sufficient with that.

The wife was standing ﴿and his wife was standing﴾ behind the screen, so that she could hear their conversation, or standing over their heads to serve them, as was customary. The clause is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl, a clause describing the state of the subject at the time of the action) referring to the pronoun in "qālū" (they said). That is, they said it while she was standing and hearing their words. ﴿So she laughed﴾ out of joy at the removal of fear, or at the destruction of the people of corruption, or at both together. It was also said that she laughed at the fulfilment of the matter, as she had been saying previously: she used to say to Ibrahim, "Take Lut to yourself, for I see that punishment is about to descend upon these people." It was also said that ﴿ḍaḥikat﴾ means that she menstruated, and from this comes the expression "ḍaḥikat al-shajaratu" (the tree laughed) when its gum flows, but this is far-fetched. It was also read with a fatḥa on the ḥāʾ (ḍaḥakat). ﴿So We gave her good news of Isaac﴾, meaning We followed her joy with a greater joy through the tongues of Our messengers. ﴿And after Isaac, Jacob﴾ is read with the accusative (naṣb), as the object of what is indicated by His saying "bashsharnāhā" (We gave her good news), meaning: and We granted her, after Isaac, Jacob. It was also read with the nominative (rafʿ) as a subject (mubtadaʾ, the topic of a nominal sentence) whose predicate is the adverbial phrase, meaning: after Isaac, Jacob is born or existent. Both names fall within the good news, like Yahya (John), or they occur in the narrative after both had been born and were named accordingly. The direction of the good news here toward her, although the origin of such news is Ibrahim, peace be upon him, to whom it was addressed where it was said: (﴿We gave him the good news of a forbearing boy﴾) and (﴿We gave him the good news of a knowing boy﴾), is to indicate that what was announced would come from both of them, and because she was barren and eager for a child.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 72:

﴿She said⁠﴾ — this is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), coming as an answer to a question posed by someone who asks: "What did she do when she was given this good news?" So it is said: "She said": ﴿Oh, woe is me!﴾ The root meaning of "wayl" (woe) is disgrace (khizy), and then it became commonly used for any dreadful matter. The alif (ا) in it is substituted for the ya' of possession (ya' al-idafa), as in "ya lahafan" (oh, my grief!) and "ya 'ajaban" (oh, how strange!). Al-Hasan read it according to the original form (with the ya' retained), Abu 'Amr and 'Asim in one narration read it with imalah (inclination of the alif), and its meaning is: "Oh my woe! Present yourself, for this is the time of your presence." It is also said that the alif is the alif of lamentation (alif al-nudba), and it is pausally stopped upon with the silent ha' (ha' al-sakt).

﴿Shall I give birth while I am an old woman⁠﴾ — of ninety, or ninety-nine years of age — ﴿and this⁠﴾ whom you see ﴿is my husband⁠﴾, i.e., my spouse; the root of "ba'l" is one who is in charge of the matter, ﴿an old man⁠﴾, and he was one hundred and twenty years old. His being in the accusative is as a circumstantial clause (hal), and the governing element is the sense of the demonstrative. It was also read in the nominative, on the basis that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "he is an old man"; or a second predicate after a predicate; or it is the predicate itself, with "ba'li" being an apposition to the demonstrative or an explanatory clarification of it. Both sentences occur as circumstantial clauses from the pronoun in "shall I give birth," to confirm and give the reason for the astonishment contained in it, i.e., "Shall I give birth while we are both in a state contrary to that?" The description of her state was placed before the description of his state — upon him be prayer and peace — because the incompatibility of her state with the mentioned birth is greater, for it may happen that children are born to old men from young women, but as for old women, their condition is barrenness. Also, because the good news was directed to her explicitly; and also because reversing the order in the explanation might give the impression, at first, that the obstacle to birth was attributed to Abraham's side — upon him be prayer and peace — and in this there is a danger that is not hidden. Her restricting the astonishment to her own giving birth, without addressing the state of the granddaughter, is because she is the one deemed unlikely; as for the birth of her child, no astonishment attaches to it.

﴿Indeed, this⁠﴾ — i.e., what has been mentioned of the obtaining of a child from two decrepit persons like us — ﴿is truly a wondrous thing⁠﴾ in relation to the customary way of Allah the Exalted, practiced among His servants. This sentence is for giving the reason for the astonishment by way of a verifying resumptive clause (istinaf tahqiqi), and its purpose is to magnify the blessing of Allah the Exalted upon her within the framework of ordinary wonder, not to deem that thing unlikely in relation to His power, glorified and exalted is He.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 73:

﴿They said: "Do you wonder at the command of Allah?"﴾ That is, at His power, His wisdom, His creating, or His affair. They disapproved of her wondering at that, because she had grown up in the house of prophethood (bayt al-nubuwwa), the place where revelation and signs descended, and the source of miracles and matters that break customary patterns. Her duty was to be dignified and not to be excited by what excites other women of this kind of extraordinary event, which comes from Allah's hidden kindnesses and subtle workings, bestowed on everyone, and which is connected to His eternal will. This is especially so for the People of the House (ahl al-bayt), whose rank with Allah, glorified is He, is not like the ranks of other people. She should instead glorify, praise, and extol Allah, the Exalted. To this they pointed with His words, Exalted is He: "the mercy of Allah," which encompasses everything and entails every good. The apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun only to increase her honor. ﴿And His blessings﴾: that is, His good things, which grow and multiply in every respect, among which is the granting of children. It was also said: the mercy is prophethood, and the blessings are the tribes (asbat) of the Children of Israel, because the prophets were among them, and all of them are descendants of Ibrahim, upon him be peace. ﴿Upon you, O People of the House﴾ is in the accusative as a term of praise or specification, because they are the household of the Friend of the Most Merciful (Khalil al-Rahman). The address shifts from the singular form to the masculine plural in order to extend the ruling to Ibrahim, upon him be peace, as well, so that their answer to her is also an answer to him, in case the same thought occurred to him as occurred to her. The sentence is a resumed statement, which gives the reason for denying her wonder, as if it were said: this is not a situation for wonder, for Allah is powerful over everything. And you, O People of the House of prophethood, dignity, and nearness, are not like the other groups; rather, His mercy, which entails every good and encompasses everything, and His blessings, that is, His good things, which grow and overflow from Him through that vast mercy, are bound to you and will not leave you.

﴿Indeed, He is Praiseworthy﴾, doer of what deserves praise, ﴿Glorious﴾, abundant in goodness and beneficence toward His servants. This sentence gives the reason for what preceded in His words: ( ﴿The mercy of Allah and His blessings upon you﴾ ).

﴿When fear had left Abraham﴾, that is, the fear he had felt of them had gone, and his heart was reassured by recognizing them and recognizing the reason for their coming. The *fa'* (then) links some of Abraham's states, peace be upon him, to others after their separation, by means of something that is not wholly foreign in every respect but has a full connection to the preceding passage and its context. The subject (*al-fa'il*) is placed after the adverbial phrase (*al-zarf*), "from Abraham," because that is where the benefit lands. By delaying what should come first, the soul waits for its arrival, so when it arrives it settles there with greater firmness. ﴿And good news came to him﴾. If the good news (*al-bushra*) is explained as their saying, "Do not fear," then the causal link between the departure of fear (p-227) and the arrival of joy is due to the argument implied by His saying, ﴿He argues with Us concerning the people of Lot﴾, meaning he argued with Our messengers about their affair. The form is shifted to the present tense to bring its image before the mind, or it means "he began to argue with Us." This is apparent. As for if the good news is explained as the good news of a son, or as something that encompasses it, then its causal link to the arrival of joy may be that it yields greater tranquility of heart through the safety of himself and his whole household, together with his argument with them. When they said to him, ﴿Indeed, we are going to destroy the people of this town﴾, he said to them: "Have you seen? If there were fifty righteous men among its people, would you destroy it?" They said, "No." He said, "Then forty?" They said, "No." He said, "Then thirty?" They said, "No." And this continued until he reached ten. They said, "No." He said, "Have you seen? If there were a single Muslim man in it, would you destroy it?" They said, "No." At that point he said, ﴿Indeed, Lot is in it.﴾ They said, ﴿We know best who is in it. We will surely save him and his family﴾.

If it is objected that the apparent meaning of this discourse is that Abraham, peace be upon him, knew that they were sent to destroy the people of Lot before fear left him, but he was unable to argue with them about their affair because he was occupied with his own situation, and so when fear left him he turned to it. Yet the departure of fear was before he knew this, as shown by His saying, ﴿They said, "Do not fear. We have been sent to the people of Lot"﴾. We say: Lot, peace be upon him, was upon the law of Abraham, peace be upon him, and his people were obligated to it. When he saw what he saw from the angels, he feared for himself and for the whole of his community, of which the people of Lot were a part. There is no doubt that this fear preceded their saying, ﴿Do not fear.﴾ As for what he, peace be upon him, knew after the prohibition against fear, it was that the people of Lot were singled out for destruction, not that they were included under the general category. So reflect. And Allah is the Granter of success.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 75:

﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was forbearing, grieving, and turning back (to Allah).﴾ ﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was forbearing⁠﻿﻿﻿—﻿﻿﻿not hasty to seek retribution against one who had wronged him. ﴿Grieving⁠﻿﻿﻿—﻿﻿﻿much lamenting over sins and sorrowing over people. ﴿Turning back⁠﻿﻿﻿—﻿﻿﻿returning to Allah, exalted is He.

The purpose of enumerating his beautiful attributes mentioned here is to explain what moved him, peace be upon him, to the dispute that proceeded from him.

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 76:

﴿O Ibrahim﴾. That is: the angels said, "O Ibrahim, ﴿turn away from this﴾ dispute, ﴿for it﴾, that is, the matter, ﴿has indeed come, the command of your Lord﴾, that is, His decree proceeding in accordance with His eternal judgment, which is an expression for the eternal will and the divine providence that necessitates the order of existent things in a particular arrangement, according to its relation to things at their appointed times, and this is what is expressed by the term qadar (divine decree). ﴿And indeed they will be struck by a punishment that cannot be turned back﴾, neither by dispute, nor by supplication, nor by anything else."

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 77:**

﴿And when Our messengers came to Lot﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: They set out from Ibrahim, peace be upon him, to Lot, peace be upon him, and the distance between the two towns was four farsakh. They entered upon him in the form of beardless young men of handsome faces. Therefore ﴿he was distressed on their account﴾, meaning his coming troubled him, because he thought they were men. He feared that his people would target them and that he would be unable to defend them.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Amr read *wa-si'a* and *si'at* with *ishmam* (a partial rounding of the lips, indicating the original *damma*) on the *sin*, i.e., *wa-sī'a* and *sī'at*, with the *sin* pronounced as if it were vowelled with a *damma*. Both forms are the passive of *sā'a* (to be distressed), in which the *sin* is given the sound of *damma* as an indication of the passive.

It is narrated that Allah, exalted is He, said to the angels: "Do not destroy them until Lot bears witness against them four times." So when he walked with them, leading them to his house, he said to them: "Has the matter of this town not reached you?" They said: "What is its matter?" He said: "I bear witness that it is the worst town on earth in its deeds," saying this four times. Then they entered his house with him, and no one knew of this. His wife went out and informed her people, and she said: "In Lot's house there are men whose faces I have never seen the likes of."

﴿And he felt constrained for them﴾, meaning his chest, or his heart, or his capacity and strength was constrained by their presence. This is a metaphor for intense distress, arising from his inability to repel the harm and to devise a way to deal with it. It was also said: his soul was constrained by this event. The mention of *dhar‘* (the forearm, or reach) is a figure of speech, referring to measurement, as though it were the measure of the body, meaning: his body's measure was constrained from bearing what had befallen him. It was also said: *dhirā‘* (the forearm) is the name of the limb from the elbow to the fingertips, and *dhar‘* is its extension. The meaning of the constriction of the *dhar‘* in the words of the Most High, "he felt constrained for them *dhar‘an*," is the shortness of it, just as the meaning of its expansion and extension is its length. The reason for the illustration by this is that the short-armed person, when he extends his arm to reach what the long-armed person reaches, falls short of it and is unable to reach it. So it is used as a figure for one whose capacity falls short of attaining the matter.

﴿And he said, "This is a distressing day."﴾ *'Asib*: severe, from *'asabahu* when he tightened it (i.e., bound it tightly).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 78:

﴿And his people came hastening towards him﴾, that is, to Lut, while he was in his house with his guests. ﴿They were hastening towards him﴾, that is, they were rushing, as if they were being driven forcibly to seek indecency with his guests. The clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring back to ﴿his people﴾. Likewise, the words of the Exalted: ﴿And before this they used to do evil deeds﴾, that is, before this time. ﴿They used to do evil deeds﴾, that is, they came hastening while they were, in fact, immersed in doing evil deeds. They had become accustomed to them and trained themselves in them, until its ugliness no longer remained in their hearts; for this reason they did not feel shame at what they did, in coming to him hastening and openly.

﴿He said: O my people, these are my daughters; they are purer for you﴾, so marry them. They had previously been seeking them, but he would not give them to them because of their wickedness and their unsuitability, not because it was not legally permissible, for marrying believing women to unbelievers was permitted. The Prophet (ﷺ) gave his two daughters in marriage to ʿUtbah ibn Abi Lahab and Abu al-ʿAs ibn al-Rabiʿ, before the revelation, and both of them were unbelievers. It was also said: they had two respected leaders whom they obeyed, so he wished to marry his daughters to them. Whichever it was, he intended by it the protection of his guest, and that is the utmost of generosity. It was also said: that statement of his was not meant literally as an intention to marry; rather it was an exaggeration of humility toward them and a display of his intense distress at what they had put before him, hoping that they would feel shame before him and be softened toward him when they heard that, and so desist from what they had undertaken, especially since the matter was evident and it was established knowledge to him and to them all that there was no lawful union between them. This is most fitting to their words: ﴿You certainly know that we have no right in your daughters﴾, as you will come to see.

﴿So fear God﴾ by abandoning the indecencies, or by preferring them over themselves. ﴿And do not disgrace me regarding my guests﴾, that is, do not shame me concerning them, for humiliating a man's guest and neighbour is humiliating him. Or: do not make me ashamed, from ''khizaya'' (disgrace), which is shame. ﴿Is there not among you a man of sound judgement﴾, who is guided to the clear truth and refrains from the ugly falsehood?!

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 79:

﴿They said﴾, turning away from what he had advised them of, namely fearing God and refraining from disgracing him, and answering the beginning of his speech: ﴿You certainly know that we have no claim on your daughters﴾, appealing to his knowledge of that, meaning: you certainly know that there is no way to marriage between us and you, that your offer is nothing but the offer of a sābiri, and that we have no desire for that. ﴿And indeed you know what we want﴾, namely having intercourse with males. And when he, peace be upon him, had despaired of their turning back from the error they were in.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 80:

﴿He said: "If only I had power against you"﴾ That is: I would do to you what I did, and accomplish what I accomplished, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if there were a Qur'an by which the mountains were set moving, or the earth were split asunder, or the dead were made to speak...﴾ ﴿Or that I could take refuge in a mighty pillar﴾ is coordinated with ﴿(If only I had power against you)﴾ and so on to its end, because of the sense of verb it contains. That is: if I were strong enough to repel you by myself, or if I had taken refuge with a mighty, powerful helper by whom I could protect myself from you, he compared that to the base of a mountain in firmness and protection.

It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "May Allah have mercy on my brother Lut, he used to take refuge in a mighty pillar."

It is narrated that he (peace be upon him) closed his door upon his guests, and began to argue with them from behind the door, so they climbed over the wall. When the angels saw the distress that had come upon Lut...

They said, meaning the messengers, when they saw his inability to repel his people: "O Lot, we are messengers of your Lord. They will never reach you [to harm you or cause you any injury]. So open the door and leave us and them to deal with each other." He opened the door, and they entered. Gabriel, peace be upon him, asked his Lord, the Lord of Might, exalted is His majesty, for permission to punish them, and He granted it. So he stood in the form in which he appears, spread his wing, and he has two wings. Upon him was a sash of strung pearls, and he was bright-toothed. He struck their faces with his wing, obliterated their eyes, and blinded them, as the Mighty and Exalted said: ﴿And We obliterated their eyes﴾. So they could no longer find the way. They went out saying: "Haste! Haste! For in the house of Lot there are sorcerers."

﴿So travel with your family﴾ with a cut (qat') from al-isra' (travelling by night). Ibn Kathir and Nafi' read it with wasl (connecting the initial hamza) wherever it occurs in the Qur'an, from al-sura. The fa' (so) indicates that the command to travel is ordered upon the information about their being messengers, which signals that commands and prohibitions were coming to him from His presence, peace be upon him. ﴿At a portion of the night﴾, meaning a part of it. ﴿And let not any of you turn back﴾, meaning do not lag behind, or do not look behind you, ﴿anyone﴾ of you and your family. They were forbidden from that so that they would press on with the journey, for whoever looks back at what is behind him cannot avoid a brief pause. Or [they were forbidden] lest they see the punishment descending upon their people and feel pity for them. ﴿Except your wife﴾ is an exception from His saying, "So travel with your family." What supports this is that it was read: (So travel with your family at a portion of the night, except your wife). It was also read with the raf' (nominative) as a badal (substitution) from ﴿anyone﴾ (ahad). Thus al-iltifat (turning back) means lagging behind, not looking backward, so that there is no contradiction between the two mutawatir (widely transmitted) readings. The nasb (accusative) implies that he, peace be upon him, was not commanded to travel with her, while the raf' implies that he was commanded to do so. The excuse that the implication of the raf' is merely her being with them, and that this does not require a command to travel with her, so that no contradiction arises because she may travel on her own, is [as it is] narrated: when he travelled with his family she followed them, and when she heard the crash of the punishment she turned and said, "O my people!" A stone overtook her and killed her. And [the excuse holds] that he, peace be upon him, travelled with her without a command to do so, since the implication of the nasb is only the absence of a command to travel with her, not a prohibition against travelling with her, such that his travelling with her would contradict a prohibition. This does not help, because making the exception refer to al-iltifat requires that the family remain in its general sense, so travelling with her would be definitely commanded. Interpreting ahliyyah (familyhood) in one reading as religious kinship and in the other as lineal kinship, despite what is plainly arbitrary and forced in it, is a return to the very contradiction that was being avoided. Therefore, the better course is to make the exception, in both readings, from His saying "la yaltafit" (let none turn back), like the one in His saying, ﴿what they did not do except a few of them﴾ (ma fa'aluhu illa qalilun minhum). Ibn 'Amir read it with the nasb, though the raf' is more eloquent as a badal, and it is not far-fetched that most readers follow what is less eloquent. It does not follow from this that she was commanded to turn back; rather, he was not forbidding her from it, as a matter of expediency. For this reason, he gave the reason in a resumptive (istinaf) form, saying:

﴿Indeed, what befalls them will befall her﴾ of the punishment, namely the rain of stones, even if the sinking did not befall her. The pronoun in innahu (indeed he) is the dhamir al-sha'n (pronoun of the matter). Musibuha (one who befalls her) is the khabar (predicate), and ma asabahum (what befell them) is the mubtada' (subject). The clause is the predicate of inna, whose subject is the pronoun of the matter. In this there is, as is not hidden, a magnification of the matter of what befell them. It is not good to make the exception disconnected (istithna' munqati', an exception not of the same kind as what precedes it) on the raf' reading.

﴿Indeed their appointed time is the morning﴾, meaning the appointed time of their punishment and destruction. This is a reason for the command to travel and the prohibition against turning back, which conveys an urging to hasten. ﴿Is not the morning near?﴾ is an emphasis of the reason, for the nearness of the morning calls for hastening the journey, to get far from the sites of the punishment. It is narrated that he said to the angels, "When is the appointed time of their destruction?" They said, "The morning." He said, "I want it sooner than that." So they said that. The appointed time of their destruction was made the morning because it is the time of ease and rest, so the descent of punishment at that time is more dreadful. And because it is more fitting for that to be a lesson for those who look on.

﴿When Our command came﴾, that is, the time of Our punishment and its appointed hour, which was the morning, ﴿We turned it upside down﴾, that is, the highest part of the towns of the people of Lot, which are the ones referred to as the Mu'tafikat (the overturned cities). They were five cities containing four hundred thousand thousands. ﴿Its highest part became its lowest﴾, that is, We overturned them into that state. "Its highest part" is the first object (maf'ul awwal, the first object of the verb) of the verb "ja'ala" (to make), and "its lowest part" is the second object (maf'ul thani, the second object) of it. This is for the sake of magnifying the matter and emphasizing the severity of the calamity, even though the overturning also occurs in the reverse sense. This is because making their highest part, which was their place of settlement and their homes, into their lowest part is more grievous and harder for them than making their lowest part into their highest, although the latter implies the former.

It is narrated that Jibril, peace be upon him, placed his wing beneath them, then lifted them up to the sky until the people of the sky heard the barking of dogs and the crowing of roosters. Then he overturned them upon them. The attribution of the making and the raining to His pronoun, glorified is He, is based on the fact that He is the one who causes it, for the sake of magnifying the matter and emphasizing the severity of the calamity.

﴿And We rained down upon it﴾, upon the people of the towns or their outliers, ﴿stones of sijjil﴾, that is, of clay that has been hardened into stone, like His saying: ﴿stones of clay﴾. Its origin is (سِنْكْ كُلْ), which was Arabicized. It was also said that it is from "ajsalahu", meaning he sent it, or "adarra 'ataahu", meaning he made his gift abundant, and the meaning is "of the like of a thing sent," or "like a gift in abundance." It was also said that it is from the "sijjil" (register), meaning from what God, may He be exalted, had written that He would punish them with. It was also said that its origin is from "sijjin" (a place of punishment), meaning from Hell, and its nun was changed to a lam. ﴿Layered﴾: it was arranged in the sky in layers, prepared for the punishment. It was also said that some of it was sent following one another, like a train of rains.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 83:

﴿Marked﴾, meaning marked for the punishment. It was also said: marked with white and red, or with a sign by which it is distinguished from the stones of the earth, or with the name of the one it is to strike. ﴿With your Lord﴾, in His treasuries, which no one else may dispose of, the Mighty and Majestic. ﴿And it is not﴾, that is, the stones described, ﴿far from the wrongdoers﴾, from every wrongdoer. ﴿For they, because of their wrongdoing, deserve it and are bound to it.﴾ In this is a severe warning to all people of wrongdoing.

«It is narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he asked Jibril (peace be upon him), and he said: "He means the wrongdoers of your community. There is none among them but that he is at the edge of a stone which falls upon him from one hour to another."» It was also said that the pronoun refers to the towns, meaning that they are near to the wrongdoers of Makkah, who pass by them on their journeys and travels to al-Shām. The masculine form of ﴿far﴾ is used either because ﴿stones﴾ is treated as a collective noun (حجر), or because it is taken as agreeing with a masculine described noun, meaning "a far thing" or "a far place." For although the stones were in the sky, which is at the greatest distance from the earth, yet when they fall from it they are the swiftest thing to reach them, so it is as if they were in a place near to them. Or it is because the word is on the pattern of the verbal noun (مَصْدَر), like الزَّفِير and الصَّهِيل, and verbal nouns are used as descriptions for both masculine and feminine alike.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 84:

﴿And to Madyan﴾: i.e., to the descendants of Madyan ibn Ibrahim, peace be upon him; or the name has been made, by predominance, the name of the tribe; or [it means] the people of Madyan, and it is a town which Madyan built, so it was named after him. ﴿Their brother﴾: i.e., their kinsman, ﴿Shu'ayb﴾. He is the son of Mikil ibn Yashjur ibn Madyan. He was called "the orator of the prophets" (khatib al-anbiya') because of the excellence of his argumentation with his people. The sentence is conjoined with the Most High's saying: ﴿And to Thamud [We sent] their brother Salih﴾, i.e., and We sent to Madyan their brother Shu'ayb.

﴿He said﴾: a resumptive sentence (isti'naf), which occurs as an answer to a question arising from the opening of the discourse, as if it were said: "What did he say to them?" So it is answered: He said, as the messengers before him, peace be upon them, said: ﴿O my people, worship Allah﴾, make Him one and do not associate anything with Him, ﴿you have no god other than Him﴾, a confirmation of monotheism (tahqiq al-tawhid) and a reason (ta'lil) for the command to it. After commanding them with that which is the foundation of the religious affair and the first thing incumbent upon the responsible persons, he forbade them from the arrangement of the beginnings of what they had customarily practised of diminishing [others' due] and cheating in measure as a continuous habit, so he said: ﴿And do not diminish the measure and the balance﴾, so that you may not use that as a means to usurping people's rights. ﴿Indeed, I see you in prosperity﴾: i.e., possessing wealth and abundance which suffice you from that; or [in] a blessing from Allah, the due of which is that it be met with other than what you do, namely leniency and graciousness toward people, in gratitude for it; or: I see you in good, so do not remove it by the evil you are upon. In every case, this is a reason for the prohibition, followed by another reason, namely His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And indeed, I fear for you﴾ if you do not desist from that, ﴿the punishment of an encompassing day﴾, from which no one among you will escape. It was said: the punishment of a destroying day, from the saying of the Most High: ﴿And its fruit was encompassed [by destruction]﴾; its origin is from the encompassing of an enemy. The intended meaning is the punishment of the Day of Resurrection, or the punishment of annihilation. The attribution of encompassing to the day, while the encompassing is a state of the punishment, is a metaphorical attribution (al-isnad al-majazi), and in it is an exaggeration that is not hidden: for the day is a time which contains the events that occur in it; so when it encompasses its punishment, there is gathered for the one punished all that it contains of it, just as when it encompasses its blessing. It is also permissible that this be a reason for the command and the prohibition together.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 85:

﴿And O my people, give full measure and weight with justice﴾. That is, with equity, without excess or deficiency. For excess in measure and weight, although it is a voluntary favour that is recommended, is in the instrument forbidden just like deficiency. Thus the one who gives more does so for use at the time of measuring out, and the one who gives less does so for use at the time of weighing. He was commanded explicitly to equalise and balance them after being forbidden to diminish them, as an intensification in urging full measure and in preventing defrauding (bakhs), and as an alert that mere abstention from deficiency and defrauding is not sufficient for them; rather it is obligatory upon them to rectify what they have corrupted, and to make it a standard for their injustice and a law for their transgression.
