﴿And do not defraud people﴾ by means of their deficiency and lack of balance ﴿of their things﴾ which they buy with them. The prohibition of defrauding has been stated explicitly, although it was already understood within the prohibition of diminishing the standard and the command to fulfil it, out of concern for the matter and as encouragement to give full rights after the warning and deterrence against diminishing them. It is also permissible that what is meant by the command to give full measure (p-232) and weight is the command to give full measure of things measured and weighed, and that the prohibition of defrauding is general, covering deficiency in quantity and otherwise, as a generalisation after specification, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not commit corruption on the earth, being mischief-makers﴾, for corruption (al-'athy) encompasses the diminishing of rights and other kinds of corruption. It has also been said that bakhs means the maks, such as the taking of tithes in transactions. Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma said:

"Is there a tax (itawa) in all the markets of Iraq, and on everything a man sells, a dirham's maks?"

Corruption on the earth (al-'athy) is theft, highway robbery and raiding. The benefit of the qualifying phrase is to exclude what is done with the aim of reform, as al-Khidr, peace be upon him, did in piercing the ship and killing the boy. It has also been said that its meaning is: "And do not commit corruption on the earth, being mischief-makers" of the affair of your Hereafter and the interests of your religion.

"Allah's remainder" (baqiyyat Allah): that is, what He has left for you of what is lawful, after abstaining from engaging in the forbidden things, ﴿is better for you﴾ than what you gain through cheating and short-measuring, for that is ﴿scattered dust﴾ (haba'an mansuran). Rather, it is pure evil, even if you think it contains good, like His saying, ﴿Allah destroys usury and makes charities grow﴾. ﴿If you are believers﴾, on condition that you believe, for its being better, through bringing reward together with salvation, is necessarily conditional upon faith. Or the meaning is: if you are ones who give credence to me in what I tell you. It has been said: "the remainder" (al-baqiyyah) refers to acts of obedience, like His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿But the enduring good deeds are better in the sight of your Lord﴾. It was also read as (taqiyyat Allah) with a taa' on top [i.e., with a ta' rather than a ba'], meaning His piety against sins. ﴿And I am not a guardian over you﴾: I do not guard you from ugly deeds, or I do not keep account of your deeds so as to requite you. I am only a counselor and a conveyor of the message, and I have given a warning, having excused myself by warning, and I have spared no effort in that. Or the meaning is: I am not one who guards and withholds from you the blessings of Allah, the Exalted, if you do not abandon what you are upon of evil conduct.

They said: "O Shu'ayb, does your prayer command you that we abandon what our fathers worshipped?" [of the idols]. They answered his command, peace be upon him, to worship God alone, which implied forbidding them to worship the idols, with this. They went to great lengths in this, and reached the furthest degrees of licentiousness, debauchery and misguidance, for they did not content themselves with denying the revelation that commanded it, but went so far as to claim that there was no command for it from reason or intellect at all, and that it was among the judgments of whispering (waswasah) and madness. On this they based their question, and they said in mockery: "Does your prayer, which is one of the products of whispering and the deeds of madmen, command you to abandon the worship of idols, which we have inherited from father to grandfather?" They made him, peace be upon him, the one commanded, although what issued from him was in fact the command to worship God Most High and other laws, because he, peace be upon him, did not command them of his own accord, but on the basis of revelation, and he informed them that he was commanded to convey it to them. They singled out the attribution of the command to the prayer from among all the other rulings of prophethood because he, may God bless him and grant him peace, was much given to prayer and was known for it, and when they saw him praying they would wink at one another and laugh, so that it became, among all the rites of the religion, a source of laughter for them. It has also been read as ﴿أصَلَواتُكَ﴾ (your prayers, in the plural).

﴿أوْ أنْ نَفْعَلَ في أمْوالِنا ما نَشاءُ﴾ (or that we do with our wealth what we wish). This is a reply to his command, peace be upon him, to give full measure and dues, and his prohibition of defrauding and diminishing. It is coordinated ('atf, grammatical coordination) with ما, meaning: or that we be left to do with our wealth what we wish, of taking and giving, increasing and decreasing. It has also been read with the letter ta' in both verbs, coordinated on the object of (تَأْمُرُكَ), meaning: your prayer commands you that you do with our wealth what you wish. The coordination with ما, as has been said, requires that "abandonment" be understood in two different senses, and what is meant by his action, peace be upon him, is the obligation of full measure and justice in their dealings, not the act of giving full measure itself, for that is not one of his actions, peace be upon him, but one of theirs.

As for why we did not say it is coordinated with (أنْ نَتْرُكَ): abandonment is not, in the strict sense, something commanded, rather what is commanded is his imposing upon them and his ordering them to it. The meaning is: your prayer commands you to impose upon us that we abandon what our fathers worshipped. Interpreting it to mean: your prayer commands you to do what is beyond your capacity and responsibility, namely the actions of others, so that this would be an insinuation from them about the weakness of his opinion, peace be upon him, and mockery of him from that angle, is refuted by the placing of the interrogative hamza (همزة الاستفهام) before the prayer and not before the command, and it requires that he, peace be upon him, have said during his preaching something that indicates this or gives that impression. How could that be? So reflect.

It has also been read with nun in the first and ta' in the second, coordinated with (أنْ نَتْرُكَ): or that we do, in our dealings, with our wealth what you wish of equalization and full measure. ﴿إنَّكَ لأنْتَ الحَلِيمُ الرَّشِيدُ﴾ (Indeed, you are surely the forbearing, the rightly guided). They described him, peace be upon him, with these two attributes in the manner of mockery, and they intended by that to ascribe to him the opposites of them, like the words of the guardians of Hell: ﴿ذُقْ إنَّكَ أنْتَ العَزِيزُ الكَرِيمُ﴾ (Taste, indeed you are the mighty, the noble). It may also be that it is a justification for what preceded of their deeming unlikely what they mentioned, meaning: (indeed, you are the forbearing, the rightly guided) according to your claim. As for describing him with them in reality, the context of mockery precludes it, except that by "prayer" is meant the religion, as has been said.

He said: "O my people, have you considered: if I am upon a clear proof (*bayyinah*), meaning a manifest argument and a luminous demonstration, by which He expressed what God, exalted is He, had given him of prophethood (*nubuwwah*) and wisdom (*hikmah*), in reply to their hideous saying, in which they made his commands and prohibitions unsupported by any authority, **from my Lord**, the Lord and Owner of my affairs, and the use of the conditional particle along with his certainty, peace be upon him, that he is in the state of the clear proofs and arguments, is in order to take into account the condition of those addressed and to observe good dialogue with them, as we mentioned in its parallels. **And He has provided me from Himself** — that is, from His presence — **with a goodly provision (rizq hasan)**, which is also prophethood and wisdom. He expressed these by that term to draw attention to the fact that these two, together with being a clear proof, are a goodly provision. How could they not be, when they are the basis of eternal life for him and for his community? The answer to the conditional is omitted, and the sense of the speech indicates it, meaning: 'Will you say about me what you say?' The meaning is that you have counted me among the foolish and the misguided, and you have regarded the commands and prohibitions issuing from me as of the kind that no rational person could utter, and you have made them of the rulings of whispering and madness. You have mocked me and my actions, to the point that you said: 'What he commands you, of monotheism (*tawhid*), of abandoning the worship of idols, and of avoiding fraud and short-weighing, is not what the commander of reason commands or the judge of insight decides, but what commands it is your prayer, which is one of the rulings of whispering and madness.' So inform me: if I am, from the side of my Lord and Owner of my affairs, established upon prophethood and wisdom, beyond which there is no further end of perfection nor any aim for an aspirant, and He has provided me thereby with a goodly provision, will you say about me and my actions what you say, of things in which there is no good and beyond which there is no evil? This is the answer demanded by the preceding and following context and supported by the noble composition. As for what has been said, that the omitted part is: 'Is it proper for me not to command you to abandon the worship of idols and to refrain from sins, or can I, with this bounty comprising the spiritual and bodily felicities, betray His revelation and oppose His command and prohibition?', then he is far removed from that. Its supposition would only suit if their speech is taken literally, and by 'prayer' is meant 'religion', in the sense: 'Does your religion command you to impose upon us the abandonment of our ancient gods and the abandonment of absolute freedom in our wealth, and to oppose us in that and split our ranks?' This is something that should not proceed from you, for you are the one renowned among us for excellent forbearance and complete rectitude, just as the saying of the people of Salih was: ﴿You were among us a man of hope before this﴾, recounted in that same manner. He was then answered with what they were answered. On this interpretation, the goodly provision means the lawful wealth that God, exalted is He, has given him, and the sense then is: 'Inform me: if I am a prophet from God, exalted is He, and He has provided me with lawful wealth, by which I am sufficient without the worlds, is it proper that I oppose His command and agree with you in what you do and what you leave undone?'

﴿And I do not desire﴾ by my forbidding you what I forbid you from, of fraud and short-weighing, ﴿to oppose you to that which I forbid you﴾, that is, to aim at it after you have turned away from it, and to be selfish with it apart from you. It is said: 'I opposed Zayd to such-and-such' when you aim at it while he has turned away from it, and 'I opposed him from such-and-such' when the matter is the reverse.

﴿I desire only﴾, that is, what I intend by what I undertake of command and prohibition is ﴿nothing but reform (al-islah)﴾, except that I reform you by sincere counsel and admonition ﴿as much as I am able﴾, that is, to the measure of the reform I am able to achieve. The restriction by it is to guard against being content with reform in general, not against desiring what is beyond his capacity. ﴿And my success is not but through God﴾, that is, my being granted success in realizing the reform I intend for you, ﴿only through God﴾, that is, through His support and help. Indeed, reform, from the standpoint of creation, is ascribed to Him, glorified is He, and I am only one of its apparent starting points. He, peace be upon him, said this to establish the truth and to remove what the ascription of ability to him might suggest, by way of his will, of independence in that. ﴿Upon Him I have relied﴾ in this, turning away from all else, for He is the Capable of every capable thing, while all else is utterly powerless in itself, indeed nonexistent, fallen from the rank of consideration, far from the station of seeking help from Him and relying upon Him.

﴿And to Him I turn in repentance﴾, that is, I return in what I am engaged in. It is also permissible that the meaning is: my being granted success in hitting the truth and the right in everything I do and leave undone is only through His guidance and help. ﴿Upon Him I have relied﴾ points to pure tawhid, both essential and actional. ﴿And to Him I turn in repentance﴾, that is, upon Him I turn with the depths of my soul in the midst of my affairs. The choice of the present-tense form over the past tense is more suitable for establishment and certainty, as in "I rely" (tawakkul), to evoke the image and to indicate continuity. It is not hidden what his answer, peace be upon him, contains of observing gentleness in return, gentleness in drawing them down, preserving the rules of good engagement and dialogue, paving the way for the truth by seeking success from the presence of God, exalted is He, and seeking His help in his affairs, cutting off the hopes of the disbelievers, displaying indifference toward them, and not caring about their enmity. As for their threat by returning to God, exalted is He, for judgment, as has been said, this is not so, because repentance is only the voluntary return by action to God, exalted is He, not the compelled return for judgment, or what encompasses it.

﴿وَيا قَوْمِ لا يَجْرِمَنَّكُمْ﴾ means: "O my people, let not my opposition to you bring upon you..." That is, let it not cause you to earn (yaksibannakum) a sin, from "jaramtuhu dhanban," as in "kasabtuhu malan" (I earned him wealth). ﴿شِقاقِي﴾ means my enmity toward you. The root sense of both words is that one of two opponents is on one side or slope, and the other is on another. ﴿أنْ يُصِيبَكُمْ﴾ is the second object (maf'ul thani) of "yajrimannakum." The meaning is: let not your enmity toward me earn for you that there befall you ﴿مِثْلُ ما أصابَ قَوْمَ نُوحٍ﴾ "like what befell the people of Noah" from the drowning, ﴿أوْ قَوْمَ هُودٍ﴾ "or the people of Hud" from the wind, ﴿أوْ قَوْمَ صالِحٍ﴾ "or the people of Salih" from the blast and the quake.

Ibn Kathir read "yajrimannakum" with a damma on the yā' (ya'), from "ajramtuhu dhanban," when you make him one who commits it, that is, one who earns it. This is derived from "jarama" when it is transitive to one object, just as "uksibuhu al-mal" (I cause him to earn wealth) is derived from "kasaba al-mal." Just as there is no difference in meaning between "kassabtuhu malan" and "aksabtuhu iyyahu," there is no difference in meaning between "jarramtuhu dhanban" and "ajramtuhu iyyahu." However, the first is more correct and more common on the tongues of the eloquent. Abu Haywa read "mithla ma asaba" with a fatha, because it is attached to a word that is indeclinable (ghayr mutamakkin), as in the verse:

Nothing prevented them from drinking from it, except that a dove called out among branches of a tree bearing awqāl (a kind of fruit).

Although this, outwardly, is a prohibition of opposition for fear of incurring the punishment, in reality it is a prohibition to the disbelievers from opposing him (peace be upon him), in the most gentle and most inventive manner, as has passed in Surah al-Ma'idah at the words of Him, Exalted: ﴿وَلا يَجْرِمَنَّكم شَنَآنُ قَوْمٍ﴾ ... the verse.

﴿وَما قَوْمُ لُوطٍ مِنكم بِبَعِيدٍ﴾ "The people of Lot are not far from you," in time or in place. If you do not take warning from the nations before them that were enumerated, then take warning from them. It seems that he only changed the style of warning with them and did not state explicitly what befell them, but was content with mentioning their nearness, indicating that this suffices in place of mentioning it, because it is well known that they are arranged in the string of the calamities of the nations already mentioned. Or, they are not far from you in disbelief and sins, so it is not unlikely that there befall you the like of what befell them. The singular "ba'id" is used with its masculine form because the intended sense is "wa ma ihlakuhum" (and their destruction is not...), with an implied noun (mudaf, construct), or "wa ma hum bi-shay'in ba'id" (and they are not a distant thing), because the aim is to convey that they are not distant in any absolute sense, not with regard to the particular quality of being a people. Or, they are not in a distant time or a distant place. It is not unlikely that this is because it follows the pattern of verbal nouns (masadir), like "nahiq" and "shahiq."

When he (peace be upon him) warned them of the evil end of their conduct, he followed it, hoping they would turn back from their transgression in which they were wandering, by urging them toward seeking forgiveness and repentance, so he said:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 90:

﴿And seek forgiveness from your Lord, then turn to Him in repentance.﴾ The explanation of the like of this has passed at the beginning of the surah. ﴿Indeed, my Lord is Most Merciful﴾, of great mercy towards those who repent, ﴿Most Loving﴾, exaggerating in doing what one does who is intensely loving (wadud) towards the one he loves, in kindness and benevolence. This is a justification (ta'lil) for the command to seek forgiveness and repent, and an exhortation (hath) to both.

﴿They said, "O Shu'ayb, we do not understand much of what you say."﴾ Fiqh (comprehension; knowing the speaker's purpose from his words) means knowing what the speaker intends by his speech. That is, "we do not understand what you mean." They said this after they had heard from him the clear proofs of the truth, presented in the best and most eloquent manner. Their stratagems were exhausted and their pretexts failed them, so they found no way to engage him in discussion except by turning away from the path of truth and taking the road to wretchedness. This is the habit of one who is silenced and overcome by argument: he meets clear evidence with abuse, threats, and intimidation. So they treated his speech, which contained every kind of wisdom, admonition, and type of knowledge and insight, as if its meaning could not be understood and its substance could not be grasped. They also included in this the implication that his words contained things that deserve the utmost punishment and retribution, and perhaps this was because of his warning against the fates of the earlier nations. For this reason they said: ﴿"And indeed we see you among us as weak"﴾, meaning among us, ﴿weak﴾, having no strength and no power to bring harm or benefit, to inflict or to repel. ﴿"And were it not for your clan"﴾, meaning were it not for our regard for their side, not because they would prevent us or defend you against us, ﴿"we would have stoned you"﴾. The prevention of a clan, a term for three to seven or up to ten people, by people who are in fact thousands in number, is something that can hardly be imagined. This is confirmed by the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿"And you are not against us one of honor"﴾, meaning not one who is respected or esteemed such that we would refrain from stoning you. We refrain from him only out of consideration for the sanctity of your clan, who remained steadfast in our religion, did not choose you over us, and did not follow you rather than us. The placing of the pronoun (ḍamīr) before the negative particle (ḥarf al-nafy), even though the predicate is not a verb, still indicates that the negation returns to the agent rather than to the verb, especially with the accompanying context of his saying, "and were it not for your clan." It is as if it were said: "And you are not against us one of honor, rather your clan are the honored ones among us." Since their purpose in this boasting was to negate what he possessed of the divine strength and honor, which is required by his being upon clear evidence from his Lord and supported by Him, and which is demanded by the matter of seeking success from Him, relying upon Him, and turning to Him, and to remove all of that from the level of being considered or regarded.

Abu al-Su'ud, *Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim*, on Surah 11, verse 92:

﴿He said﴾, peace be upon him, in reply to them: ﴿O my people, is my clan more esteemed by you than God?﴾ The belittling of One who is not made mighty except by Him, Mighty and Majestic, is a belittling of His mighty presence. He denied them the greater esteem of his clan over God, Exalted, even though what they affirmed was only the general might of his clan and not that they were more esteemed than Him, Mighty and Majestic, although both share the same basic might. This was to double the rebuke and repeat the reproach. He first denied their preference for the side of the clan over the side of God, Exalted, and then denied any might at all. The meaning is: "Is my clan more esteemed by you than God? This is something that can hardly be true, since you have not assigned to Him, Exalted, any share of might whatsoever."

﴿And you have taken Him﴾ (by reason of your not regarding the One who neither brings nor returns anything except by His command) ﴿cast behind your backs﴾, that is, as something discarded, forgotten behind the back and not cared for. The word *ẓihriyyan* is a relative noun derived from *ẓahr* (back), with the vowel changed to mark the change in the nisba, like *amsiyy* as the nisba of *ams* (yesterday). ﴿Indeed my Lord encompasses what you do﴾, that is, the evil deeds, among which is your failure to respect His side. ﴿Encompasses﴾: nothing hidden from Him escapes Him, and even if you have made Him forgotten, He will requite you for them.

It is also possible that the denial is meant as a rejection and a refutation. When they claimed that they would not refrain from stoning him, peace be upon him, because of his strength and might, but out of regard for his clan's side, he rebutted them: you have not measured God with His true, mighty measure, and you have not shown regard for His strong presence, so how can you show regard for the side of my humble clan?

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 93:

﴿O my people, act﴾. When he (peace be upon him) saw their persistence in disbelief, and that they would not desist from the sins they were committed to, to the point that they had become bold enough to commit the grave offence of making light of him and resolving to stone him, were it not for the sanctity of his kinsmen, he said to them, in the manner of a threat: act ﴿according to your position﴾. That is: to the utmost of your ability and capacity. It is said: "makana makanatan" when one becomes firmly established to the highest degree. He (peace be upon him) said this in response to their claim that they were strong and capable of stoning him, and that he was weak among them and had no power. Or it means according to your direction and your course, from their saying "makan" and "makanah," like "maqam" and "maqamah." The meaning is: remain upon what you are upon of disbelief and opposition to me, and all else you are upon that has no good in it, and exert your effort in harming me and carrying out what is in your intention and bringing into action from potential into actuality what is in your wish. ﴿Indeed, I am acting﴾ according to my position, as God supports me and grants me success with all kinds of support and success. ﴿You will soon know﴾. When he (peace be upon him) threatened them with his saying: (act according to your position, indeed I am acting), it was likely that someone among them would ask, "Then what will happen after that?" So it was said: you will soon know ﴿who will receive a punishment that disgraces him﴾. The punishment is described as disgracing as an allusion to what they had threatened him (peace be upon him) with, namely stoning, for although it is a punishment, it contains a clear disgrace, since it is not inflicted except for a grave crime that necessitates it. ﴿And who is a liar﴾. This is coordinated with (who will receive) and not as its counterpart (qasim). Rather, since they had threatened him with stoning and called him a liar, it was said: you will soon know who is the one punished and who is the liar. In this there is an allusion to their lying in their claim to strength and power to stone him (peace be upon him), and in attributing to him weakness and humiliation, and in their claim that they spared him out of regard for the side of his kinsmen. The difference between the two coordinated clauses in being verbal and nominal is because the lying of a liar is not something awaited in the way the arrival of punishment is, rather what is awaited is the manifestation of the prior, continuing lie. As for "man" (who), it may be an interrogative (ism istifhamiyyah) suspending the knowing from acting (mu'allaqah), as if it were said: you will soon know which of us will receive a punishment that disgraces him and which of us is a liar. Or it may be a relative (mawsulah), meaning: you will soon recognize the one who will receive a punishment and the one who is a liar. ﴿And watch﴾, and wait for the outcome of what I say. ﴿Indeed, I am with you a watcher﴾, awaiting, the form "fa'il" here meaning "one who watches" like "sarim" (one who cuts), or "one who observes" like "'ashir" (companion), or "one who is awaited" like "rafi'" (elevated). The addition of "with you" (ma'akum) shows his (peace be upon him) complete confidence in his matter.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 11, verse 94:**

﴿When Our command came﴾, that is, Our punishment, as His saying, exalted is He, ﴿You will soon know who will receive a punishment that disgraces him﴾ indicates. Or it means its time, for the expectation (al-irtiqab) implies this. ﴿We saved Shu'ayb and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us﴾, which is the faith to which We guided them, or by a mercy coming from Us to them. It is mentioned with the conjunction "wa" (and), as in the story of 'Ad, because no promise preceded it that would function as a cause requiring the particle "fa'" (then) before its effect, as in the stories of Salih and Lut. In those stories a prior promise had come, in His saying, ﴿That is a promise not to be denied﴾, and His saying, ﴿Indeed their appointed time is the morning﴾.

﴿And the cry seized those who had done wrong﴾. The noun is used instead of a pronoun to record their wrongdoing against them, and to indicate that what seized them was due to their wrongdoing, whose kinds were detailed earlier. ﴿The cry (al-sayha)﴾: it is said that Jibril, peace be upon him, shouted at them, and they perished. In Surah al-A'raf, ﴿the earthquake (al-rajfa) seized them﴾, and in Surah al-'Ankabut, ﴿the earthquake seized them﴾, that is, the quaking (al-zalzala). Perhaps it is among the concomitants (rawadif) of the cry, which entails the agitation of the air that leads to it, as was mentioned before.

﴿So they were found in their homes, lying prostrate (jathimin)﴾, dead, remaining in their places, with no escape from them.

Since the object of knowledge in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿You will soon know who will receive a punishment...﴾ and so on, is not the arrival of the punishment itself, but rather who will be struck by it, its arrival was made a matter whose occurrence is certain, needing no report about it, since it was made a condition. The saving of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, and the destruction of the disbelievers were made its answer and the intended point of the statement. The saving of Shu'ayb was placed first out of concern for his matter, and as a declaration that mercy, which is what lordship requires, precedes wrath, whose effect appears according to the consequence of their misdeeds and crimes.

(p-238) ﴿As if they had never flourished therein.﴾ That is: they did not dwell (*lam yuqimu*) in it, moving about freely in its regions and roaming in its environs.

﴿Away with Madyan, just as Thamud was taken away!﴾ The shift from the implicit pronoun (*al-idmar*) to the explicit noun (*al-izhar*) is so that it would more clearly indicate their transgression (*tughyan*), which led them to this state, and so that it would be more fitting for those whose destruction is compared to theirs, namely Thamud. Their destruction was compared to theirs because both were destroyed by a kind of punishment, namely the shout (*al-sayhah*), except that these were struck with the cry from above them, whereas those were struck from beneath them.

It is also read as *ba'udat* with a damma, according to the original form. The kasra in *ba'idat* is an alteration that restricts the meaning of distance to that which causes destruction and remoteness, and it is a verbal noun for both of them. The *bu'd* (with damma) is the verbal noun of the kasra form.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 96:

"And We certainly sent Musa with Our signs" — "signs" here means the nine clear signs (al-ayat al-tis'a al-mufassalat), which are the staff, the white hand, the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, the reduction of fruits, and the souls (al-anfus). Some have counted them as one sign and reckoned among them the overshadowing of the mountain (idhlal al-jabal), but this is not so, for it was [a means of] accepting the rulings of the Torah when the Children of Israel refused them. The bi' (with) is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the object of (﴿We sent﴾), or as a qualifier (na't) of its emphasized verbal noun (masdar). That is: We sent him while he was accompanied by Our signs, or We sent him with a sending accompanied by them.

"And a manifest authority" (﴿wa-sultanin mubin﴾) is the striking miracles among them, or it is the staff. The singling out of it by mention is to show its nobility, because it was the most dazzling of them. Or the intended meaning of "signs" is what is other than it. Or the two expressions refer to one thing, meaning: We sent him combining in him being Our signs and being a manifest authority for his prophethood, clear in itself, or making it clear, from abana (which is intransitive and transitive). Or it is dominance and power, as in His saying, exalted is He: "And We will give you both an authority" (﴿wa-naj'alu lakuma sultanan﴾). It may also be that what is meant is what he, peace be upon him, made clear in the course of his call when Pharaoh said to him: "Who is your Lord?" (﴿man rabbukuma﴾), so what of the former generations? [...] Of the refined realities and fitting subtleties. Taking it as an expression for the Torah, or including it among the signs, is refuted by His saying, mighty and majestic:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 97:

﴿To Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾. Its revelation came only after the destruction of Pharaoh and his people entirely, so that the Children of Israel might act upon it in what they do and what they refrain from. As for Pharaoh and his people, they were commanded to worship the Lord of the worlds, exalted is His authority, and to abandon the monstrous grandeur that the tyrant claimed and that his rebellious faction accepted from him, and to send the Children of Israel away from captivity and coercion. The specific mention of his chiefs (mala'), although his mission (may peace be upon him) was addressed to his entire people, is because of their eminence in opinion and in managing affairs, and because others followed them in what they approached and what they withdrew from.

The commentary does not explicitly state Pharaoh's disbelief in the signs of God Most High and his immersion in the misguidance and misleading that he was upon. Instead it confines itself to mentioning the matter of his chiefs, so it says: ﴿they followed the command of Pharaoh﴾, that is, his command to disbelieve in what Moses (peace be upon him) brought of the clear truth. This is to signal the clarity of his condition, so that his disbelief and his command to his chiefs to do so are, as it were, a matter of certain existence, not in need of explicit mention. What needs to be mentioned is the matter of his chiefs, who vacillated between one who guides to the truth and one who calls to misguidance, so He censured them for their poor choice.

The use of the particle fa' (then/so) in their following, which follows from Pharaoh's command, which is based on his disbelief, which was preceded by the conveying of the message, indicates the suddenness of their following and the haste of Pharaoh in disbelief and in commanding them to it. It is as if all of that did not delay after the sending and the conveying, but rather all of it occurred at one time, so their following occurred immediately after that. It is also permissible that the command of Pharaoh be intended as his well-known matter and his deviant course, so the meaning of "they followed" would be that they persisted in following. The fa' here is like what is in your saying: "I admonished him, but he did not heed, and I shouted at him, but he did not desist." For bringing about a thing after the arrival of what requires abstaining from it, even if it is continuation upon it, is in terms of its description a new act and a fresh deed. So reflect.

The avoidance of the pronoun is to dispel the illusion of a return to Moses (peace be upon him) from the beginning of the matter, and to intensify the disgrace of the condition of those who followed. Pharaoh is a byword for corruption, causing corruption, misguidance and misleading, so their following him is due to extreme ignorance and lack of insight. The same applies to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and the command of Pharaoh was not rightly guided﴾. Rushd (right guidance) is the opposite of ghayy (error), and it may also be intended as praiseworthy outcome. On the first meaning, meaning "one who guides" or "one possessed of rushd", it is a literal linguistic usage (haqiqa lughawiyya) and the attribution is figurative (majaz); on the second, it is figurative and the attribution is literal.

﴿He will lead his people﴾ all of them, from the nobles and others, ﴿on the Day of Resurrection﴾. That is, he will go before them, from *qadama* in the sense of *taqaddama* (to go ahead). This is a new clause (*istiʾnaf*, a resumptive sentence, one that begins a fresh statement) explaining his state in the Hereafter: just as he was their leader in misguidance, so too he will go before them into the Fire, and they will follow him. Or it serves to clarify that the outcome of his affair is not good and that its end is evil. ﴿So he will bring them to the Fire﴾, that is, he will bring them. The use of the past tense form (*fa-awradahum*) indicates that the event will certainly occur without doubt. Pharaoh is likened to the forerunner (*al-fārit*) who goes ahead of those coming to water, his followers to those coming to water, and the Fire to the water they come to. Then it is said: ﴿And wretched is the watering-place to which they are brought﴾, that is, wretched is the watering-place that they approach, which is the Fire. This is because the watering-place is sought for quenching thirst and cooling the hearts, whereas the Fire is the opposite of that.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 99:

﴿And they were made to follow﴾: i.e., the chiefs (al-mala') who followed the command of Pharaoh (Fir'awn). ﴿In this [world]﴾: i.e., in the worldly life (al-dunya), ﴿a curse﴾ (la'nah) ʿaẓīmah (great), in that those who came after them among the nations curse them until the Day of Resurrection. ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection﴾ as well, in that all the people of the place of standing (al-mawqif) curse them altogether. So the curse follows them wherever they go, and revolves with them wherever they turn in the place of standing. Just as they followed Pharaoh, the curse followed them in both abodes, as a fitting recompense (jaza' wifaqan). The description of their dreadful state and their shameful condition was sufficient, and there was no need to describe the state of Pharaoh, since when their state was thus, what then is your thought about the state of the one who misled them and cast them into this far-reaching error? And since it is the nature of followers to be helpers of the one they follow, the curse was made their ʿifd (reward/support) in the manner of mockery (al-tahakkum). So it is said: ﴿Wretched is the gift that is given﴾, i.e., wretched is the help that is helped. The word rifd has been explained as "gift" (ʿaṭa'), but the context does not suit this. Its original meaning is that which is added to something else to strengthen it. The object of dispraise is omitted, i.e., their rifd, which is the curse in both abodes. That it is "marfud" (given as support) is because each curse among them assists and strengthens its companion and supports it.

That (﴿ذَلِكَ﴾) is a reference to what has been related of the accounts of the nations, and its distance is in terms of its having passed in mention and address to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). It is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is ﴿مِن أنْباءِ القُرى﴾ ("of the news of the towns"), those destroyed for what their own hands had earned, ﴿نَقُصُّهُ عَلَيْكَ﴾ ("We relate it to you") being a predicate following a predicate. That is: that story is among the accounts of the towns that are related to you. ﴿مِنها﴾ ("of them") means of those towns, ﴿قائِمٌ وحَصِيدٌ﴾ ("some still standing and some reaped"), that is: and of them there is some reaped, the second part being omitted because the first indicates it. What remains of them is likened to a crop standing on its stalk, and what has been effaced and perished is likened to the reaped harvest. The clause is resumptive (mustanna'afah) and has no place in terms of i'rab.

(p-240) ﴿And We did not wrong them﴾ by destroying them, ﴿but they wronged themselves﴾ by making themselves liable to destruction through committing what necessitates it. ﴿So their gods, whom they invoked besides Allah, did not avail them﴾, meaning: they did not benefit them, nor did they repel the punishment (ba's) of Allah the Exalted from them. ﴿Their gods which they called upon﴾, i.e., which they worshipped, ﴿besides Allah﴾. The present tense (yad'una) is chosen to relate a past state, or to indicate the continuity of their worship of them. ﴿Anything﴾ is in the position of a verbal noun (masdar), i.e., any kind of avail. ﴿When the command of your Lord came﴾, i.e., at the time of the coming of His punishment. It is in the accusative governed by (aghnat). It has also been read as (ālihatuhumu al-lātī) and (yudʿawna) in the passive voice. ﴿And they added nothing to them but ruin﴾, i.e., destruction and loss, for they were destroyed and lost only because of their worship of them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 102:

﴿And thus﴾ i.e., like that seizing which has already been explained. It is in the nominative case as a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is His saying ﴿is the seizing of your Lord﴾. It is also read as (akhadha Rabbuka), in which case the kaf (ka) is in the accusative, being an emphatic infinitive (masdar mu'akkad). ﴿When He seizes the towns﴾ i.e., their people. The seizing is attributed to the towns only to indicate that its effect extends to them, as has been mentioned. It is also read as (idh akhadha). ﴿while they are wrongdoing﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the towns; in reality, however, it refers to their people, but since the towns have been placed in their stead in the seizing, the circumstantial description has been applied to the towns. Its benefit is to indicate that they were seized only because of their wrongdoing, so that this would be a lesson for every wrongdoer. ﴿Indeed His seizing is painful, severe﴾ i.e., grievous and difficult for the one seized, from which there is no hoped-for escape; and in it is what is not hidden of threat and warning.

﴿Indeed in that﴾, i.e., in His, the Exalted's, seizing of the destroyed nations, or in their stories, ﴿is a sign﴾, a lesson ﴿for whoever fears the punishment of the Hereafter﴾, for it is he who takes heed from it, since one reasons from the severe punishment that befell them because of the evil deeds they committed to the states of the punishment of the Hereafter.

As for him who denies the Hereafter and deems the annihilation of the world impossible, and claims that neither it nor any of its states is attributable to a chooser who acts by will, and that whatever events occur in it happen only through causes that necessitate them, from celestial configurations that coincide at certain times, and not because of the sins mentioned that the destroyed nations committed, he is far removed from this lesson. Perdition to them and to the ideas they hold!

﴿That﴾ is a reference to the Day of Resurrection, indicated by the mention of the Hereafter. ﴿It is a Day for which mankind will be gathered﴾, i.e., mankind will be gathered for it, for reckoning and recompense. The shift to the passive form serves to indicate the constancy of the meaning of gathering, the certainty of its occurrence without doubt, and that people cannot be separated from it. It is more emphatic than the saying of God, Exalted: ﴿the Day He gathers you for the Day of Assembly﴾.

﴿And that﴾, i.e., the Day of Resurrection, while noting the title of the gathering of mankind for it, ﴿is a Day witnessed﴾, i.e., witnessed in it, for the inhabitants of the heavens and the earths witness in it. The attribution was extended by treating the verb as though it were the object, as in the line of verse:

*In an assembly of the foreheads of people, witnessed*

That is, many witness it. Had the day itself been made the thing witnessed, the purpose of exalting and magnifying the day and distinguishing it from others would be lost, for all other days are likewise.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 104:

﴿And We do not delay it﴾ i.e., that Day, which is regarded under the two aspects of gathering and witnessing, ﴿except for a term already counted﴾ — except for the expiry of a fixed, limited period, determined as wisdom requires.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 105:**

﴿On the day it comes﴾ means: when that delayed day comes, at the completion of its appointed term, as in His saying, exalted is He: "that the Hour should come upon them." It was also said: "the day on which the recompense that takes place in it comes." It was also said: the subject is God, exalted and majestic is He, since the context is one of magnifying the matter of the day. A reading retains the yā' in its original form (*bi-ithbāt al-yā' 'alā al-aṣl*). ﴿No soul shall speak﴾ means: no soul shall speak with anything that benefits or saves it, whether an answer or an intercession. The governing element of the adverbial phrase (*al-ẓarf*) is either the implied verb of termination (*al-intihā'*) in His saying: ﴿except for a term appointed﴾, meaning the term ends on the day it comes, or the understood implied verb known from context, namely "remember" (*udhkur*). ﴿Except by His permission﴾, exalted is His authority, refers to speech, as in His saying: ﴿They shall not speak except one whom the Most Merciful has permitted﴾. This applies to one of the stations of that day. His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿This is a day when they will not speak﴾ and ﴿nor will they be permitted to offer excuses﴾ refers to another station of its stations, just as His saying, glorified is He: ﴿on the day every soul comes pleading for itself﴾ refers to another of them. Or what is permitted is the true answers, and what is forbidden is the false excuses. Indeed, permission may also be given for them in order to make their falsehood manifest, as in the saying of the disbelievers: ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ and its like.

﴿Among them is the wretched﴾, for whom the Fire has become due by the requirement of the threat, ﴿and the blessed﴾, i.e., and among them is the blessed. The predicate has been omitted because the first part indicates it. It refers to the one for whom Paradise has become due by the requirement of the promise. The pronoun refers to the people of the station, which is indicated by His saying: ﴿no soul shall speak﴾, or to mankind. The wretched is placed before the blessed because the context is one of warning and admonition.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 106:

﴿As for those who are wretched﴾ i.e., wretchedness has preceded for them, ﴿they will be in the Fire﴾ i.e., they will abide therein, ﴿for them therein will be groaning (zafir) and wailing (shahiq)﴾. The zafir is the expelling of breath, and the shahiq is its drawing back. Both are used for the beginning and the end of the braying (nahiq) of a donkey. Al-Shammakh says, describing a wild ass:

Far from the melody, the first of its voice is a zafir, and following it is a shahiq, hoarse.

What is meant by them is a description of the intensity of their distress, and a comparison of their state to that of one whose heart is overcome by heat and whose spirit is confined within it; or a comparison of their screaming to the voices of donkeys. It is also read (shuqu) with a damma, and the clause is then resumed (mustanafa), as if a questioner had said: "What is their condition therein?" and it was answered: "For them therein is such and such." Or it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the Fire, or to the pronoun in the prepositional phrase, like the saying of His, exalted is His name:

**Qur'an 11:107:** ﴿abiding therein﴾ with an exception: if what is meant is the occurrence of their being in the Fire, then the state is one of future becoming (*ḥāl muqaddara*). ﴿As long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾, that is, for the duration of their continuance. This time-limitation is an expression of perpetuity (*ta'bīd*) and the negation of cessation, in accordance with the method (*minhāj*) of the Arabs' speech: *mā dāma Tu'ār*, *mā aqāma Thabīr*, *mā lāḥa kawkabun*, *mā ikhtalafa al-layl wa'l-nahār*, *mā ṭamā al-baḥr*, and other expressions of perpetuity. It does not make their abiding in the Fire contingent upon the continuance of these heavens and this earth, since the decisive texts indicate the perpetuity of their abiding therein and the cessation of the continuance of these two. If, however, a contingency is intended, then what is meant is the heavens and earth of the Hereafter, as the texts indicate, such as His saying: ﴿The Day the earth will be changed to other than the earth, and the heavens﴾ (14:48), and His saying: ﴿And He has caused us to inherit the land, to dwell in Paradise wherever we will﴾ (39:74). Everyone is certain that the people of the Hereafter (p-242) must have a canopy and a foundation that endure, so the contingency of their abiding therein on their enduring suffices, and there is no need to investigate the details of their states and modes.

**﴿Except what your Lord wills﴾:** an exception from the eternity (*khulūd*), in the manner of His saying: ﴿They will not taste death therein, except the first death﴾ (44:56), and His saying: ﴿And do not marry those whom your fathers married, except what has already passed﴾ (4:22), and His saying: ﴿until the camel passes through the eye of the needle﴾ (7:40). However, the impossibility of the aforementioned matters is known by the judgment of reason, and the impossibility of the will's being attached to the non-eternity is known by the judgment of transmitted texts. The meaning is that they are fixed in the Fire at all times except during the time of God's will, for their non-abiding therein. Since neither that will nor its time is possible, by the judgment of the decisive texts that necessitate eternity, there is no possibility of the end of the period of their abiding therein. And to repel what might be imagined, namely that the impossibility of God's will being attached to the non-eternity is a necessity upon God, He said: ﴿Indeed your Lord is the Effecter of what He intends﴾. The meaning is that in the eternal punishment of the wretched in the Fire, such that the opposite of it is impossible to occur, He is the Effecter according to the requirement of His will, the Decider according to the demand of His will which proceeds upon the ways of His wisdom, which calls for the arrangement of recompenses upon the deeds of the servants. The shift from the pronoun to the explicit noun is to cultivate awe and to increase the affirmation.

It has also been said that this is an exception from eternity in the punishment of the Fire, for they are not eternally punished therein, but rather they are punished with *al-zamharīr* (extreme cold) and with other kinds of punishment, and with what is more severe than all of them, namely God's wrath upon them, His rejection of them, and His humiliating them.

**And you know** that we, even if we concede that what is meant by "the Fire" is not the whole abode of punishment comprising all kinds of torment, but the Fire itself, nonetheless: what is free of the punishment of *al-zamharīr* among those kinds accompanies the punishment of the Fire, so there is no instance of the exception in that. And you may say: they are not eternally in the physical punishment which is the punishment of the Fire, but for them there are, of the varieties of punishment, what none knows except God, the Glorified. These are the spiritual punishments and pains, which those immersed in the judgments of nature in this lowly life do not comprehend, whose perception is confined to the physical conditions to which they are accustomed, and who have no readiness to receive what lies beyond that of the spiritual conditions when it is communicated to them. For this reason its explanation was not addressed, and it was sufficient to rely upon this general rank which indicates terror. And these punishments, although they befall them while they are in the Fire, yet through them they forget the punishment of the Fire and do not feel it. This rank is sufficient to realize the meaning of this exception.

It has been said that *illā* (except) means *siwā* (other than), and this is more fitting to what has been mentioned. It has also been said that *mā* means *man* (those who), taking the sense of description. The meaning would then be: those who are wretched in the Fire, who are destined for eternity therein, except those whom God willed not to be eternal therein, and they are the sinful believers.

And as for those who were made happy, they will be in the Garden, abiding therein for as long as the heavens and the earth endure. The discussion of it is like the discussion of what preceded, except that it is not mentioned here that they have in it joy and delight, as was mentioned regarding the people of the Fire, that they have in it groaning and wailing, because the context is one of warning and admonition. ﴿Except what your Lord wills.﴾ If it is taken in the manner of conditioning on the impossible (ta'liq bil-muhal), then His words, ﴿a gift never cut off﴾, are in the accusative as a verbal noun (maf'ul mutlaq) from the sense of the sentence, because His words, "So in the Garden they will abide therein," imply a giving and a bestowal. It is as if it were said: He gives them a gift. This is either a noun of action (ism masdar), which is the giving, or a verbal noun with its augmenting letters removed, like His words ﴿He brought you forth from the earth as a growing﴾. If it is taken to mean what God has prepared for His righteous servants of spiritual bliss, which is expressed by "what no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has occurred to the heart of any human," then it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the implied object of the willing, or as a specifier (tamyiz). The attribution of the will (of the exception) to God Most High may be in the sense of "a cut-off gift" or in the sense of "a gift not cut off," so it removes the ambiguity regarding the attribution. Ibn Zayd said: God Most High told us what He wills for the people of the Garden, when He said: ﴿a gift never cut off﴾, and He did not tell us what He wills for the people of the Fire. It is permissible that it be connected to both kinds of bliss or to the first only, to avert what might be imagined from the apparent sense of the exception, namely that it is discontinuous (munqati', a disjunctive exception).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 11, verse 109:

﴿So do not be in doubt﴾ means: in uncertainty. The *fa'* (ف) here indicates that the prohibition follows from what has been related of the narratives and what was made clear within them of the worldly and otherworldly consequences. ﴿of what these worship﴾ means: concerning the worship of these polytheists and its evil outcome, or concerning the state of the idols they worship, namely that they do not benefit them. Since the context of the noble composition (*nazm*, the arrangement of the Qur'anic text) just before the narratives begins is to show the extreme evil state of the disbelievers and the perfect good state of the believers, and an example was struck for them, saying: ﴿The likeness of the two groups is like the blind and the deaf, and the seeing and the hearing. Are they equal in likeness? Will you not then take heed?﴾, and after that were related reports of past nations with their messengers sent to them, which whoever takes heed would be warned by, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was forbidden from being in doubt about the fate of the affair of these polytheists, both in the immediate and in the eventual. Then the reason for this was given by way of resumption (*isti'naf*, a new sentence that answers an implied question), saying: ﴿They worship only as their fathers worshipped before﴾, referring to those whose narratives were related to you. ﴿Before﴾ means: they and their fathers are equal in polytheism. They worship no worship except like their worship, or they worship nothing except the like of the idols that they worshipped. The shift to the present tense (*al-mudari'*) is to narrate a past state and to bring its image to mind. Alternatively, the sense is "like what they used to worship," so *kana* (كان) is elided, the phrase ﴿before﴾ indicating it. And indeed, what befell their fathers has reached you, so something similar will befall them, for the similarity of causes requires the similarity of effects. ﴿And indeed We will pay them﴾, meaning these disbelievers, ﴿their portion﴾, meaning their specified share determined for them according to their crimes and misdeeds, of punishment in the immediate and the eventual, just as We paid their fathers their allotted portions. Or it means the provision apportioned to them, so this would explain why the punishment is delayed from them despite the certainty of what necessitates it. ﴿undiminished﴾ is an emphatic circumstantial phrase (*hal mu'akkadah*) modifying "portion," like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then you turned back, retreating﴾ (9:25). Its benefit is to repel the suspicion of metaphorical usage. Making it a restrictive qualifier (*muqayyidah*) to repel the possibility that the portion is diminished in itself is based on overlooking that the governing element is the paying. So reflect.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 110:

﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book﴾, i.e., the Torah, ﴿but differences arose concerning it﴾, i.e., concerning its status and whether it was from Allah the Exalted: some believed in it and others disbelieved in it. So do not be concerned about the disagreement of your people concerning what We have given you of the Qur'an, nor about their saying, "Why has a treasure not been sent down to him, or an angel not come with him?" and their claim that you have fabricated it. ﴿And had it not been for a word that had preceded (p-244) from your Lord﴾, which is the word of decree to respite them until the Day of Resurrection, in accordance with the wisdom that calls for that, ﴿the matter would have been decided between them﴾, i.e., the judgment would have been carried out between the disputing ones among your people by sending down the punishment that the falsifiers deserve, so that they would be distinguished thereby from the truthful. It has also been said: between the people of Moses, but this is not the intended meaning. ﴿And indeed they﴾, i.e., and indeed the disbelievers among your people, the pronoun referring to some of those who returned to them (the antecedent being "between them," the pronoun being used because there is no risk of confusion), ﴿are in grave doubt﴾ ﴿concerning it﴾, i.e., concerning the Qur'an, even though it has not been mentioned explicitly; for the mention of the giving of the Book of Moses and the occurrence of disagreement concerning it, especially in the context of consolation, loudly proclaims this without being hidden, ﴿disquieting﴾, i.e., causing unease and suspicion.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 111:

﴿And indeed, all﴾ The tanwin (nunation) here is a substitute (ʿiwad) for the genitive noun that was omitted after it; that is: and indeed all of those who differ concerning it, both the believers among them and the disbelievers. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', and Abu Bakr read it with the lightened (takhfif) form together with its operative function (i'mal), considering the original form (i'tibaran li-l-asl). ﴿Surely, your Lord will fully repay them for their deeds﴾ That is: the recompense of their deeds. The first lam is a preface to the oath (muwatti’a li-l-qasam), and the second is the answer to the omitted oath. Lamma (لَمّا) is composed of the preposition la (لَ) and the relative or qualifying ma (ما), and its original form was lamin, whereupon the nun was changed into a mim for assimilation, so three mims came together, and the first of them was deleted. The meaning is: "by Him in whom" or "by a creature who" or "by a group who"; by Allah, your Lord will surely repay them. It has also been read as (lamā) with the lightened form, where ma is an extra particle inserted to separate the two lams, and the meaning is: and indeed all of them, by Allah, (surely He will repay them), and so on. It has also been read as (lammān) with tanwin, meaning "all together," as in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and you devour the heritage, devouring all together﴾. Ubayy read: (wa-in kullun lamma la-yuwaffiyannahum), where "in" is a negation and "lamma" means "illa" (except); this has also been read so.

﴿Indeed, He is Acquainted with what they do﴾ That is: with what each individual of those who differ does, of good and evil, ﴿Aware﴾ in such a way that nothing of its great or minute details is hidden from Him. This is a reason for what preceded concerning the full payment of the recompense of their deeds, for comprehending the details of the deeds of both groups, and what each deed merits by the requirement of wisdom of the specific recompense, necessitates giving every entitled one his due: if good, then good; and if evil, then evil.

﴿So be steadfast as you have been commanded﴾. When it had been made clear, within the narratives recounted about past nations, how evil the end of disbelief and disobedience toward the messengers is, and it had been indicated that the state of these disbelievers in unbelief, error, and deserving punishment is like that of those who were punished, that their share of punishment will reach them without any reduction, that their denial of the Qur'an is like the denial of the people of Moses, peace be upon him, toward the Torah, and that, had the decree not preceded to postpone their general punishment and their complete reckoning until the Day of Resurrection, they would have been dealt with as their forefathers were dealt with before them, and that they will be paid their share in full, and that each one of the believers and the disbelievers will be repaid for his deeds, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was commanded to be steadfast, as he was commanded in the beliefs and actions shared between him and the rest of the believers, and especially the actions specific to him, peace be upon him: conveying the legal rulings, carrying out the duties of prophethood, and bearing the burdens of the message, such that included in it is what he was commanded in the previous words of the Exalted: "So perhaps you will leave out some of what is revealed to you, and your breast will be constricted by it" ... the verse. In sum, this command encompasses all the excellent qualities of the fundamental and subsidiary rulings and the theoretical and practical perfections, and discharging its obligation is extremely difficult. For this reason the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Hud has made me grey."

﴿And those who have turned in repentance with you﴾: that is, those who repented from polytheism and disbelief and joined you in faith, and it is these who are meant by "with you." It is conjoined to the pronoun concealed in "So be steadfast" (fastaqim), and it was permissible without emphasis because of the intervening element that stands in its place. In reality, this is the conjoining of a sentence to a sentence, since the meaning is: "And let those who have repented with you be steadfast." It has also been said that it is in the accusative as an object of accompaniment (maf'ul ma'ahu), as Abu al-Baqa said, and the meaning is: "Be steadfast, accompanied by those who have repented with you."

﴿And do not transgress﴾: do not deviate from what has been set as limits for you, by excess or by deficiency, for both extremes of the course of affairs are blameworthy. Transgression (tughyan), which is going beyond the limit, has been so named as an intensification, or as a predominance of the condition of the rest of the believers over his condition, peace be upon him.

﴿Indeed, He is Seeing of what you do﴾: He will therefore recompense you for it. This is a reason given for the command and the prohibition. The verse indicates the obligation to follow what is explicitly stated without deviation by mere opinion, for that is transgression and error. As for acting in accordance with ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning, exertion to derive rulings) that follows the underlying causes (ʿilal) of the texts, that falls under steadfastness, just as one is commanded to do so according to the requirements of the texts that enjoin ijtihad.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 113:

﴿And do not incline﴾ — that is, do not incline even the slightest inclination — ﴿toward those who have wronged﴾ — that is, toward those among whom wrongdoing has been found in general. The basis of the prohibition is wrongdoing, and the plural is in accordance with the plurality of those addressed. As for what has been said, that this is for emphasis in the prohibition, insofar as being a group is a likely reason for leniency in flattering them, this would only hold if the intended meaning were the prohibition of inclining toward them as a group, and that is not the case.

﴿Then the Fire will touch you﴾ — because of that. If the state of merely inclining, in general, toward one in whom some wrongdoing has been found leads to the touch of the Fire in this way, then what is your opinion of one who inclines greatly toward those who are firmly rooted in wrongdoing and transgression, who throws himself eagerly into their company and their drinking-companionship, who casts his whole self upon their friendship and fellowship, who rejoices in imitating their outward appearance, who fixes his eyes upon their fleeting splendour, and who envies them for what they have been given of near-hanging fruits?! And he, in truth, is as slight as a grain and as light as a gnat's wing, far from whose inclination hearts would turn, the seeker and the sought both being weak.

The verse is the most eloquent that can be conceived in prohibiting wrongdoing and warning against it. Its address to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and those with him among the believers is for steadfastness in uprightness, which is justice, for inclining toward either extreme of excess or deficiency is a wrong to oneself or to others. It has been read as ﴿Turkanu﴾ according to the dialect of Tamim, and as ﴿Turkanu﴾ in the passive form from arkanahu.

﴿And you have no protectors besides God﴾ — that is, no helpers who would rescue you from the Fire. The clause is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from his saying "then the Fire will touch you." The negation of protectors is not by way of negating that each one of them has protectors, such that it would be true that he has a protector; rather, it is by way of the distribution of the singular over the singulars, due to the position of (lakum). Yet it is not in the sense of negating that each of them independently possesses a helper, but in the sense of negating that any one of them has a helper, by the indication of the context.

﴿Then you will not be helped﴾ — from the side of God, glory be to Him; since it has already preceded in His judgment that He would punish you for your inclining toward them, and not spare you. The "then" (thumma) is for the remoteness of the rank of their not being helped by God after He had threatened them with punishment and made it obligatory upon them. It is also permissible that it be treated as occupying the place of "fa" (so), in the sense of remote improbability, for when it was made clear that God the Exalted punishes them and that other than Him does not rescue them, it was concluded that they are not helped at all.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 114:

﴿And establish the prayer at the two ends of the day﴾, that is, at morning and evening. Its being in the accusative as an adverb of time is because it is annexed to a time-word. ﴿And at the approaches of the night﴾, that is, hours of it close to the day, for it derives from azlafahu, "he brought it near," and is the plural of zulfah. It is conjoined to "the two ends of the day." What is meant by praying at these two is the prayer of the dawn (al-ghadah) and the afternoon ('asr). It has been said that it is the noon prayer (zuhr) in place of the afternoon prayer ('asr), since what follows the decline of the sun is evening (ʿashiyy). By the prayer at the approaches is meant the sunset prayer (maghrib) and the night prayer ('isha'). It is also read zulufan with two dammas, and with a damma and a sukun, like busr and busur, and zulfa in the sense of zulfah, like qurba in the sense of qurbah.

﴿Indeed, good deeds﴾, among which, indeed, the chief of them, are what you have been commanded of the prayers, ﴿remove bad deeds﴾, which humankind rarely is free from, that is, they expiate them. In a hadith: "Prayer from one prayer to the next is an expiation for what lies between them, so long as major sins are avoided." It has also been said that it was revealed concerning Abu al-Yasar al-Ansari when he kissed a woman and then regretted it, so he came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and informed him of what he had done. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I will wait for the command of my Lord." When he had prayed the afternoon prayer, it was revealed. He (ﷺ) said: "Yes, go, for it is an expiation for what you have done." Or they prevent one from committing them, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, prayer forbids indecency and wrongdoing﴾.

﴿That﴾ refers to His saying, exalted is He, "So be steadfast," and what follows it. It has also been said that it refers to the Qur'an. ﴿A reminder for those who remember﴾, that is, an admonition for those who take heed.

﴿And be patient﴾ over the hardships of what you have been commanded in the course of the preceding commands. As for what he was forbidden from, namely transgression and inclining toward those who did wrong, there is no hardship in refraining from it, so there is no basis for generalizing patience to it. Except that it may be meant as that which humans cannot ordinarily be free of: the slightest inclination, by the dictate of nature, away from the uprightness that is commanded, and a slight inclination, by the dictate of human nature, toward whoever has committed some wrong. For guarding against the like of these involves a hardship that is not hidden. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not waste the reward of the good-doers﴾, meaning: He pays them the wages of their deeds without any diminution at all. This is expressed by the negation of waste, although not giving the reward is not truly waste, how could it be, since deeds do not necessitate reward such that their failure to be rewarded would entail their being wasted, in order to show the perfection of His exaltedness above that, by portraying it in the form of what is impossible for Him, glorified be He, to do of ugly things, and by presenting reward in the guise of matters incumbent upon Him. The pronoun was deliberately avoided so that it would serve as evidence for the intended meaning while conveying a general benefit for everyone who possesses this attribute. This is a justification for the command to be patient, and it implies that patience in what has been mentioned is a form of ihsan (excellence).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 116:

﴿Then why were there not﴾ (fa-hallā kāna): why was there not (fa-hallā kāna) ﴿among the generations﴾ (min al-qurūn) that existed ﴿before you﴾ (min qablikum), according to the opinion of those who permit omitting the relative pronoun together with part of its relative clause; or [the phrase may be read as] "existing before you" (kā'inatan min qablikum), ﴿people of remainder﴾ (ulū baqiyyatin), of judgment and intellect; or people of virtue and goodness. They were so named because a man naturally retains from what he produces customarily its finest and best part, so it became a proverbial expression for excellence and virtue. It is said: "So-and-so is of the remainder of the people," meaning, of their choicest. From this is the saying: "In corners are hidden treasures, and among men are remnants" (fi al-zawāyā khabāyā wa fi al-rijāl baqāyā).

It is also possible that al-baqiyyah has the meaning of al-baqwā, like al-taqiyyah from al-taqwā, meaning: why were there not among them people of self-preservation, guarding themselves from the wrath of God Most High and His punishment? This is supported by the reading "ulū biqyatin" (with a kasrah on the ba' and without the yā' after the qāf... in the form of a single occurrence), which is the single-instance noun (al-marrah) from the verbal noun of baqqāhu, yubaqqīhi, meaning: he watched over him and awaited him; that is, people of watchfulness and fear of the punishment of God Most High, as though they were waiting for its descent out of their apprehension.

﴿who forbade corruption in the land﴾ (yanhawna 'an al-fasād fi al-arḍ), the corruption that occurred among them as related about them, ﴿except a few of those whom We rescued from among them﴾ (illā qalīlan mimman anjaynā minhum). This is an exceptive clause of disconnection (istithnā' munqaṭi'), meaning: but a few of them whom We rescued, because they were of that quality. The "min" here is explanatory (li al-bayān), not partitive (li al-tab'īd), because all those rescued are forbidders; and there is no soundness in connecting it to the apparent sense of the speech, because that would make it an exhortation (taḥḍīḍ) to the people of remainder to forbid the aforementioned, except for the few of the rescued among them, as when you say: "Why did your people not recite the Qur'an, except the righteous among them," intending to exclude the righteous from those urged to recite. Yes, that is correct if it is taken as an exception from the necessary negation implied by the exhortation, so that it is as if it were said: "There were not, among the generations, people of remainder, except a few of them." However, the nominative (raf') is then the more eloquent, as a substitution (badaliyyah).

﴿And those who did wrong followed﴾ (wa-ittaba'a alladhīna ẓalamū), by directly engaging in corruption and abandoning its prohibition, ﴿what they were made to enjoy therein﴾ (mā ut'rifū fīhi), that is, they were granted luxuries from desires and were preoccupied with attaining them. As for the direct perpetrators, it is evident; and as for the lax, it is because they gain their corrupt portions thereby. It is also said that what is meant by them is those who abandoned the prohibition, and you know that this entails that the direct perpetrators of corruption are not included in the sense of "wrongdoing" and "criminality" by expression. ﴿And they were criminals﴾ (wa-kānū mujrimīn), that is, disbelievers. So this is an explanation of the cause of the destruction of the annihilated nations, namely the spread of wrongdoing and following of caprice among them, and the prevalence of abandoning the forbidding of evil alongside disbelief. The phrase "wa-ittaba'a" is coordinated with an implied element indicated by the speech, that is: "they did not forbid, and [they] followed..." etc. Thus the shift to the explicit noun serves to include the direct perpetrators with them in the ruling and in the attribution of wrongdoing to them, and to indicate that this is the reason for what befell them of punishment. Or it is taken as a resumptive statement (isti'nāf) that follows from the phrase "except a few," meaning: "except a few of those whom We rescued from among them, who forbade corruption, and those who did wrong followed" — those who directly perpetrated corruption and those who abandoned its prohibition — so the explicit noun is the requirement of the apparent sense.

And His saying "wa-kānū mujrimīn" is coordinated with "ut'rifū" (were made to enjoy), that is, they followed luxury, and their being criminals is because one who follows desires is immersed in sins; or criminality is meant as their neglect of gratitude. Or it is coordinated with "ittaba'a," that is, they followed their desires, and by that following they were criminals. It is also permissible for it to be a parenthetical clause (i'tirāḍ) and a condemnation of them as a criminal people. It is also read "wa-ut'biʿa" (and they were made to follow), that is, they were made to follow the requital of what they were made to enjoy, so the "wa" is for circumstance (li al-ḥāl). The famous reading may be interpreted in this way, and the preceding mention of the rescue supports it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 117:

﴿And your Lord would never destroy the towns﴾. That is: it is not valid or proper; rather, it is impossible in wisdom that He should destroy the towns that He destroyed, as far as what has reached you of their accounts, and from this the condition of the rest of the wrongdoing towns is known. The lam is for emphasizing the negation. His saying ﴿with wrongdoing﴾ means: while associated with it. It has been said that it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the agent, meaning: wronging them. The indefiniteness (of ﴿wrongdoing﴾) is for magnification and to signal that destroying the reformers is a great wrong. The purpose is to declare God exalted above that entirely, by depicting it in the form of what cannot proceed from Him, exalted is He. Otherwise there is no injustice in what God does to His servants, whatever it may be, according to the established principle of the Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah, the orthodox Sunni school). Its detailed explanation has passed in surah Al 'Imran at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And that Allah is not unjust to the servants﴾.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿while its people are reformers﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the object, and its governing element is the same governing element (of the earlier hal), but not by way of its being restricted by what occurred as a hal from its agent, namely (﴿with wrongdoing﴾), because that would indicate that the negation of destruction as wrongdoing is restricted to the condition of its people being reformers. There is no doubt about its corruption; rather (it is) absolute, free of that. It has been said: the intended meaning of the wrongdoing is polytheism (shirk), and the ba' is causal, meaning: He does not destroy the towns because of the polytheism of their people while they are reformers who practice justice among themselves and do not add to their polytheism another corruption. That is due to the abundance of His mercy and His leniency regarding His own rights. For this reason the jurists, when rights conflict, gave precedence to the rights of the poor servants over the rights of God, the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy.

It has also been said: sovereignty remains with polytheism but does not remain with wrongdoing. You know that the context of forbidding the reprehensible acts, the most abominable of which is associating partners with God, does not suit this, since polytheism is included in corruption on earth in the first place. For this reason each of the Messengers whose accounts are related began by forbidding his community from polytheism, then from (p-248) the rest of the sins they were engaged in. Therefore the correct reading is to take wrongdoing as general corruption, encompassing polytheism and other kinds of sins, and to take reform as their reforming it and desisting from it, by some of them being those who take on the task of forbidding it, and some of them being those who turn to admonition, not persisting in what they are upon of polytheism and other kinds of corruption.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 118:

﴿And if your Lord had willed, He would have made mankind one community﴾, united upon the truth and the religion of Islam, such that scarcely anyone would differ concerning it. But He did not will that, so they were not agreed upon the truth. ﴿And they will not cease to be differing﴾ concerning the truth, i.e., opposing it, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And none differed concerning it except those who were given it, after clear proofs had come to them, out of rebellion among themselves﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 11, verse 119:

﴿Except those upon whom your Lord has mercy﴾ — (They are) a people whom Allah, exalted is He, has guided by His grace to the truth, so they agreed upon it and did not differ concerning it; that is, they did not oppose it. Taking it to mean absolute difference, encompassing what proceeds from the one who is right and the one who is wrong, is rejected by the aforementioned exception. ﴿And for that He created them﴾ — that is, for the difference mentioned; the ones who remain after the exception, namely those who differ. The lam here indicates outcome (al-'aqibah) or purpose of mercy (al-tarahhum).
